Immutable Infrastructure — Why You Never SSH Into a Server

The concept of immutable infrastructure is fundamental to cloud native platform engineering: once a resource is created, it is NEVER modified. If you need to change something, you create a NEW resource and replace the old one. This eliminates configuration drift and "snowflake servers":

❌ Mutable Infrastructure (Traditional)

"SSH into the server, update the package, edit the config file, restart the service."

  • Server-1: patched last Tuesday
  • Server-2: patched 3 months ago (oops)
  • Server-3: "Bob manually fixed something at 3 AM"
  • Result: 3 servers, 3 different states. Chaos.
✅ Immutable Infrastructure (Cloud Native)

"Build a new container image with the updated package. Deploy it. The old container is destroyed. Never modify a running container."

  • Every anihpj pod is identical — built from the same image
  • No "drift" — a pod is replaced, never modified
  • Rollback = deploy the previous image version
  • Result: Every instance is identical. Predictable.

💡 CNPA Principle: Immutable infrastructure + declarative management + GitOps = the foundation of platform engineering. These three concepts together eliminate the "snowflake server" problem forever.

4.3 Containers vs Virtual Machines — Understanding the Difference

Containers and VMs are both isolation technologies, but they work at different layers of the stack. The CNPA exam expects you to understand the architectural differences and when to use each:

CONTAINERS vs VIRTUAL MACHINES — Architectural Comparison
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  VIRTUAL MACHINES                     CONTAINERS                │
  │  ┌────────────────────────┐          ┌────────────────────────┐│
  │  │  App A    │  App B     │          │  App A    │  App B     ││
  │  │  ┌────────┴────────┐   │          │  ┌────────┴────────┐   ││
  │  │  │  Bins/Libs      │   │          │  │  Bins/Libs      │   ││
  │  │  ├─────────────────┤   │          │  └────────┬────────┘   ││
  │  │  │  Guest OS       │   │          │           │            ││
  │  │  │  (Full kernel)  │   │          │  ┌────────┴────────┐   ││
  │  │  ├─────────────────┤   │          │  │ Container Engine│   ││
  │  │  │  Hypervisor     │   │          │  │ (containerd)    │   ││
  │  │  ├─────────────────┤   │          │  ├─────────────────┤   ││
  │  │  │  Host OS Kernel │   │          │  │ Host OS Kernel  │   ││
  │  │  ├─────────────────┤   │          │  ├─────────────────┤   ││
  │  │  │  Hardware       │   │          │  │ Hardware        │   ││
  │  │  └─────────────────┘   │          │  └─────────────────┘   ││
  │  │                        │          │                         ││
  │  │  Size: GBs             │          │  Size: MBs              ││
  │  │  Startup: Minutes      │          │  Startup: Seconds       ││
  │  │  Isolation: Full OS    │          │  Isolation: Process +   ││
  │  │             kernel     │          │    Namespace + Cgroups  ││
  │  │  Density: 10s/host     │          │  Density: 100s/host     ││
  │  │  Portability: OVF/OVA  │          │  Portability: OCI Image ││
  │  └────────────────────────┘          └────────────────────────┘│
  │                                                                 │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

When to Use Containers vs VMs — Decision Guide

ScenarioContainersVMsWhy
Microservices / cloud native apps✅ YESOverkillContainers are designed for this — fast, portable, orchestratable
Strong multi-tenant isolationPossible but complex✅ YESVMs provide hardware-level isolation. Containers share a kernel.
Legacy monolithic appsPossible with adaptation✅ EASIERVMs match the original deployment model. Containerizing monoliths is complex.
Different OS kernels needed❌ NO✅ YESContainers share the host kernel. Windows + Linux on same host = VMs.
CI/CD build agents✅ YESOverkillContainers spin up in seconds. Perfect for ephemeral CI runners.
Untrusted workloads (user code)Risky✅ SAFERContainer escape is possible. VMs provide stronger boundaries.

💡 CNPA Focus: The CNPA world is primarily container-based (Kubernetes). But you should understand VMs for hybrid scenarios — especially when running K8s control plane components or stateful workloads that require strong isolation.

How Containers Actually Work — Linux Namespaces and cgroups

A container is NOT a "mini VM." It's a Linux process with boundaries enforced by two kernel features. Understanding this helps you debug container issues and design better platforms:

📦
Linux Namespaces — What a Container CAN See

Namespaces limit what a process can SEE:
• PID namespace: Container sees only its own processes (PID 1 = container's main process)
• NET namespace: Container has its own network interfaces, routing table
• MNT namespace: Container has its own filesystem mount points
• UTS namespace: Container has its own hostname
• IPC namespace: Container has isolated inter-process communication
• USER namespace: Container can have different UIDs than the host (root in container ≠ root on host)

⚖️
cgroups — What a Container CAN Use

Control Groups (cgroups) limit what a process can USE:
• CPU cgroup: cpu.shares (requests), cfs_quota_us/cfs_period_us (limits)
• Memory cgroup: memory.limit_in_bytes — when exceeded → OOMKilled
• Block I/O cgroup: limits disk read/write bandwidth
• Network cgroup: (managed by CNI, not cgroups directly)
• PIDs cgroup: limits number of processes per container

Key insight: When you set resources: {requests: {cpu: "250m"}, limits: {memory: "512Mi"}} — you're configuring CGROUPS. The kubelet writes these values to the cgroup filesystem.

💡 CNPA Debugging: If a container can't see another process → check PID namespace. If a container can't reach another pod → check NET namespace (NetworkPolicy). If a container is killed → check cgroup memory limit (OOMKilled). The kernel features map 1:1 to the symptoms.

4.4 Kubernetes as the Universal Control Plane — One API, Any Cloud

Kubernetes abstracts the underlying infrastructure behind a single, consistent API. Whether your cluster runs on AWS, GCP, Azure, or bare metal — kubectl apply -f deployment.yaml works the same. This is WHY platform engineering uses Kubernetes: it's the universal abstraction layer.

📖 Universal Control Plane Defined

Kubernetes as a universal control plane means using the K8s API not just for container orchestration, but for managing ALL infrastructure — compute (nodes, clusters), networking (services, ingress), storage (PVCs), security (RBAC, policies), and even cloud resources (via Crossplane). Everything is a K8s resource. Everything is managed declaratively. Everything is in Git.

How K8s Masks Cloud Differences — Crossplane in Action

KUBERNETES AS UNIVERSAL CONTROL PLANE — One API, Multiple Clouds
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  YOU WRITE (once):                                              │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ apiVersion: database.anihpj.io/v1                         │ │
  │  │ kind: PostgreSQL                                           │ │
  │  │ metadata:                                                  │ │
  │  │   name: anihpj-db                                          │ │
  │  │ spec:                                                      │ │
  │  │   version: "15.4"                                          │ │
  │  │   storage: 20Gi                                            │ │
  │  │   ha: true                                                 │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  THE SAME K8s MANIFEST WORKS ON ANY CLOUD:                      │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐         │
  │  │     AWS      │  │     GCP      │  │    Azure     │         │
  │  │              │  │              │  │              │         │
  │  │ Provisions:  │  │ Provisions:  │  │ Provisions:  │         │
  │  │ AWS RDS      │  │ Cloud SQL    │  │ Azure DB     │         │
  │  │ (PostgreSQL) │  │ (PostgreSQL) │  │ (PostgreSQL) │         │
  │  │              │  │              │  │              │         │
  │  │ Crossplane   │  │ Crossplane   │  │ Crossplane   │         │
  │  │ AWS Provider │  │ GCP Provider │  │ Azure Prov.  │         │
  │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘         │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 This is the power of the universal control plane:           │
  │     • Developers write the SAME YAML everywhere                 │
  │     • Platform team configures providers per cloud              │
  │     • Cloud-agnostic by default, cloud-specific when needed     │
  │     • Switching clouds = changing provider config, not app code │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
💡 The Platform Engineer's Role in the Universal Control Plane

As a CNPA, YOU configure the Crossplane providers and define the Compositions (XRD) that developers use. You write the "PostgreSQL" CRD once. Developers use it anywhere. When the org switches from AWS to GCP, YOU update the Composition — developers never notice. The universal control plane is YOUR abstraction layer.

How the K8s API Server Processes a Request — The Full Auth Chain

Every kubectl command goes through a 3-stage pipeline inside the API server. Understanding this chain is critical for debugging "why can't I create this resource?" issues and for designing platform security:

K8s API SERVER REQUEST FLOW — AuthN → AuthZ → Admission
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  $ kubectl apply -f anihpj-deployment.yaml                      │
  │       │                                                         │
  │  ┌────▼────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  STAGE 1: AUTHENTICATION (AuthN) — "WHO are you?"       │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │   │
  │  │  │ • X.509 client certificate (from kubeconfig)      │  │   │
  │  │  │ • Bearer token (ServiceAccount token)            │  │   │
  │  │  │ • OIDC (OpenID Connect) token                    │  │   │
  │  │  │ • Webhook token authentication                   │  │   │
  │  │  │                                                   │  │   │
  │  │  │ Result: User "alice@anihpj.io" OR "system:        │  │   │
  │  │  │         serviceaccount:anihpj-prod:anihpj-api"    │  │   │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │   │
  │  └────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                           │                                    │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  STAGE 2: AUTHORIZATION (AuthZ) — "WHAT can you do?"    │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │   │
  │  │  │ • RBAC (Role-Based Access Control)               │  │   │
  │  │  │   Role: "anihpj-api-deployer"                     │  │   │
  │  │  │   Rules:                                           │  │   │
  │  │  │   - apiGroups: ["apps"]                            │  │   │
  │  │  │   - resources: ["deployments"]                    │  │   │
  │  │  │   - verbs: ["get", "list", "create", "update"]   │  │   │
  │  │  │                                                   │  │   │
  │  │  │ • Node Authorization (kubelet permissions)        │  │   │
  │  │  │ • Webhook authorization (external policy engine)  │  │   │
  │  │  │                                                   │  │   │
  │  │  │ Result: ALLOW (alice can create Deployments)      │  │   │
  │  │  │   OR: DENY (bob cannot create Deployments)        │  │   │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │   │
  │  └────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                           │ ALLOW                              │
  │  ┌────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐   │
  │  │  STAGE 3: ADMISSION CONTROL — "Is this VALID?"         │   │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │   │
  │  │  │ MUTATING Webhooks (run FIRST, can CHANGE object): │  │   │
  │  │  │ • Inject sidecars (Istio, Linkerd)               │  │   │
  │  │  │ • Add default resource limits (LimitRange)       │  │   │
  │  │  │ • Add labels/annotations                         │  │   │
  │  │  │                                                   │  │   │
  │  │  │ VALIDATING Webhooks (run SECOND, can only DENY):  │  │   │
  │  │  │ • Kyverno: "All images must be signed"           │  │   │
  │  │  │ • Kyverno: "All pods must have resource limits"  │  │   │
  │  │  │ • OPA/Gatekeeper: custom Rego policies           │  │   │
  │  │  │                                                   │  │   │
  │  │  │ Result: ALLOW → object written to etcd            │  │   │
  │  │  │   OR: DENY → "admission webhook blocked request"  │  │   │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │   │
  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘   │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 CNPA INSIGHT: When kubectl fails with "forbidden":          │
  │     • 401 Unauthorized → STAGE 1 (AuthN) failure                │
  │     • 403 Forbidden → STAGE 2 (AuthZ/RBAC) failure              │
  │     • "admission webhook denied" → STAGE 3 (Admission) failure │
  │     Knowing WHICH stage failed tells you WHERE to look.         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

4.5 Cluster API (CAPI) — Managing Clusters with Kubernetes

Cluster API is meta-Kubernetes: you use Kubernetes to manage Kubernetes clusters. You define a "Cluster" CRD → the CAPI controller provisions VMs, installs K8s, configures networking → you have a working cluster. This is how platform teams manage infrastructure at scale.

📖 Cluster API Defined

Cluster API (CAPI) is a Kubernetes project that provides declarative APIs for cluster creation, configuration, and management. Instead of manually running kubeadm init or clicking through cloud consoles to create EKS/AKS/GKE clusters, you define a Cluster object in YAML. CAPI controllers reconcile this desired state with actual infrastructure — provisioning VMs, installing Kubernetes, and configuring networking automatically.

CAPI — "The Platform That Builds Platforms"

CLUSTER API — Declarative Cluster Management
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  MANAGEMENT CLUSTER (runs CAPI controllers)                     │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  $ kubectl apply -f anihpj-cluster.yaml                   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1                     │ │
  │  │  kind: Cluster                                            │ │
  │  │  metadata:                                                │ │
  │  │    name: anihpj-prod                                      │ │
  │  │  spec:                                                    │ │
  │  │    clusterNetwork:                                        │ │
  │  │      pods: {cidrBlocks: ["192.168.0.0/16"]}              │ │
  │  │    controlPlaneRef:                                       │ │
  │  │      kind: AWSManagedControlPlane                         │ │
  │  │    infrastructureRef:                                     │ │
  │  │      kind: AWSManagedCluster                              │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  CAPI Controller reads this → provisions in AWS:          │ │
  │  │  • 3 EC2 instances (control plane)                        │ │
  │  │  • 5 EC2 instances (worker nodes)                         │ │
  │  │  • Installs Kubernetes 1.32 on all nodes                  │ │
  │  │  • Configures networking (Calico CNI)                     │ │
  │  │  • Joins workers to control plane                         │ │
  │  │  • Registers cluster in management cluster                │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  RESULT:                                                         │
  │  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐         │
  │  │  anihpj-dev  │  │anihpj-stage  │  │ anihpj-prod  │         │
  │  │  (EKS, 1.32) │  │ (EKS, 1.32)  │  │ (EKS, 1.32)  │         │
  │  │  3 nodes     │  │  5 nodes     │  │  10 nodes    │         │
  │  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘  └──────────────┘         │
  │                                                                 │
  │  All created declaratively. All version-controlled in Git.      │
  │  All managed through the SAME kubectl you already know.         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

CAPI Providers — One API, Multiple Infrastructures

☁️
Infrastructure Providers

CAPI supports all major platforms through providers: AWS (CAPA) for EKS, GCP (CAPG) for GKE, Azure (CAPZ) for AKS, vSphere (CAPV) for on-prem VMware, OpenStack (CAPO), and Docker (CAPD) for local testing. Each provider translates the generic Cluster CRD into cloud-specific API calls.

🔧
Bootstrap Providers

CAPI needs a way to turn VMs into K8s nodes: Kubeadm (CABPK) — the standard bootstrap provider. Generates cloud-init scripts that install containerd, kubelet, kubeadm, and join the node to the cluster. You never run kubeadm manually — the controller does it for you.

Cluster API Cluster Manifest — K8s Managing K8s

Here's the actual CAPI Cluster manifest that provisions an EKS cluster for anihpj production. This YAML replaces clicking through the AWS console:

capi-anihpj-prod-cluster.yaml 
# ─── Cluster: WHAT you want ───
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: Cluster
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod
  namespace: platform
spec:
  clusterNetwork:
    pods:
      cidrBlocks: ["192.168.0.0/16"]
    services:
      cidrBlocks: ["10.96.0.0/12"]
  controlPlaneRef:
    apiVersion: controlplane.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
    kind: KubeadmControlPlane
    name: anihpj-prod-cp
  infrastructureRef:
    apiVersion: infrastructure.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2
    kind: AWSManagedCluster
    name: anihpj-prod-aws

# ─── Control Plane: 3 etcd nodes → tolerates 1 failure ───
---
apiVersion: controlplane.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: KubeadmControlPlane
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod-cp
  namespace: platform
spec:
  replicas: 3
  version: v1.32.0
  machineTemplate:
    infrastructureRef:
      apiVersion: infrastructure.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2
      kind: AWSMachineTemplate
      name: anihpj-prod-cp-mt

# ─── Worker Nodes: MachineDeployment ───
---
apiVersion: cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
kind: MachineDeployment
metadata:
  name: anihpj-prod-workers
  namespace: platform
spec:
  clusterName: anihpj-prod
  replicas: 5
  template:
    spec:
      bootstrap:
        configRef:
          apiVersion: bootstrap.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta1
          kind: KubeadmConfigTemplate
          name: anihpj-prod-bootstrap
      clusterName: anihpj-prod
      infrastructureRef:
        apiVersion: infrastructure.cluster.x-k8s.io/v1beta2
        kind: AWSMachineTemplate
        name: anihpj-prod-worker-mt
      version: v1.32.0

# $ kubectl apply -f capi-anihpj-prod-cluster.yaml
# CAPI provisions: 3 CP + 5 workers on AWS → running EKS!
# Same pattern for GCP, Azure, vSphere — change infrastructureRef.

CAPI vs Managed Kubernetes (EKS/GKE/AKS) — When to Use Which

The CNPA exam expects you to understand when to use Cluster API and when to use a cloud-managed Kubernetes service:

AspectCluster API (CAPI)Managed K8s (EKS/GKE/AKS)
Control planeYou manage it (on your VMs)Cloud provider manages it
UpgradesYou control when and how via GitProvider schedules and executes
Multi-cloud✅ Same API on AWS, GCP, Azure, vSphereDifferent APIs and consoles per cloud
CostYou pay for VMs only (no control plane fee)~$73/month per cluster (EKS) + VMs
Operational burdenHigher — you manage etcd, API server upgradesLower — provider handles etcd backups, API server HA
Best forMulti-cloud strategy, cost optimization, on-prem, full GitOps controlTeams prioritizing operational simplicity, single-cloud
CNPA FocusThe exam covers BOTH. Know that CAPI is the declarative, GitOps-friendly approach. Managed K8s is simpler but less flexible.

4.6 Namespaces, Labels, and Annotations — Organizing Your Platform

Kubernetes provides three metadata systems to organize your platform. The CNPA exam expects you to know when to use each — especially the critical distinction between labels (for selection) and annotations (for metadata):

Namespaces — Virtual Clusters Within a Cluster

Namespaces provide logical isolation within a single physical cluster. Think of them as "virtual clusters" — each with its own resource quotas, RBAC policies, and network policies:

📁
anihpj Namespace Strategy

• anihpj-dev — Dev team workspace. ResourceQuota: 4 CPU, 8Gi RAM. PSA: baseline.
• anihpj-staging — Integration testing. ResourceQuota: 8 CPU, 16Gi RAM. PSA: restricted.
• anihpj-prod — Production. ResourceQuota: 16 CPU, 32Gi RAM. PSA: restricted. NetworkPolicy: strict.

🛡️
What Namespaces Isolate

• ResourceQuota — caps total CPU/memory per namespace
• NetworkPolicy — controls pod-to-pod communication
• RBAC — RoleBindings are namespace-scoped
• Pod Security Admission — enforces security standards
• Namespaces do NOT isolate: Nodes (all pods share nodes), CRDs (cluster-scoped), PersistentVolumes (cluster-scoped)

Labels vs Annotations — The Critical Distinction

LABELS vs ANNOTATIONS — Use Each Correctly
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  LABELS (for SELECTION & GROUPING)                              │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ metadata:                                                  │ │
  │  │   labels:                                                  │ │
  │  │     app: anihpj              ← Service selector uses this  │ │
  │  │     tier: api                ← NetworkPolicy filters this  │ │
  │  │     env: production          ← kubectl -l env=production  │ │
  │  │     version: v1.2.3          ← Canary routing uses this    │ │
  │  │     team: jobpost-team       ← Cost allocation uses this   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ✅ Can SELECT with labels:                                │ │
  │  │     kubectl get pods -l app=anihpj,tier=api               │ │
  │  │     Service selector: app=anihpj → routes to these pods   │ │
  │  │     NetworkPolicy: podSelector: tier=api → targets these   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  Rules: 63 char max, alphanumeric + hyphens + underscores │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ANNOTATIONS (for METADATA & TOOLING)                           │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ metadata:                                                  │ │
  │  │   annotations:                                             │ │
  │  │     prometheus.io/scrape: "true"     ← Prometheus config   │ │
  │  │     prometheus.io/port: "8000"                              │ │
  │  │     backstage.io/component: "anihpj-api" ← Catalog entry  │ │
  │  │     kubernetes.io/change-cause: "Fix DB pool" ← History   │ │
  │  │     cert-manager.io/issuer: "letsencrypt-prod" ← TLS      │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ❌ CANNOT select with annotations:                        │ │
  │  │     kubectl get pods -l prometheus.io/scrape=true ← FAILS │ │
  │  │     Service selectors cannot use annotations               │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  Rules: Can be large. Unstructured data OK. For TOOLS.    │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

4.7 Resource Requests, Limits & Quality of Service (QoS)

Setting resource requests and limits is NOT optional in production. Without them, one misbehaving pod can consume all CPU/memory on a node and starve every other pod. The CNPA exam tests your understanding of how Kubernetes prioritizes pods under resource pressure:

📖 Requests vs Limits Defined

Requests: The MINIMUM resources guaranteed to a container. The scheduler uses this to decide which node can fit the pod. "This pod needs at least 256Mi of RAM — place it on a node with at least 256Mi free."

Limits: The MAXIMUM resources a container is allowed to use. If a container exceeds its CPU limit, it's throttled (slowed down). If it exceeds its memory limit, it's OOMKilled (terminated).

QoS Classes — Who Gets Evicted First Under Memory Pressure

QOS CLASSES — Pod Eviction Priority
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  Node Memory Pressure: RAM is running out!                      │
  │  K8s must evict (kill) pods to free memory.                     │
  │                                                                 │
  │  EVICTION ORDER (Last to First):                                │
  │                                                                 │
  │  🥇 GUARANTEED (requests == limits for CPU AND memory)          │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ • Killed LAST — K8s tries HARD to keep these alive         │ │
  │  │ • Only evicted if no Burstable or BestEffort pods exist   │ │
  │  │ • Example: anihpj-db (StatefulSet)                         │ │
  │  │   requests: {cpu: "1", memory: "2Gi"}                     │ │
  │  │   limits:   {cpu: "1", memory: "2Gi"}  ← REQUESTS==LIMITS │ │
  │  │   QoS: Guaranteed ✅                                        │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  🥈 BURSTABLE (request < limit for ANY container)               │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ • Killed if memory pressure persists, after BestEffort     │ │
  │  │ • Most common QoS for production workloads                │ │
  │  │ • Example: anihpj-api (Deployment)                         │ │
  │  │   requests: {cpu: "250m", memory: "256Mi"}                │ │
  │  │   limits:   {cpu: "500m", memory: "512Mi"} ← REQ != LIMIT │ │
  │  │   QoS: Burstable                                           │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  🥉 BESTEFFORT (no requests or limits set)                      │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │ • Killed FIRST — no guarantees at all                      │ │
  │  │ • Only use for dev/test, NEVER for production apps         │ │
  │  │ • Example: ephemeral debug pod                              │ │
  │  │   resources: {}  (nothing set)                             │ │
  │  │   QoS: BestEffort ⚠️                                        │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 CNPA BEST PRACTICE:                                         │
  │  • Always set requests + limits for production workloads       │
  │  • Use LimitRange to enforce defaults in namespaces            │
  │  • Use ResourceQuota to cap total resources per namespace      │
  │  • Monitor actual usage vs requests with Prometheus            │
  │  • Set requests to AVERAGE usage, limits to PEAK usage         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
QoS ClassConditionEviction PriorityUse For
Guaranteedrequests == limits for CPU AND memory on ALL containers🥇 Last (safest)Databases, stateful services, critical workloads
BurstableAt least one container has request < limit🥈 MiddleStateless apps (anihpj-api), most production workloads
BestEffortNo requests or limits set🥉 First (riskiest)Dev/test only. NEVER production.

CPU Throttling — The Silent Performance Killer

CPU throttling is often misunderstood. When a container exceeds its CPU limit, Kubernetes does NOT kill it (unlike memory). Instead, it throttles the CPU — slowing the container down. This causes mysterious latency spikes that look like application bugs but are actually infrastructure limits:

CPU THROTTLING — What Actually Happens When You Hit the Limit
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  anihpj-api: requests={cpu: "250m"}, limits={cpu: "500m"}       │
  │                                                                 │
  │  NORMAL OPERATION (below 500m):                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  CPU Usage: ████████░░░░  (400m / 500m) — No throttling   │ │
  │  │  Latency: P95 = 200ms ✅                                    │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  TRAFFIC SPIKE (hits 500m limit):                               │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  CPU Usage: ████████████████ (500m/500m) — THROTTLED!     │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  What happens:                                             │ │
  │  │  1. Container tries to use 700m CPU                       │ │
  │  │  2. CFS (Completely Fair Scheduler) limits to 500m        │ │
  │  │  3. Container's threads are PAUSED for throttle periods   │ │
  │  │  4. Application experiences: "random" latency spikes      │ │
  │  │     • P95 latency: 200ms → 2,000ms 😱                      │ │
  │  │     • Looks like a code bug — actually CPU throttling     │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  How to detect:                                            │ │
  │  │  $ kubectl top pod anihpj-api-abc123                      │ │
  │  │  CPU: 498m (near limit!)                                   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  Prometheus metric:                                        │ │
  │  │  container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total > 0            │ │
  │  │  → Throttling IS happening! Increase CPU limit.            │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  CNPA BEST PRACTICE:                                            │
  │  • Monitor container_cpu_cfs_throttled_seconds_total           │
  │  • If throttling > 1% of total CPU time → INCREASE limit       │
  │  • CPU throttling causes latency → users suffer                │
  │  • Memory OOM → pod dies → K8s restarts → users briefly affected│
  │  • CPU throttling → pod LIVES but SLOW → users suffer ALWAYS   │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

OOMKilled — Decoding the Dreaded Exit Code 137

When a container exceeds its memory limit, the kernel's OOM (Out-Of-Memory) killer terminates it with exit code 137. Understanding this is essential for debugging production issues:

🔍
How to Detect OOMKilled

kubectl describe pod anihpj-api-abc123
Look for:
• State: Terminated
• Reason: OOMKilled
• Exit Code: 137 (128 + 9 = SIGKILL)

Check history:
Last State: Terminated (Reason: OOMKilled)
→ Pod was killed and restarted. K8s auto-restarts by default.

🛠️
How to Fix OOMKilled

1. Increase memory limit: limits: {memory: "1Gi"}
2. Fix memory leak: Use Prometheus to track container_memory_working_set_bytes over time
3. Add HPA: Scale out instead of scaling up
4. Set appropriate requests: If requests are too low, the scheduler places too many pods on one node
5. NEVER remove limits — that's BestEffort, which gets killed first under node pressure

💡 CNPA Debugging Rule: OOMKilled (exit 137) = MEMORY problem. CPU Throttled = LATENCY problem. Never confuse the two. The fix for each is different.

LimitRange and ResourceQuota — Enforcing Resource Discipline at the Namespace Level

Setting requests/limits on individual pods is good. Enforcing them AUTOMATICALLY across entire namespaces is what platform engineering demands:

📏
LimitRange — Defaults Per Pod/Container

Sets default requests/limits for pods that don't specify them and enforces min/max bounds. If a developer deploys a pod without setting resources, LimitRange applies sensible defaults automatically.

Example: Default CPU request=200m, limit=500m. Default memory request=256Mi, limit=512Mi. Max CPU=2, Max memory=4Gi. Min CPU=50m. Pods without resources get defaults. Pods exceeding max are BLOCKED.

📊
ResourceQuota — Caps Per Namespace

Limits TOTAL resources across all pods in a namespace. Prevents one team from consuming the entire cluster.

Example: anihpj-prod namespace: max 16 CPU, 32Gi RAM, 20 pods, 10 ConfigMaps. When the quota is reached, new resource creation is BLOCKED until existing resources are deleted.

LimitRange + ResourceQuota — anihpj-prod Production Example

anihpj-prod-resource-policies.yaml 
# ─── LimitRange: Enforces defaults per pod ───
apiVersion: v1
kind: LimitRange
metadata:
  name: anihpj-limits
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  limits:
  - type: Container
    default:
      cpu: "500m"           # Default CPU limit (if pod doesn't specify)
      memory: "512Mi"       # Default memory limit
    defaultRequest:
      cpu: "200m"           # Default CPU request
      memory: "256Mi"       # Default memory request
    max:
      cpu: "2"              # No pod may exceed 2 CPU cores
      memory: "4Gi"         # No pod may exceed 4Gi memory
    min:
      cpu: "50m"            # Every pod must request at least 50m CPU
      memory: "64Mi"        # Every pod must request at least 64Mi

# ─── ResourceQuota: Caps total per namespace ───
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: anihpj-quota
  namespace: anihpj-prod
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: "16"      # Sum of all pod CPU requests ≤ 16 cores
    requests.memory: "32Gi" # Sum of all pod memory requests ≤ 32Gi
    limits.cpu: "32"        # Sum of all pod CPU limits ≤ 32 cores
    limits.memory: "64Gi"   # Sum of all pod memory limits ≤ 64Gi
    pods: "30"              # Max 30 pods in this namespace
    configmaps: "20"        # Max 20 ConfigMaps
    secrets: "20"           # Max 20 Secrets
    persistentvolumeclaims: "10"  # Max 10 PVCs

# RESULT: Developers CANNOT:
# • Deploy pods without resource declarations (LimitRange fills defaults)
# • Deploy pods exceeding 2 CPU / 4Gi (LimitRange max blocks it)
# • Deploy more than 30 pods (ResourceQuota blocks creation)

Vertical Pod Autoscaler (VPA) — Let K8s Set Your Resource Values

Setting requests/limits manually is error-prone. Set them too low → OOMKilled. Set them too high → wasted resources. VPA observes actual pod usage over time and recommends (or automatically applies) optimal values:

✅ VPA in Practice — anihpj-api Optimization
  • Without VPA: You guessed requests=256Mi, limits=512Mi. Actual usage: 180Mi. You're wasting 76Mi per pod. 10 pods = 760Mi wasted.
  • With VPA (Recommend mode): VPA observes 180Mi average, 350Mi peak. Recommends: requests=200Mi, limits=400Mi. You review and apply manually.
  • With VPA (Auto mode — NOT recommended with HPA): VPA automatically updates pod resources. Pods are evicted and recreated with new values. ⚠️ Do NOT use VPA Auto with HPA — they fight over replica count vs resource size.
  • Best Practice: Use HPA for horizontal scaling (add/remove pods). Use VPA Recommender for resource tuning (adjust requests/limits). Manually apply VPA recommendations.

4.8 Service Discovery & Load Balancing — How Pods Find Each Other

In Kubernetes, pod IPs are ephemeral — they change when pods restart. Services provide stable, discoverable endpoints that abstract away the underlying pod IPs. This is declarative networking: you declare "I want a Service named anihpj-db on port 5432" — and K8s makes it happen.

How anihpj-api Finds anihpj-db — The Full DNS Resolution

SERVICE DISCOVERY — DNS Resolution Step by Step
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  STEP 1: anihpj-api pod needs to connect to PostgreSQL          │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  anihpj-api pod (IP: 10.244.1.5)                          │ │
  │  │  Python code: psycopg2.connect(host="anihpj-db")          │ │
  │  │  DNS query: "anihpj-db.anihpj-prod.svc.cluster.local"    │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              │                                   │
  │  STEP 2: CoreDNS resolves the name                              │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  CoreDNS (runs in kube-system namespace)                   │ │
  │  │  Looks up: anihpj-db.anihpj-prod.svc.cluster.local        │ │
  │  │  Returns: ClusterIP = 10.96.100.50                         │ │
  │  │  This IP is VIRTUAL — no interface has this IP             │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              │                                   │
  │  STEP 3: kube-proxy translates ClusterIP → Pod IP                │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  kube-proxy (iptables rules on every node)                 │ │
  │  │  DNAT rule: 10.96.100.50:5432 → random backend pod        │ │
  │  │  Backend pods (Ready, matching Service selector):          │ │
  │  │  • anihpj-db-0 (10.244.2.10:5432) — Primary PostgreSQL    │ │
  │  │  • anihpj-db-1 (10.244.2.11:5432) — Read replica          │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              │                                   │
  │  STEP 4: Traffic flows to the pod                                │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  anihpj-api (10.244.1.5) → anihpj-db-0 (10.244.2.10)     │ │
  │  │  Connection established. Query executed. Result returned.  │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 KEY INSIGHT: Pods don't know each other's IPs. They use     │
  │     DNS names. Services provide stable endpoints. This is       │
  │     DECLARATIVE networking — you declare the Service, K8s      │
  │     handles the rest.                                           │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

anihpj Ingress + Service — External Traffic to Pod

Here's the complete external-to-internal traffic flow for anihpj. An Ingress routes HTTPS to a ClusterIP Service, which load-balances to the API pods. cert-manager handles TLS automatically:

anihpj-api-svc-ingress.yaml 
# ─── ClusterIP Service (internal only, pod selector) ───
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  labels: {app: anihpj, tier: api}
  annotations:
    prometheus.io/scrape: "true"
    prometheus.io/port: "8000"
spec:
  type: ClusterIP             # Internal-only (not exposed externally)
  selector:
    app: anihpj-api           # Routes to pods with this label
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 80                  # Service port
    targetPort: 8000          # Container port (Django Gunicorn)
    protocol: TCP

# ─── Ingress (External HTTPS → Internal ClusterIP) ───
---
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Ingress
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api-ingress
  namespace: anihpj-prod
  annotations:
    cert-manager.io/cluster-issuer: "letsencrypt-prod"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/ssl-redirect: "true"
    nginx.ingress.kubernetes.io/rate-limit: "100r/s"
spec:
  ingressClassName: nginx
  tls:
  - hosts:
    - api.anihpj.io
    secretName: anihpj-api-tls   # cert-manager auto-provisions
  rules:
  - host: api.anihpj.io
    http:
      paths:
      - path: /
        pathType: Prefix
        backend:
          service:
            name: anihpj-api    # → Routes to the ClusterIP above
            port:
              number: 80

# FULL FLOW: User → https://api.anihpj.io
#   → Ingress (TLS terminated by cert-manager)
#   → ClusterIP Service (anihpj-api:80)
#   → kube-proxy iptables DNAT → Pod IP:8000
#   → Django responds

Service Types — When to Use Each

Service TypeAccessible FromUse Caseanihpj Example
ClusterIPWithin cluster onlyInternal communication between servicesanihpj-api → anihpj-db (port 5432)
NodePortExternal (node IP:30000-32767)Development, debugging, simple external accessDev environment: access anihpj-api on node IP:30080
LoadBalancerExternal (cloud LB)Production external accessProduction: AWS NLB → anihpj-api Service
ExternalNameDNS alias (CNAME)Proxying to external servicesanihpj-external-db → mydb.rds.amazonaws.com
HeadlessNo ClusterIP, returns pod IPs directlyStatefulSets, service discovery per podanihpj-db-headless → direct pod DNS (for StatefulSet)
💡 The Platform DNS Convention

Every Service in Kubernetes gets a DNS name: <service-name>.<namespace>.svc.cluster.local. This means anihpj-api in the anihpj-prod namespace can reach anihpj-db simply by connecting to anihpj-db (if in the same namespace) or anihpj-db.anihpj-prod.svc.cluster.local (from anywhere in the cluster). This is how microservices discover each other without hardcoded IPs.

kube-proxy — iptables vs IPVS Performance Comparison

kube-proxy is the component that translates Service ClusterIPs to pod IPs. It has two modes with significantly different performance characteristics. As a CNPA managing production clusters, you need to know when to switch:

Aspectiptables (Default)IPVS (High-Performance)
How it worksCreates iptables rules for each Service endpoint. Every packet traverses the rules sequentially.Uses Linux IP Virtual Server — a kernel-level load balancer with multiple scheduling algorithms.
Performance at scale⚠️ Degrades beyond ~1,000 services. O(n) rule traversal.✅ Scales to 10,000+ services. O(1) hash table lookup.
LatencyIncreases with rule count. Each packet checks every rule.Consistent regardless of service count.
Load balancing algorithmRandom only (statistical distribution).Multiple: rr (round-robin), lc (least connection), sh (source hash), dh (destination hash).
Connection trackingUses conntrack — can overflow under high load.More efficient connection tracking. Less conntrack pressure.
When to switchSwitch to IPVS when: >1,000 services, high packet rates, or iptables rule latency becomes noticeable. Most production clusters benefit from IPVS.

💡 CNPA Configuration: kube-proxy --proxy-mode=ipvs --ipvs-scheduler=lc (least connection). The platform team configures this in the golden path — developers never need to know about it, but they benefit from the performance.

Ingress vs Service Type LoadBalancer — Routing External Traffic Correctly

A common confusion: should you expose your application via a Service of type LoadBalancer, or via an Ingress? The CNPA exam tests this distinction:

❌ Service Type LoadBalancer Per App

Creates one cloud load balancer PER service.

  • anihpj-api → AWS NLB #1 ($20/month)
  • anihpj-web → AWS NLB #2 ($20/month)
  • anihpj-admin → AWS NLB #3 ($20/month)
  • 10 services = 10 load balancers = $200/month
  • Each LB has its own TLS configuration
  • Each LB has its own DNS record
✅ One Ingress + ClusterIP Services

One Ingress routes ALL traffic to ClusterIP Services.

  • 1 Ingress Controller (NGINX) → 1 AWS NLB ($20/month)
  • anihpj.io/api → Ingress → anihpj-api (ClusterIP)
  • anihpj.io → Ingress → anihpj-web (ClusterIP)
  • anihpj.io/admin → Ingress → anihpj-admin (ClusterIP)
  • 100 services = 1 load balancer = $20/month
  • One TLS certificate for all routes
  • One DNS record, path-based routing
💡 CNPA Rule of Thumb

Use Ingress for HTTP/HTTPS traffic. One Ingress Controller handles ALL your HTTP services via path-based or host-based routing. Use Service Type LoadBalancer only for non-HTTP protocols (TCP, UDP, gRPC without HTTP/2 negotiation) or when the Ingress Controller itself needs a load balancer. The platform team deploys the Ingress Controller once — developers just create Ingress resources.

NetworkPolicy — The Firewall for Your Pods

By default, all pods in Kubernetes can communicate with all other pods. NetworkPolicies restrict this communication — they are the firewall rules of your platform. Without them, a compromised frontend pod can directly access your database:

NETWORKPOLICY — Restricting Pod Communication
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  WITHOUT NetworkPolicy (Default: ALLOW ALL) ❌                   │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  anihpj-web ──── can reach ────▶ anihpj-api (expected)    │ │
  │  │  anihpj-web ──── can reach ────▶ anihpj-db  😱 (BAD!)     │ │
  │  │  anihpj-api  ──── can reach ────▶ anihpj-db  (expected)   │ │
  │  │  external-z ──── can reach ────▶ anihpj-db  😱 (WORSE!)   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  Any pod can talk to any pod. No segmentation.             │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  WITH NetworkPolicy (Default: DENY, Explicit ALLOW) ✅           │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  # Policy 1: Allow web → api (ingress on api pods)        │ │
  │  │  apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1                          │ │
  │  │  kind: NetworkPolicy                                       │ │
  │  │  metadata:                                                 │ │
  │  │    name: allow-web-to-api                                  │ │
  │  │    namespace: anihpj-prod                                  │ │
  │  │  spec:                                                     │ │
  │  │    podSelector: {matchLabels: {tier: api}}  ← APPLIES TO   │ │
  │  │    policyTypes: ["Ingress"]                                 │ │
  │  │    ingress:                                                 │ │
  │  │    - from:                                                 │ │
  │  │      - podSelector: {matchLabels: {tier: web}}  ← FROM    │ │
  │  │      ports: [{port: 8000, protocol: TCP}]                  │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  # Policy 2: Allow api → db (ingress on db pods)          │ │
  │  │  kind: NetworkPolicy                                       │ │
  │  │  metadata:                                                 │ │
  │  │    name: allow-api-to-db                                   │ │
  │  │  spec:                                                     │ │
  │  │    podSelector: {matchLabels: {tier: database}}            │ │
  │  │    ingress:                                                 │ │
  │  │    - from:                                                 │ │
  │  │      - podSelector: {matchLabels: {tier: api}}            │ │
  │  │      ports: [{port: 5432, protocol: TCP}]                  │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  RESULT: web→api ✅, api→db ✅, web→db ❌ BLOCKED           │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 CNPA BEST PRACTICE: Apply a "default-deny" NetworkPolicy    │
  │     to every namespace. Then explicitly ALLOW only required     │
  │     traffic. This follows the principle of least privilege.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

4.9 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of application environments and infrastructure concepts.

Core Fundamentals Q1 of 10
A developer says "It works on my machine!" but the application fails in staging. What principle would have prevented this?
A) Use a more powerful laptop so it matches production hardware
B) Deploy directly to production to avoid staging issues
C) Environment parity — use the same K8s version, CNI, policies, and container runtime across dev/staging/prod
D) Write more unit tests to catch machine-specific bugs
✅ Correct Answer: C — Environment parity

"It works on my machine" happens when dev and production environments differ. Environment parity means using the same K8s version, same CNI, same policies across all environments. The image is built ONCE and promoted — so what runs in staging is EXACTLY what runs in production.

Core Fundamentals Q2 of 10
Which is the CORRECT artifact promotion strategy for anihpj?
A) Build separate images for dev, staging, and production with environment-specific flags
B) Build the container image ONCE in CI. Promote the SAME image through dev→staging→production, changing only K8s configuration
C) Use the latest tag and redeploy in each environment
D) Build in staging, then copy the binary to production servers
✅ Correct Answer: B — Build once, deploy everywhere

The image is built ONCE with a unique digest (SHA256). The EXACT same image is promoted through environments — only K8s configuration (ConfigMaps, Secrets, replica count) changes. Rebasing per environment creates different artifacts, defeating the purpose of staging validation.

Core Fundamentals Q3 of 10
You need to run Windows and Linux workloads on the same set of servers. Which isolation technology should you use?
A) Virtual Machines — containers share the host kernel and cannot run different OS kernels on the same host
B) Containers — Docker supports both Windows and Linux containers on any host
C) Kubernetes with mixed node pools
D) WebAssembly — it's OS-agnostic
✅ Correct Answer: A — VMs for different OS kernels

Containers share the host OS kernel. You cannot run a Windows container on a Linux host (or vice versa). VMs each have their own OS kernel, so you can mix Windows and Linux VMs on the same hypervisor. In K8s, you CAN have mixed Windows/Linux node pools — each pool has nodes running the appropriate OS.

Core Fundamentals Q4 of 10
What is the primary benefit of using Kubernetes as a universal control plane?
A) Kubernetes is faster than cloud-specific APIs
B) Kubernetes replaces the need for cloud providers entirely
C) Kubernetes has better security than cloud IAM systems
D) One consistent API for all infrastructure — kubectl works the same on AWS, GCP, Azure, and bare metal. Cloud-specific differences are abstracted away.
✅ Correct Answer: D — One consistent API across all clouds

The universal control plane means developers write the SAME YAML regardless of the underlying cloud. Crossplane translates K8s resources into cloud-specific API calls. The platform team configures providers; developers just use kubectl apply. This is the core value proposition of platform engineering on Kubernetes.

Core Fundamentals Q5 of 10
What does Cluster API (CAPI) enable that manual cluster provisioning does not?
A) Faster cluster creation using pre-built AMIs
B) Declarative cluster lifecycle management — define clusters as K8s resources, version-control them in Git, and let controllers reconcile desired state
C) Automatic application deployment to new clusters
D) Free Kubernetes clusters without paying cloud providers
✅ Correct Answer: B — Declarative cluster lifecycle management

CAPI brings the same declarative model to cluster management that K8s brings to container management. You declare "I want a cluster with 3 control plane nodes and 5 workers on AWS." CAPI controllers provision the VMs, install K8s, and maintain the desired state. If a node fails, CAPI replaces it. All cluster config is in Git.

Core Fundamentals Q6 of 10
A Service needs to find all pods with app=anihpj AND tier=api. Which metadata mechanism should be used?
A) Annotations — they are designed for service discovery
B) Namespace labels — namespaces automatically propagate to pods
C) Labels — Services use label selectors to identify which pods to route traffic to
D) Pod name prefix matching
✅ Correct Answer: C — Labels (for selection)

Labels are designed for SELECTION and GROUPING. Services use label selectors to find pods. NetworkPolicies use podSelectors to filter traffic. Annotations are for metadata/tooling and CANNOT be used for selection. This is the most important distinction between labels and annotations.

Core Fundamentals Q7 of 10
A node is under extreme memory pressure. In what order are pods evicted?
A) BestEffort first → Burstable next → Guaranteed last
B) Guaranteed first → Burstable next → BestEffort last
C) Random order — all pods are equal under pressure
D) Newest pods first, oldest pods last
✅ Correct Answer: A — BestEffort → Burstable → Guaranteed

QoS classes determine eviction priority: BestEffort pods (no requests/limits) are killed FIRST because they have no resource guarantees. Burstable pods are killed next. Guaranteed pods (requests==limits for all containers) are killed LAST. This is why production databases should always use Guaranteed QoS.

Core Fundamentals Q8 of 10
anihpj-api pod connects to anihpj-db using the hostname "anihpj-db". What actually resolves this name?
A) The pod's /etc/hosts file, which is updated by kubelet
B) An external DNS provider like Route53
C) The K8s API server acts as a DNS resolver for pods
D) CoreDNS — resolves anihpj-db.anihpj-prod.svc.cluster.local → ClusterIP → kube-proxy → pod IP
✅ Correct Answer: D — CoreDNS resolution chain

CoreDNS (running in kube-system) resolves the Service DNS name to the ClusterIP. kube-proxy (iptables rules on every node) then translates the ClusterIP to a random Ready pod IP. The pod never needs to know another pod's IP — it just uses the DNS name.

Core Fundamentals Q9 of 10
anihpj-api has requests={cpu:250m, mem:256Mi} and limits={cpu:500m, mem:512Mi}. What QoS class is this?
A) Guaranteed — requests are set, so resources are guaranteed
B) Burstable — requests are less than limits for both CPU and memory
C) BestEffort — limits exceed requests, so it's best-effort scheduling
D) No QoS class — you need to specify a QoS class explicitly
✅ Correct Answer: B — Burstable

Guaranteed requires requests==limits for CPU AND memory on ALL containers. Since anihpj-api has requests < limits, it falls into Burstable. This is the most common QoS class for production workloads — it allows bursting above requests when resources are available, while still providing a guaranteed baseline.

Core Fundamentals Q10 of 10
You need to manage anihpj configuration across dev/staging/prod. What approach follows the "same config, different values" principle?
A) Maintain three completely separate YAML files for each environment
B) Use environment variables set manually in each cluster
C) Use Kustomize with a base/ directory for common config and overlays/dev, overlays/staging, overlays/prod for environment differences
D) Build separate Docker images with environment-specific configuration baked in
✅ Correct Answer: C — Kustomize base + overlays

Kustomize lets you define a common BASE (deployment, service, ingress) and environment-specific OVERLAYS (replica counts, resource sizes, debug flags). The base is shared; overlays patch differences. kubectl apply -k overlays/prod applies the base + prod patches. No duplication, no drift.

📊 Chapter 4 Summary — Key Takeaways

🌐Environment StrategyLocal→Staging→Production. Same config, different values via Kustomize overlays.
📦Build Once, Deploy EverywhereSame image promoted through envs. Never rebuild per environment.
📦 vs 🖥️Containers vs VMsContainers share kernel (fast, dense). VMs isolate kernel (stronger security).
☸️Universal Control PlaneOne K8s API across all clouds. Crossplane provisions cloud resources via kubectl.
🏷️Labels vs AnnotationsLabels = selection (Services). Annotations = metadata (tools). Never confuse them.
🥇🥈🥉QoS ClassesGuaranteed (last killed) → Burstable → BestEffort (first killed). Set limits!

Chapter 5: Platform Architecture & Capabilities — Designing the Blueprint

Platform architecture is the art of hiding complexity behind simple, self-service interfaces. Every layer — Infrastructure, Orchestration, Delivery, Observability, Developer Experience — abstracts the layer below it. This chapter teaches you how to design a platform that serves multiple teams safely (multi-tenancy), stays available under load (HA/scalability), extends to new use cases (CRDs/Operators), defends against threats (defense-in-depth security), and supports any workload (networking/storage). We'll use anihpj/jobpost to make every architectural decision concrete.

🟡 Intermediate ⏱️ ~3 hours 🏛️ Architecture 🎯 Domain 1: 36% 🛡️ Security

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Platform architecture layers — how Infrastructure → Orchestration → Delivery → Observability → DevEx stack together
  • ✅ The CNCF Platforms White Paper — the industry-standard reference architecture and its key attributes
  • ✅ Platform capabilities matrix — the minimum viable capabilities every IDP must provide
  • ✅ Multi-tenancy — soft (namespaces) vs hard (separate clusters) isolation for multiple teams on one platform
  • ✅ High availability and scalability — etcd quorum, Cluster Autoscaler, HPA, VPA, node pools
  • ✅ Platform extensibility — CRDs, Operators, and Admission Webhooks to extend K8s for platform-specific needs
  • ✅ Defense-in-depth security — the 10-layer security model from NetworkPolicy to etcd encryption
  • ✅ Networking and storage architecture — CNI, Service Mesh, Ingress, CSI drivers, backup/DR
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Platform Engineering Core Fundamentals 36% Foundation for Security (Ch 7-11) Foundation for APIs & Provisioning (Ch 17-20)

5.1 What is Platform Architecture?

Platform architecture is the blueprint for your Internal Developer Platform — how all the components (Kubernetes, CI/CD, GitOps, observability, security, developer portal) fit together into a cohesive, self-service system. It's the "big picture" that guides every platform decision:

📖 Platform Architecture Defined

"Platform architecture is the art of hiding complexity behind simple, self-service interfaces." A developer at the DevEx layer should never need to know how Kubernetes schedules pods, how cert-manager provisions TLS, or how Crossplane creates databases. The architecture ensures that each layer abstracts the complexity of the layer below — making the platform USABLE by developers while remaining POWERFUL enough to run production workloads.

The 5-Layer Platform Architecture — The Universal Blueprint

PLATFORM ARCHITECTURE — The 5 Layers (Top to Bottom)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  LAYER 5: 👨‍💻 DEVELOPER EXPERIENCE (DevEx)                       │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Backstage Portal | CLI (anihpj-cli) | API | IDE Plugin  │ │
  │  │  "What developers SEE and TOUCH"                          │ │
  │  │  → Click "Create Django Service" → everything happens     │ │
  │  │  → View all services, docs, metrics, costs in one place   │ │
  │  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │  ABSTRACTION: Hides Layers 1-4 complexity                 │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              │                                  │
  │  LAYER 4: 📊 OBSERVABILITY                                      │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Prometheus (metrics) | Grafana (dashboards) | Loki (logs)│ │
  │  │  Tempo (traces) | Alertmanager (alerts) | PagerDuty       │ │
  │  │  "Is everything working? How do we know?"                  │ │
  │  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │  ABSTRACTION: Auto-instrumented. Every service gets        │ │
  │  │  metrics, logs, traces, and dashboards by default.        │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              │                                  │
  │  LAYER 3: 🚀 DELIVERY (CI/CD + GitOps)                         │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  GitHub Actions (CI) | ArgoCD (GitOps) | Helm/Kustomize   │ │
  │  │  Container Registry (GHCR/Harbor) | Image Scanning (Trivy)│ │
  │  │  "How does code get from Git to Production?"              │ │
  │  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │  ABSTRACTION: Push code → everything auto-builds, tests,  │ │
  │  │  scans, signs, and deploys. No manual steps.             │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              │                                  │
  │  LAYER 2: ☸️  ORCHESTRATION (Kubernetes + Extensions)           │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Kubernetes | Crossplane (cloud resources) | CAPI         │ │
  │  │  cert-manager (TLS) | external-dns | Kyverno (policies)  │ │
  │  │  "How are containers and infrastructure managed?"         │ │
  │  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │  ABSTRACTION: One API for containers AND cloud resources. │ │
  │  │  kubectl creates both Pods AND RDS databases.            │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                              │                                  │
  │  LAYER 1: 🏗️ INFRASTRUCTURE (Cloud / Bare Metal)                │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  Compute (EC2/GCE) | Network (VPC/Subnets) | Storage (EBS)│ │
  │  │  DNS (Route53) | Load Balancers (NLB/ALB) | IAM           │ │
  │  │  "Where does everything physically run?"                  │ │
  │  ├───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤ │
  │  │  ABSTRACTION: Provisioned via Terraform or Crossplane.    │ │
  │  │  Developers never touch cloud consoles.                   │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 KEY PRINCIPLE: Each layer abstracts the layer below it.     │
  │     DevEx (L5) users never see Infrastructure (L1) complexity.  │
  │     Platform team works at L1-L4 to make L5 delightful.         │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Architectural Decision Records (ADRs) — Documenting Platform Decisions

Platform architecture involves hundreds of decisions. Which CNI? Which Service Mesh? Which Ingress Controller? ADRs capture WHY each decision was made — so future engineers understand the context:

📝
What Is an ADR?

An Architectural Decision Record is a short document capturing a significant architectural decision, the context, the options considered, the chosen option, and the consequences. Stored in Git alongside the code it affects.

Example: "ADR-005: Choose Cilium as CNI over Calico" — documents the eBPF performance advantage, Hubble observability, and NetworkPolicy enforcement that led to the decision.

🔍
Why ADRs Matter for Platform Teams

• New team members understand WHY Cilium was chosen, not just THAT it was chosen
• When revisiting decisions, you have the original context
• Auditors can trace platform design decisions
• Prevents "why did we do it this way?" conversations
• Lives in the platform Git repo — version controlled

The Strangler Fig Pattern — Migrating to a Platform Without a Big Bang

Organizations rarely build platforms from scratch. The Strangler Fig Pattern — named after a vine that gradually envelops and replaces a host tree — is the recommended approach for migrating existing infrastructure to a platform:

THE STRANGLER FIG PATTERN — Gradual Platform Migration
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  PHASE 1: Identify First Candidate                               │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  • Pick a low-risk service (internal tool, not customer-   │ │
  │  │    facing). Migrate it to the platform.                    │ │
  │  │  • Prove: the platform works, deploys are faster,          │ │
  │  │    monitoring is better.                                   │ │
  │  │  • Example: anihpj's internal admin dashboard → platform   │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                          ↓                                      │
  │  PHASE 2: Expand Gradually (Service by Service)                  │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  • Migrate services ONE AT A TIME. Never big-bang.         │ │
  │  │  • Each migration: build golden path → migrate → validate  │ │
  │  │  • Old and new run SIDE BY SIDE during transition          │ │
  │  │  • Example: anihpj-api (week 2), anihpj-web (week 3),      │ │
  │  │    anihpj-db (week 4)                                      │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                          ↓                                      │
  │  PHASE 3: Strangle the Old System                                │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  • When ALL services are migrated → decommission old infra │ │
  │  │  • Old servers, old pipelines, old monitoring → shut down  │ │
  │  │  • Platform is now the ONLY way to deploy                  │ │
  │  │  • Legacy: 0% traffic. Platform: 100% traffic.             │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 CNPA PRINCIPLE: Never "big bang" a platform migration.      │
  │     Strangle the old system one service at a time. Each         │
  │     migration builds confidence and validates the platform.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

5.2 The CNCF Platforms White Paper — The Industry Standard

The CNCF Platforms White Paper defines the reference architecture for cloud native platforms. Every CNPA-certified engineer should know its key attributes and use them to evaluate platform designs:

📖 CNCF Platform Definition

"A platform is a curated set of capabilities, presented through consistent APIs and tooling, that enables development teams to deliver software at scale." — CNCF Platforms White Paper

Key Attributes of a Cloud Native Platform

📦
Platform as a Product

Treated like a SaaS product — with users (developers), features (golden paths), roadmap, and success metrics. Not an internal project with an end date. Continuously improved based on user feedback.

🔓
Self-Service

Developers provision their own infrastructure without tickets. The platform provides portals, CLIs, and APIs — not manual gateways. "Click. Deploy. Done."

🔌
API-Driven

All platform capabilities exposed through consistent, versioned APIs. kubectl, Backstage API, platform CLI — all backed by the same APIs. Programmable and automatable.

📝
Declarative

Users declare WHAT they want. The platform figures out HOW. YAML manifests, Terraform files, Kyverno policies — all declarations of desired state. Controllers reconcile continuously.

🧩
Composable

Built from best-of-breed CNCF tools — not a monolithic vendor suite. ArgoCD for GitOps, Prometheus for metrics, Backstage for portal. Each component can be swapped independently.

CNCF Platform Reference Architecture — Mapped to anihpj
