#     {"name": "python3.12", "version": "3.12.1", "type": "library"},
#     {"name": "django", "version": "5.0.1", "type": "library", "purl": "pkg:pypi/django@5.0.1"},
#     {"name": "libcurl4", "version": "7.88.1", "type": "library"},
#     ... (145 components total)
#   ]
# }

# SBOM standards:
# • CycloneDX (OWASP) — JSON/XML, lightweight
# • SPDX (Linux Foundation) — ISO standard, more metadata

# Why SBOM matters for CNPA:
# • Compliance: Executive Order 14028 requires SBOMs for federal software
# • Incident response: "Do we use log4j?" → grep SBOM → answer in seconds
# • Supply chain transparency: Know exactly what's in your images
# • CVE matching: Match SBOM components against vulnerability databases
📖 SBOM in the CNPA Context

The CNPA exam expects you to understand SBOM as a supply chain security tool. Key points: (1) SBOM is generated at BUILD time (by Syft in CI), not at runtime. (2) SBOM is stored as a CI artifact alongside the image — not inside the image. (3) When a critical CVE (like Log4Shell) is announced, you query your SBOM repository — not your running clusters — to find affected images. (4) SBOM + vulnerability scanner = complete vulnerability management. SBOM says what's IN the image; the scanner says what's VULNERABLE.

SBOM Formats — SPDX vs CycloneDX: Which One Should anihpj Use?

Two SBOM standards dominate the industry. The CNPA exam expects you to know both exist and understand their differences — the choice impacts tooling compatibility, compliance reporting, and ecosystem integration:

📋 SPDX (Software Package Data Exchange)

Creator: Linux Foundation. Standard: ISO/IEC 5962:2021.

Strengths:

  • ISO standard — required for government compliance (Executive Order 14028)
  • Rich legal metadata: licenses, copyrights, attributions
  • Relationship tracking: "Library X DEPENDS_ON Library Y"
  • Mature ecosystem: Linux kernel, Yocto Project, Zephyr

Best for: Organizations needing ISO-standard compliance. Legal/license compliance teams. Government contractors.

📦 CycloneDX (OWASP)

Creator: OWASP Foundation. Standard: OWASP flagship project.

Strengths:

  • Security-focused: includes vulnerability info, exploitability data
  • Lightweight JSON — smaller files, faster parsing
  • Native support in Syft, Trivy, Dependency-Track
  • Extended beyond SBOM: SaaSBOM, HBOM (hardware), OBOM (operations)

Best for: Security teams. DevSecOps pipelines. Organizations using Syft + Trivy + Dependency-Track (all natively support CycloneDX).

💡 anihpj Recommendation: Generate BOTH. Syft with --output spdx-json for compliance/legal teams. Syft with --output cyclonedx-json for the security pipeline (Dependency-Track, Trivy integration). Storage is cheap. Compliance requirements change. Having both formats future-proofs your SBOM strategy.

Why Supply Chain Security Matters — The SolarWinds Anatomy

In 2020, attackers compromised SolarWinds' build pipeline and injected malicious code into a SIGNED software update. 18,000 organizations — including US government agencies — installed the trojaned update because it was "trusted." This is why every step in the CI/CD pipeline needs verification: signing, SBOM, and SLSA aren't academic concepts — they're defenses against the most dangerous class of attacks:

SUPPLY CHAIN ATTACK ANATOMY — How SolarWinds Happened (And How We Prevent It)
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  THE SOLARWINDS ATTACK (2020) — What Went Wrong                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  1. Attacker compromises CI/CD build server               │ │
  │  │  2. Attacker injects malicious DLL into source code       │ │
  │  │     BEFORE compilation                                    │ │
  │  │  3. CI pipeline builds + signs the COMPROMISED binary     │ │
  │  │  4. "Signed" update distributed to 18,000 customers       │ │
  │  │  5. Customers TRUST the signature → install immediately   │ │
  │  │  6. Attacker now has backdoor access to 18,000 networks   │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ROOT CAUSE: The signature only proved "SolarWinds built  │ │
  │  │  this" — NOT that "the source code wasn't tampered with."  │ │
  │  │  Signing is necessary but INSUFFICIENT alone.            │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  HOW MODERN SUPPLY CHAIN SECURITY PREVENTS THIS (anihpj):       │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  1. Source code in Git → PR requires 2-person review      │ │
  │  │     (SLSA 4 requirement — no unilateral changes)          │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  2. CI build runs on EPHEMERAL runner (not long-lived     │ │
  │  │     server that could be compromised over time)           │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  3. Build produces:                                       │ │
  │  │     • Signed image (Cosign — proves CI built it)          │ │
  │  │     • SBOM (Syft — lists ALL components)                  │ │
  │  │     • Provenance (SLSA — records build environment)       │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  4. Kyverno VerifyImages checks AT ADMISSION:             │ │
  │  │     • Is the signature valid? ✅                           │ │
  │  │     • Was it signed by anihpj CI? ✅                       │ │
  │  │     • Is the Rekor transparency log entry present? ✅      │ │
  │  │     • Does the SBOM show unexpected new components?       │ │
  │  │       → If yes → flag for review, DON'T auto-deploy       │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  5. Falco monitors runtime: unexpected outbound           │ │
  │  │     connections? → ALERT immediately                      │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  RESULT: Even if the build server is compromised, the     │ │
  │  │  combination of PR review + ephemeral runners +            │ │
  │  │  provenance + SBOM diffing + admission verification +     │ │
  │  │  runtime detection makes the attack EXTREMELY difficult. │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 THE CNPA LESSON: Signing alone is NOT enough. You need:     │
  │     Provenance (HOW it was built) + SBOM (WHAT's inside) +      │
  │     Admission verification (SHOULD it run) + Runtime detection  │
  │     (WHAT is it doing NOW). Each answers a different question.  │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

11.5 Pipeline Security Best Practices — OIDC & SLSA

Two critical patterns define modern CI/CD security: OIDC eliminates long-lived credentials, and SLSA provides a framework for measuring supply chain integrity. Together, they address the two biggest pipeline risks: stolen credentials and tampered artifacts:

OIDC — No More Static Credentials

OIDC — Temporary Credentials Replace Static Keys
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  ❌ THE OLD WAY (DANGEROUS):                                     │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │  1. Create AWS IAM user                                     │ │
  │  │  2. Generate AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID + AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY     │ │
  │  │  3. Store in GitHub Secrets (hoping nobody leaks them)      │ │
  │  │  4. Keys NEVER EXPIRE — valid until manually rotated       │ │
  │  │  5. If keys leak (git commit, log output, CI output):      │ │
  │  │     → Attacker has PERMANENT AWS access 🔓                  │ │
  │  │     → Can provision resources, read S3, delete infra       │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  ✅ THE NEW WAY (OIDC — SECURE):                                 │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                             │ │
  │  │  GitHub Actions                    AWS IAM                  │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────┐                    ┌──────────────────┐     │ │
  │  │  │ OIDC     │─── 1. JWT token ──▶│ OIDC Provider     │     │ │
  │  │  │ Provider │     (repo+branch)  │ (trusts GitHub)   │     │ │
  │  │  └──────────┘                    └────────┬─────────┘     │ │
  │  │                                          │                 │ │
  │  │                                          ▼                 │ │
  │  │                                   ┌──────────────────┐     │ │
  │  │                                   │ IAM Role          │     │ │
  │  │                                   │ (assume-role)     │     │ │
  │  │                                   │ Condition:        │     │ │
  │  │                                   │  repo=anihpj/*    │     │ │
  │  │                                   │  branch=main      │     │ │
  │  │                                   └────────┬─────────┘     │ │
  │  │                                          │                 │ │
  │  │                    ◀── 2. Temporary ─────┘                 │ │
  │  │                        credentials (1 hour, auto-expire)   │ │
  │  │                                                             │ │
  │  │  ✅ NO static keys stored anywhere                          │ │
  │  │  ✅ Credentials auto-expire in 1 hour                       │ │
  │  │  ✅ Scoped to specific repo + branch (condition)            │ │
  │  │  ✅ If token leaks → already expired or wrong repo          │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 CNPA PRINCIPLE: OIDC is ALWAYS the answer for CI/CD auth.  │
  │     Static credentials (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID) = WRONG answer.     │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

SLSA Framework — Supply Chain Integrity Levels

SLSA (Supply chain Levels for Software Artifacts, pronounced "salsa") defines four levels of supply chain integrity. Each level builds on the previous — the CNPA expects you to understand what each level provides:

LevelNameRequirementsWhat It Protects Against
SLSA 1DocumentationBuild process is documented. Automated build. Provenance generated (who built what, when).Basic visibility. Shows intent but no integrity guarantees.
SLSA 2Tamper ResistanceVersion control. Build service (not dev laptop). Signed provenance. Hosted build platform.Prevents casual tampering. "Was this built by CI or on someone's laptop?"
SLSA 3AuditabilityIsolated builds. SLSA-compliant build platform. Provenance is non-forgeable. Source and build are auditable.Prevents build process tampering. "Can I trust the CI pipeline itself?"
SLSA 4HermeticityHermetic builds. Reproducible. All dependencies pinned. Two-person review. Everything SLSA 3 + maximum isolation.Maximum protection. "Same source ALWAYS produces the same binary." Government/military grade.

💡 CNPA Context: Most platforms target SLSA 2-3. SLSA 4 is aspirational. The exam will present scenarios where a build runs on a developer's laptop → this violates SLSA 2 (build service requirement). The fix: move builds to a hosted CI platform (GitHub Actions, Tekton, Jenkins on dedicated infra).

Runtime Security — Falco: The Last Line of Defense

All the shift-left security in the world can't guarantee 100% prevention. A zero-day CVE, a misconfigured RBAC, or an insider threat could still slip through. Falco is the CNCF-standard runtime security tool that monitors system calls in real-time, detecting anomalous behavior as it happens. If every other security layer fails, Falco is your safety net:

FALCO RUNTIME DETECTION — Catching What Slips Through
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                                                                 │
  │  HOW FALCO WORKS: System Call Monitoring at the Kernel Level    │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  KERNEL (eBPF or kernel module)                           │ │
  │  │       │                                                    │ │
  │  │       │ Every syscall is captured:                         │ │
  │  │       │ execve(), open(), connect(), bind(), ptrace()...  │ │
  │  │       ▼                                                    │ │
  │  │  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ │
  │  │  │              FALCO ENGINE (DaemonSet)                 │ │ │
  │  │  │                                                      │ │ │
  │  │  │  1. Captures syscall events from kernel               │ │ │
  │  │  │  2. Enriches with K8s metadata (pod, namespace,      │ │ │
  │  │  │     container, image)                                 │ │ │
  │  │  │  3. Evaluates against FALCO RULES (YAML)              │ │ │
  │  │  │  4. If rule matches → ALERT                            │ │ │
  │  │  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  CRITICAL FALCO RULES FOR PLATFORM SECURITY:                    │
  │  ┌───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  🐚 UNEXPECTED SHELL SPAWN                                │ │
  │  │  Rule: "A shell (bash/sh) was spawned in a container"     │ │
  │  │  Why: Production apps don't spawn shells. If someone is   │ │
  │  │       running /bin/bash in your prod container, it's      │ │
  │  │       either an attacker or a misconfig. Either way: ALERT.│ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  ⛏️ CRYPTOMINER DETECTION                                  │ │
  │  │  Rule: "Outbound connection to known mining pool ports"   │ │
  │  │  Why: Compromised containers are often used to mine       │ │
  │  │       crypto. Connections to stratum+tcp:// pools on      │ │
  │  │       ports 3333, 4444, 8888 = IMMEDIATE ALERT.          │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  📁 SENSITIVE FILE ACCESS                                  │ │
  │  │  Rule: "Reading /etc/shadow, /root/.ssh, or K8s secrets"  │ │
  │  │  Why: Production apps don't need to read /etc/shadow.     │ │
  │  │       If they try, someone is attempting privilege         │ │
  │  │       escalation or credential theft.                     │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  🌐 UNEXPECTED OUTBOUND CONNECTION                         │ │
  │  │  Rule: "Container connected to IP NOT in allowlist"       │ │
  │  │  Why: anihpj-api should only talk to anihpj-db, Redis,    │ │
  │  │       and the K8s API. Connection to unknown IP →         │ │
  │  │       potential data exfiltration or C2 channel.          │ │
  │  │                                                           │ │
  │  │  🔑 PRIVILEGED CONTAINER STARTED                          │ │
  │  │  Rule: "Container started with privileged: true"          │ │
  │  │  Why: PSA should block this at admission, but if someone  │ │
  │  │       bypassed it (or PSA is misconfigured), Falco       │ │
  │  │       catches it at runtime. Defense-in-depth.            │ │
  │  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
  │                                                                 │
  │  💡 FALCO INTEGRATION IN THE ANIHPJ STACK:                      │
  │  Falco (DaemonSet) → Alert → Prometheus Alertmanager →          │
  │  PagerDuty → On-call engineer. Runtime detection completes      │
  │  the security pipeline: Pre-commit→PR→Build→Deploy→RUNTIME.   │
  │  Every stage catches what earlier stages missed.                │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

11.6 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

Test your understanding of shift-left security, vulnerability scanning, image signing, SBOM, OIDC, and SLSA.

Security Q1 of 10
Where should secret detection (git-secrets) run in the anihpj pipeline?
A) At deploy time — Kyverno can check for secrets in pod specs
B) At build time — after the Docker image is created
C) At pre-commit time — BEFORE secrets are ever committed to Git. Shift-left means catching issues at the EARLIEST possible stage.
D) At runtime — Falco can detect when secrets are accessed
✅ Correct Answer: C — Pre-commit is the earliest (cheapest) stage

Shift-left principle: the EARLIER you catch an issue, the cheaper it is to fix. If git-secrets catches an AWS key at pre-commit: fix the file, recommit = 2 minutes. If caught at PR review: 5 minutes. At build: 30 minutes (rebuild). At deploy: 2 hours (rollback). At runtime: DAYS of incident response. The CNPA answer is always the LEFTMOST stage that can detect the issue.

Security Q2 of 10
Trivy scan finds 2 CRITICAL and 8 HIGH CVEs in your image. What should happen?
A) Deploy anyway — CVEs are common and usually not exploitable
B) FAIL the pipeline — CRITICAL CVEs must be fixed. Update the base image, rebuild, re-scan until zero CRITICAL CVEs.
C) Create a Jira ticket and deploy — fix later
D) Ignore the scan results — Trivy has many false positives
✅ Correct Answer: B — CRITICAL CVEs FAIL the pipeline

CRITICAL CVEs (CVSS 9.0+) are remotely exploitable and can lead to complete system compromise. The anihpj policy: CRITICAL → fail pipeline immediately, don't even push to registry. HIGH → block deployment to production but allow dev/staging. MEDIUM → create ticket, fix within 30 days. LOW → log for awareness. The key: fix CVEs BEFORE the image reaches the registry — not after it's running in production.

Security Q3 of 10
What is the advantage of Cosign keyless signing (Sigstore) over traditional key-based signing?
A) Keyless signing is faster — no cryptographic operations needed
B) Keyless signing doesn't require a container registry
C) Keyless signing produces smaller signatures
D) NO long-lived private keys to manage, protect, or steal. Ephemeral keys generated per signature. Identity verified via OIDC. Public auditability via Rekor transparency log.
✅ Correct Answer: D — No key management = no key theft

Traditional signing: generate a private key, store it securely (HSM, vault), distribute the public key, rotate keys, revoke compromised keys — massive operational burden. Keyless signing: Cosign authenticates via OIDC (GitHub Actions identity), Fulcio issues a SHORT-LIVED certificate (10 minutes), the ephemeral key signs the image and is discarded. The certificate + signature are recorded in Rekor (immutable public ledger). No key to steal. No key to rotate. Every signature is publicly auditable. This is the CNPA-preferred approach.

Security Q4 of 10
What does Kyverno's VerifyImages rule check at admission time?
A) That the container image has a VALID cryptographic signature from a TRUSTED identity — and rejects pods with unsigned or invalidly signed images
B) That the image has passed a Trivy scan with zero CVEs
C) That the image exists in the container registry
D) That the image tag follows semantic versioning
✅ Correct Answer: A — VerifyImages checks cryptographic signatures

Kyverno VerifyImages checks: (1) Does the image have an OCI signature? (2) Is the signature cryptographically valid? (3) Was it signed by a trusted identity (verified via public key or Fulcio certificate chain)? (4) Is there a Rekor transparency log entry? If ANY check fails → admission DENIED. This is separate from vulnerability scanning (Trivy) — signing proves WHO built it; scanning checks WHAT's in it. Both are needed for defense-in-depth.

Security Q5 of 10
What is the primary value of an SBOM in incident response?
A) SBOM automatically patches vulnerable components
B) When a critical CVE (like Log4Shell) is announced, you query your SBOM repository to find EVERY image containing the vulnerable component — in minutes instead of weeks
C) SBOM replaces vulnerability scanning — it's a more modern approach
D) SBOM is required by Kubernetes to run pods
✅ Correct Answer: B — SBOM enables rapid CVE impact analysis

Without SBOM: "Do we use Log4j?" → manually check every repo, every Dockerfile, every running container → takes WEEKS. With SBOM: grep -r "log4j" sboms/ → answer in MINUTES. SBOM is a COMPLETE inventory of every library, OS package, and dependency in every image. Generated at build time by Syft. Stored as a CI artifact. Queryable at any time. This is why Executive Order 14028 mandates SBOMs for federal software — and why CNPA expects you to understand the pattern.

Security Q6 of 10
Why are static credentials (AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID) in CI/CD dangerous?
A) They're too short — they expire too quickly
B) They require a hardware security module (HSM)
C) They can only be used once
D) They NEVER expire, are stored as plaintext in CI variables, and if leaked (git commit, logs, CI output) → attacker has permanent cloud access with no time limit
✅ Correct Answer: D — Static keys = permanent, stealable access

Static credentials are the #1 CI/CD security anti-pattern. They NEVER expire. They're stored as plaintext in CI/CD variables. If they leak (accidental git commit, debug logging, CI output capture), the attacker has PERMANENT access — no time limit, no automatic revocation. The fix: OIDC. GitHub Actions authenticates to AWS via OIDC, gets TEMPORARY credentials (1-hour expiry) scoped to the specific repo and branch. No static keys anywhere. Even if the token leaks, it's already expired. This is ALWAYS the CNPA correct answer for CI/CD authentication.

Security Q7 of 10
A developer builds Docker images on their laptop and pushes to the registry. Which SLSA level does this VIOLATE?
A) SLSA 1 — builds must be documented (the developer can document the process)
B) SLSA 4 — only hermetic builds are affected
C) SLSA 2 — requires a HOSTED BUILD SERVICE (CI platform, not developer laptop). Laptop builds are not tamper-resistant.
D) No SLSA level is violated — any build method is acceptable
✅ Correct Answer: C — SLSA 2 requires a hosted build service

SLSA 2's key requirement: builds MUST run on a HOSTED BUILD SERVICE (GitHub Actions, Tekton Pipelines, Jenkins on dedicated infra) — NOT on a developer's laptop. Why? (1) Build service provides an AUDIT TRAIL (who triggered the build, when, with what source). (2) Build service isolates the build from the developer's environment. (3) Build service generates signed provenance. A developer could tamper with the build on their laptop — SLSA 2 prevents this by requiring a trusted, auditable build platform.

Security Q8 of 10
You find an AWS access key committed to a public GitHub repository. What should you do FIRST?
A) IMMEDIATELY revoke/delete the key in AWS IAM — assume it's compromised. Then git-secrets to prevent future commits. The key has been public — revocation is urgent.
B) Delete the file from the repository and force-push — removing the commit fixes the leak
C) Add the repository to .gitignore — that prevents future leaks
D) Rotate the key — create a new one and update the application
✅ Correct Answer: A — Revoke FIRST, then fix the process

When a secret is committed to a public repo, assume it's ALREADY COMPROMISED (bots scan GitHub commits for keys within seconds). Step 1: REVOKE the key in AWS IAM immediately — stop the bleeding. Step 2: Remove the secret from Git history (BFG Repo-Cleaner, git filter-branch) — but know that if it was public, it's already been copied. Step 3: Install git-secrets to prevent future leaks. Step 4: Implement pre-commit hooks. Order matters: revoke first because every second the key is valid is a second an attacker can use it.

Security Q9 of 10
Trivy scan shows a CRITICAL CVE in openssl with CVSS 9.8 and a fix version available. What's the most efficient remediation?
A) Add a NetworkPolicy to block traffic to the affected pod — network isolation mitigates the CVE
B) Update the base image (apt-get upgrade or bump python:3.12-slim → python:3.12.2-slim), rebuild, re-scan. Fix the ROOT CAUSE — the vulnerable library.
C) Deploy a WAF to block exploit attempts — application-level protection
D) Accept the risk — CVSS 9.8 is just a number
✅ Correct Answer: B — Fix the root cause: update the vulnerable library

When a fix version EXISTS, ALWAYS fix the root cause. Updating the base image is the simplest fix: apt-get update && apt-get upgrade or bump the base image tag. Rebuild, re-scan to verify the CVE is gone. A, C, and D are compensating controls — they might reduce the attack surface but don't ELIMINATE the vulnerability. The CNPA principle: if a patch exists, APPLY IT. Only use compensating controls when no patch is available (zero-day).

Security Q10 of 10
Design the complete security toolchain for anihpj's pipeline — from pre-commit to runtime.
A) Just Trivy at build time — it covers all security needs
B) Kyverno VerifyImages at deploy time — admission control is sufficient
C) Pre-commit: git-secrets → PR: bandit + safety → Build: trivy scan + cosign sign + Syft SBOM → Deploy: Kyverno VerifyImages → Runtime: Falco. Defense-in-depth at EVERY stage.
D) Manual code review before merge — humans catch what tools miss
✅ Correct Answer: C — Defense-in-depth across ALL pipeline stages

The complete shift-left toolchain: Pre-commit (git-secrets) catches leaked credentials before they reach Git. PR review (bandit SAST + safety SCA) catches code vulnerabilities and vulnerable dependencies. Build (trivy CVE scan + cosign sign + Syft SBOM) catches OS/library CVEs, signs images for trust, and generates SBOM for compliance. Deploy (Kyverno VerifyImages) enforces only signed, trusted images run. Runtime (Falco) detects anomalous behavior. Each stage catches what earlier stages miss. This is defense-in-depth applied to the CI/CD pipeline — the CNPA ideal.

📊 Chapter 11 Summary — Key Takeaways

⬅️Shift-LeftPre-commit→PR→Build→Deploy→Runtime. Security at EVERY stage. Catch issues at the cheapest stage.
🔍Trivy ScanCRITICAL→fail pipeline. HIGH→block prod. MEDIUM→ticket. LOW→log. Fix CVEs BEFORE registry push.
✍️Cosign SignKeyless signing via Sigstore. No keys to manage. Fulcio certs + Rekor log = auditable trust chain.
📋SBOMComplete component inventory. Syft generates CycloneDX/SPDX. Rapid CVE impact analysis in minutes.
🔑OIDCNO static credentials. Temporary tokens (1hr). Scoped to repo+branch. Auto-expire. Always the CNPA answer.
🏗️SLSALevels 1-4: Documentation→Tamper Resistance→Auditability→Hermeticity. Most platforms target SLSA 2-3.

Chapter 12: Continuous Integration Pipelines Deep Dive — The Build Factory

Continuous Integration isn't just "running tests on push." It's a software factory — a pipeline that converts raw source code into production-ready artifacts through a series of automated, repeatable stages. Each stage is a GATE — if any fails, the pipeline stops. No artifacts escape the factory without passing every quality check. This chapter dissects the CI pipeline stage by stage: triggers, caching, parallelization, artifacts, notifications, and Git integration — all applied to the anihpj/jobpost GitHub Actions workflow that builds, scans, signs, and packages our Django application.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours⚙️ CI/CD🎯 Domain 3: 16%

  • ✅ CI Pipeline Complete Flow — Every stage from push to artifact. How each acts as a quality gate
  • ✅ Triggers & Stages — Push, PR, schedule, manual. Parallel vs sequential stages. GitHub Actions event model
  • ✅ Caching & Artifacts — pip/docker layer caching. Docker images, SBOMs, signatures, test reports as pipeline outputs
  • ✅ Notifications & Git Integration — Slack alerts, GitHub status checks, branch protection rules
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Continuous Delivery 16% Foundation for GitOps (Ch 15-16) Foundation for Security in CI/CD (Ch 11)

12.1 CI Pipeline — The Complete Flow

A CI pipeline is a series of automated stages that run every time code is pushed. Each stage is a gate — lint fails? Pipeline stops. Tests fail? Pipeline stops. Build fails? Pipeline stops. Only code that passes EVERY gate produces artifacts. This is the "quality factory" model: raw code in → verified artifacts out.

For the anihpj/jobpost Django application, the GitHub Actions CI pipeline runs three main stages: lint (code quality checks with ruff, ~30 seconds), test (unit + integration tests with pytest, ~2 minutes), and build-scan (Docker build + Trivy vulnerability scan + Cosign signing, ~4 minutes). Total: under 7 minutes from push to signed, scanned container image.

Why CI Exists — The Problem It Solves (Integration Hell)

Before CI, teams worked in isolation for days or weeks, then attempted a "big bang" integration. The result was predictable: merge conflicts, broken builds, and "it works on my machine." CI solves this by integrating EVERY change, IMMEDIATELY, on EVERY push. Small integrations are easy. Big integrations are painful. CI makes every integration small:

❌ Before CI — "Integration Hell"
  • Developer A works on feature for 2 weeks in isolation
  • Developer B works on different feature for 2 weeks in isolation
  • Integration day: 47 merge conflicts, 12 broken tests, 3 days to fix
  • "It works on my machine" → but not in production
  • Nobody knows whose change broke what
  • Result: Fear of merging. Infrequent, painful releases.
✅ With CI — Continuous Integration
  • Developer pushes small change → CI runs in 7 minutes
  • If it fails: developer knows IMMEDIATELY — their change is the ONLY change
  • If it passes: merged. Next developer's change is built on top of it.
  • Integration happens continuously, not on "integration day"
  • Every commit is tested. Every commit is buildable. Every commit is deployable.
  • Result: Confidence. Speed. No integration surprises.
📊 CI PIPELINE — Complete anihpj Flow
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ⚙️ ANIHPJ CI PIPELINE                               │
│                                                                       │
│  git push (trigger)                                                   │
│       │                                                               │
│  ┌────▼────┐    ┌────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐  │
│  │  LINT   │───▶│  TEST  │───▶│ BUILD + SCAN │───▶│   ARTIFACT   │  │
│  │  ruff   │    │ pytest │    │ Docker build │    │   STORE      │  │
│  │  ~30s   │    │ ~2min  │    │ Trivy scan   │    │              │  │
│  └────┬────┘    └───┬────┘    │ Cosign sign  │    └──────────────┘  │
│       │             │         │   ~4min     │                        │
│       └── FAIL ─────▶ PIPELINE STOPS ◀───── FAIL ──────────────────┘│
│                                                                       │
│  Artifacts produced (stored in GitHub Actions + ECR):                 │
│  🐳 Docker image:  anihpj/jobpost:abc1234 (signed, scanned)          │
│  📋 SBOM:          sbom.spdx.json (Software Bill of Materials)       │
│  ✍️  Signature:     cosign signature (cryptographic proof)            │
│  📊 Test report:    coverage.xml + junit.xml                         │
