│  ✅ ArgoCD detects new image tag → syncs to dev → staging → prod     │
│  ✅ Notary verifies cosign signature before deployment               │
│  ✅ Kyverno checks SBOM for prohibited licenses                      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Why Every Stage is a Gate — The "Stop Early" Philosophy

The CI pipeline is designed to fail fast. Lint runs FIRST because it's the cheapest check (30 seconds) and catches the most common issues (syntax errors, formatting, import order). If lint fails, there's no point running tests for 2 minutes. If tests fail, there's no point building a Docker image for 4 minutes. This ordering saves compute time and gives developers faster feedback:

✅ Well-Ordered Pipeline
  • Lint (30s): Cheap. Catches trivial errors first.
  • Test (2m): Medium cost. Validates logic.
  • Build+Scan (4m): Expensive. Only runs if code is clean.
  • Result: Lint failure = 30s feedback. Not 6.5 minutes.
❌ Poorly Ordered Pipeline
  • Build (4m): Expensive. Runs first.
  • Test (2m): Medium. Runs second.
  • Lint (30s): Cheap. Runs LAST.
  • Result: Typo in import = 6.5 minutes to discover.

Pipeline Debugging — When CI Fails, What Do You Do?

A red ❌ in CI is a puzzle. The CNPA exam tests your ability to diagnose WHY a pipeline failed — is it a code problem, an infrastructure problem, or a pipeline configuration problem? Here's a systematic debugging approach:

1
Read the Logs

Open the failed job. Scroll to the FIRST error. Don't guess — the error message tells you exactly what went wrong. "ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'django'" → missing dependency, not broken code.

2
Reproduce Locally

Run the SAME commands locally. pip install -r requirements.txt && pytest. Fails locally? It's a code issue. Passes locally? It's an environment issue (missing service, wrong Python version, different OS).

3
Check the Diff

What files changed? git diff origin/main. If only docs changed but the build failed → caching issue. If requirements.txt changed → dependency conflict. If Dockerfile changed → build configuration problem.

4
Check Dependencies

Did a new version of a dependency break things? Check if the failure started SUDDENLY (no code changes). Look for: pip installing a newer version than expected. Pin versions: django==5.0.1 not django>=5.0.

5
Isolate & Fix

Comment out stages to isolate the problem. Temporarily skip build to focus on test. Once root cause is found: fix the code/config, push, verify green ✅. If it's a flaky test: quarantine it (mark as xfail) and fix separately.

📖 The CNPA CI Debugging Mindset

When the pipeline is red, ask these questions in ORDER: (1) Did the CODE change? → Read the diff. Most failures are code bugs caught by tests. (2) Did the ENVIRONMENT change? → Check if a new GitHub Actions runner image was deployed. Check if a service (PostgreSQL container) failed to start. (3) Did a DEPENDENCY change? → Check if pip installed a newer version. Check pip freeze output in the logs. (4) Is it a FLAKY test? → Re-run the pipeline. If it passes on retry → flaky test. (5) Is it a PIPELINE BUG? → The pipeline YAML itself has an error (syntax, wrong action version, missing permission). The exam tests your ability to systematically narrow down the cause — not jump to conclusions.

🐙 GitHub Actions YAMLci.yml — anihpj/jobpost Complete CI Pipeline
name: CI — anihpj/jobpost
on:
  push:
    branches: [main, develop]
  pull_request:
    branches: [main]

jobs:
  # ─── STAGE 1: LINT (30s, runs first — cheapest) ───
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-ruff@v1
      - run: ruff check . && ruff format --check .
        # Fails on: unused imports, undefined names, style violations

  # ─── STAGE 2: TEST (2min, depends on lint passing) ───
  test:
    needs: lint          # ← Gate: test ONLY runs if lint passes
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      postgres:
        image: postgres:15
        env: {POSTGRES_PASSWORD: testpass}
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: {python-version: '3.12'}
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest --cov=jobpost --cov-report=xml -v
        env: {DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:testpass@localhost/test}

  # ─── STAGE 3: BUILD + SCAN + SIGN (4min, depends on test passing) ───
  build-scan:
    needs: test           # ← Gate: build ONLY runs if tests pass
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    permissions:
      id-token: write     # Needed for cosign keyless signing
      contents: read
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      # Build Docker image
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          tags: anihpj/jobpost:${{ github.sha }}
          push: true
      # Scan for vulnerabilities (Trivy)
      - uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
        with:
          image-ref: anihpj/jobpost:${{ github.sha }}
          format: sarif
          output: trivy-results.sarif
          severity: CRITICAL,HIGH  # Fail on CRITICAL or HIGH
      # Generate SBOM
      - uses: anchore/sbom-action@v0
        with:
          image: anihpj/jobpost:${{ github.sha }}
      # Sign the image (keyless via OIDC)
      - uses: sigstore/cosign-installer@v3
      - run: cosign sign --yes anihpj/jobpost:${{ github.sha }}

Pipeline as Code — Why Your CI Pipeline Lives in Git

The CI pipeline definition (.github/workflows/ci.yml) is stored IN the repository it builds. This is deliberate — it follows the same "as Code" philosophy as Infrastructure as Code and Policy as Code. The pipeline is versioned alongside the code it tests. When you change how the application is built, you change the pipeline in the same PR:

📜
Pipeline as Code Benefits
  • Version controlled: Who changed the build? Why? When? All in Git history.
  • Reviewed: Pipeline changes go through PR review. No one secretly weakens security checks.
  • Reproducible: Checkout any commit → get the EXACT pipeline that built it. No "it worked in the old Jenkins" mysteries.
  • Branch-aware: Different branches can have different pipelines. Feature branches skip deployment. Main branch deploys.
🔒
Pipeline Security
  • No secrets in pipeline YAML: Use ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK }}, never hardcode tokens.
  • Pin action versions: uses: actions/checkout@v4 (not @main — could be maliciously changed).
  • Limit permissions: GitHub Actions tokens have repo scope by default. Restrict to minimum needed.
  • Review pipeline changes: An attacker who modifies ci.yml can exfiltrate secrets. Treat pipeline YAML as security-critical code.

Common CI Pipeline Anti-Patterns — What NOT to Do

The CNPA exam tests your ability to identify and fix broken CI pipelines. Knowing what NOT to do is just as important as knowing what to do. Here are the most common CI anti-patterns seen in real platforms — and on the exam:

🚫
❌ Slowest Stage First

Running the 4-minute Docker build BEFORE the 30-second lint check. A typo costs 4+ minutes to discover. Fix: cheapest checks always run first.

🚫
❌ No Cache Strategy

Reinstalling all pip/npm dependencies from scratch on every run. Pipeline takes 8 minutes when it could take 2. Fix: implement caching with hash-based keys.

🚫
❌ Hardcoded Secrets

Database passwords, API keys, or tokens embedded directly in ci.yml. Exposed to anyone with repo read access. Fix: use ${{ secrets.* }} for all sensitive values.

🚫
❌ No Branch Protection

CI runs but developers can merge to main even when it fails. CI becomes advisory, not mandatory. Fix: enable "Require status checks" in branch protection rules.

🚫
❌ Flaky Tests Ignored

"Oh, that test fails sometimes. Just re-run the pipeline." Flaky tests erode trust in CI — when the pipeline is red 30% of the time, developers stop looking. Fix: fix or quarantine flaky tests.

🚫
❌ Monolithic Pipeline

One giant job that does lint, test, build, scan, and deploy — serially, in one step. A failure anywhere requires re-running EVERYTHING. Fix: break into independent jobs with needs dependencies.

12.2 CI Pipeline Triggers & Stages

A CI pipeline doesn't run by magic — it responds to events. Understanding what triggers your pipeline and how stages are organized is the difference between a pipeline that gives fast feedback and one that wastes compute and developer patience.

Pipeline Triggers — What Starts the Pipeline?

Trigger EventGitHub ActionsTypical UseLatency
Push to branchon: pushEvery commit triggers CI. Fast feedback on every change.~5-30s
Pull Requeston: pull_requestShows ✅/❌ status checks on PR. Blocks merge on failure.~5-30s
Scheduled (cron)on: schedule: [{cron: "0 2 * * *"}]Nightly full scan (all vulnerability databases refreshed). Security audits.At scheduled time
Manual triggeron: workflow_dispatchEmergency deploy. One-off rebuild. "Deploy to production" button.Immediate (manual)
Tag pushon: push: {tags: ["v*"]}Release event. Build + sign + publish release artifacts.~5-30s

Parallel vs Sequential Stages — Optimizing Pipeline Speed

Stages that don't depend on each other should run IN PARALLEL. Stages that depend on previous output must run SEQUENTIALLY. The anihpj pipeline optimizes this: lint and a security pre-check could run in parallel, but test depends on lint (no point testing broken code), and build depends on test (no point building failing code):

📊 PIPELINE STAGE DEPENDENCIES — Parallel vs Sequential
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    PIPELINE EXECUTION MODEL                            │
│                                                                       │
│  SEQUENTIAL (anihpj pattern — gates enforce quality):                 │
│  ┌────────┐     ┌────────┐     ┌──────────────┐                      │
│  │  LINT  │────▶│  TEST  │────▶│ BUILD + SCAN │                      │
│  │  30s   │     │  2min  │     │    4min      │                      │
│  └────────┘     └────────┘     └──────────────┘                      │
│  Total: ~6.5min. BUT: lint failure = 30s feedback.                   │
│                                                                       │
│  PARALLEL (independent stages — max speed):                           │
│  ┌──────────────┐                                                     │
│  │ LINT (30s)   │──┐                                                  │
│  └──────────────┘  │    ┌──────────────┐                             │
│                    ├───▶│ BUILD + SCAN │                             │
│  ┌──────────────┐  │    │   4min       │                             │
│  │ UNIT TEST    │──┘    └──────────────┘                             │
│  │ (2min)       │                                                     │
│  └──────────────┘                                                     │
│  Total: ~4.5min (lint + test overlap). BUT: lint failure = 4.5min.   │
│                                                                       │
│  💡 CNPA CHOICE: Sequential gates (anihpj) trade 2min for faster     │
│  failure feedback. Parallel trades faster success for slower failure. │
│  For production pipelines, sequential gates are PREFERRED — quality   │
│  gates should stop the pipeline at the earliest failure point.        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Matrix Builds — Test Against Multiple Configurations

What if your Django app needs to work on Python 3.10, 3.11, AND 3.12? A matrix strategy runs the SAME job across multiple configurations in parallel — one job definition, multiple environments. This is how you ensure cross-version compatibility without copy-pasting job definitions:

🐙 GitHub Actions YAMLMatrix Strategy — Test Against Multiple Python Versions
test:
  needs: lint
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  strategy:
    matrix:
      python-version: ['3.10', '3.11', '3.12']
      db: [postgres]        # Could also add: mysql, sqlite
    fail-fast: false        # Don't cancel other jobs if one fails
    max-parallel: 4         # Limit concurrent jobs (API rate limits)

  services:
    postgres:
      image: postgres:15

  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
      with:
        python-version: ${{ matrix.python-version }}
    - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
    - run: pytest --cov=jobpost -v

  # RESULT: 3 parallel jobs run simultaneously:
  # ✅ test (3.10, postgres) — 2min
  # ✅ test (3.11, postgres) — 2min
  # ✅ test (3.12, postgres) — 2min
  # Total: ~2min (parallel), not 6min (sequential)

  # With more combinations (3 Python × 2 DBs = 6 jobs):
  # All 6 run in parallel. Total still ~2min. Matrix = free speed.
💡 When to Use Matrix Builds

Use matrix for: testing multiple language versions (Python 3.10/3.11/3.12), multiple OSes (ubuntu/macos/windows), multiple database backends (PostgreSQL/MySQL/SQLite). Don't use matrix for: different stages of the pipeline (lint→test→build are sequential gates, not matrix variants). Matrix runs the SAME job with different PARAMETERS. Sequential gates run DIFFERENT jobs in order.

Path Filtering — Don't Run CI for Docs-Only Changes

Why run the full lint→test→build pipeline when someone only edits README.md? Path filtering lets you SKIP entire workflows or specific jobs when changed files don't warrant them. This saves compute time and avoids unnecessary pipeline "noise":

🐙 GitHub Actions YAMLPath Filtering — Skip CI for Docs, Run Full for Code
# ─── WORKFLOW-LEVEL PATH FILTERING ───
on:
  push:
    paths:                          # Only trigger if these paths change
      - '**.py'                      # Python files
      - 'requirements.txt'           # Dependencies
      - 'Dockerfile'                 # Container build
      - '.github/workflows/**'       # Pipeline itself
    paths-ignore:                    # NEVER trigger for these
      - '**.md'                      # Documentation
      - 'docs/**'                    # Docs directory
      - 'LICENSE'                    # License file

# ─── JOB-LEVEL CONDITIONAL EXECUTION ───
jobs:
  # Always run — cheap and catches style issues everywhere
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-ruff@v1
      - run: ruff check .

  # Only run full test suite if Python code changed
  test:
    needs: lint
    if: |
      !contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[skip ci]') &&
      !contains(github.event.head_commit.message, '[ci skip]')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pytest --cov=jobpost -v

  # Only build image if pushing to main or a release tag
  build:
    needs: test
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' || startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          tags: anihpj/jobpost:${{ github.sha }}
          push: true

# ─── RESULT ───
# • Push to feature branch (only .py files changed):
#   ✅ lint runs, ✅ test runs, ❌ build SKIPPED (not main)
# • Push to main (README.md changed):
#   ✅ lint runs, ✅ test runs, ✅ build runs
# • Push to main with "[skip ci]" in commit message:
#   ✅ lint runs, ❌ test SKIPPED, ❌ build SKIPPED

Self-Hosted vs GitHub-Hosted Runners — Where Your Pipeline Executes

Every CI job runs on a runner — the machine that executes your pipeline steps. GitHub provides hosted runners (free for public repos, included minutes for private). Self-hosted runners run on YOUR infrastructure. The choice impacts cost, performance, and security:

☁️ GitHub-Hosted Runners
  • Zero maintenance: GitHub manages the OS, updates, and security patches.
  • Fresh environment every run: No state leakage between builds. Clean slate.
  • Predictable specs: ubuntu-latest = 4 vCPU, 16 GB RAM, 150 GB SSD.
  • Free tier: 2,000 minutes/month for private repos. Unlimited for public.
  • Best for: Standard builds. Public repos. Teams that don't want infra overhead.
🏢 Self-Hosted Runners
  • Custom hardware: GPU runners for ML training. ARM64 for Raspberry Pi builds. 64 GB RAM for monorepos.
  • Network access: Access private VPCs, internal registries, on-prem databases.
  • No time limits: GitHub-hosted jobs timeout at 6 hours. Self-hosted = no limit.
  • Cost at scale: 10,000+ minutes/month → self-hosted is cheaper.
  • Best for: Monorepos, ML workloads, private network access, high-volume builds.
⚠️ Self-Hosted Runner Security Risk

Self-hosted runners PERSIST state between jobs. A malicious PR could: (1) Install a backdoor in one job. (2) The backdoor survives to the next job (same machine). (3) Exfiltrate secrets from subsequent jobs. Mitigation: (a) NEVER use self-hosted runners for public repos. (b) Use ephemeral runners (auto-destroyed after each job). (c) Isolate runners per team/project. (d) Regularly rotate runner credentials. GitHub-hosted runners are ephemeral by default — each job gets a fresh VM. This is the CNPA-recommended approach for security.

Reusable Workflows — Don't Copy-Paste Pipeline YAML

When an organization has 20 microservices, each with its own repository, you don't want 20 copies of the same CI pipeline. A reusable workflow is a pipeline template — define ONCE, call from everywhere. Changes to the template automatically apply to all consumers. This is the "DRY" (Don't Repeat Yourself) principle applied to CI:

🐙 GitHub Actions YAMLReusable Workflow — Define Once, Use Everywhere
# ─── FILE: .github/workflows/python-ci.yml (in platform-org/.github repo) ───
# This is the REUSABLE workflow — the template.
name: Python CI (Reusable)
on:
  workflow_call:           # ← Makes this reusable (not triggered directly)
    inputs:
      python-version:
        type: string
        default: '3.12'
    secrets:
      DOCKER_USERNAME:
        required: true

jobs:
  lint:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: astral-sh/setup-ruff@v1
      - run: ruff check .
  test:
    needs: lint
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: {python-version: '${{ inputs.python-version }}'}
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: pytest -v
  build:
    needs: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with: {push: true, tags: anihpj/${{ github.event.repository.name }}:${{ github.sha }}}

# ─── FILE: .github/workflows/ci.yml (in EACH service repo) ───
# Each service just CALLS the reusable workflow.
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  ci:
    uses: anihpj/.github/.github/workflows/python-ci.yml@main  # ← Call template
    with:
      python-version: '3.12'
    secrets:
      DOCKER_USERNAME: ${{ secrets.DOCKER_USERNAME }}
  # That's it! 8 lines. Zero copy-paste. All 20 services use the SAME pipeline.
  # When you update the template, all services get the update automatically.
💡 When to Use Reusable Workflows

Use reusable workflows when: (1) Multiple repos use the same tech stack (Python/Django microservices). (2) You need consistent CI across the organization. (3) A security fix needs to roll out to ALL pipelines immediately. Don't use when: Each service has fundamentally different CI needs (Python backend vs React frontend vs Go CLI). Reusable workflows are for STANDARDIZATION — not for making every pipeline identical. Services with unique needs should have their own workflows.

12.3 CI Pipeline Caching & Artifacts

Without caching, every CI run reinstalls every dependency from scratch — wasting minutes and network bandwidth. Without artifact management, build outputs disappear when the pipeline ends. Caching and artifacts are the pipeline's "memory" — they make pipelines FAST and make outputs AVAILABLE.

Caching — Don't Reinstall the World Every Time

Caching stores dependencies between pipeline runs. The cache key determines when to invalidate the cache (start fresh) vs when to reuse it. A well-designed cache key means 95% of runs use the cache and finish in seconds instead of minutes:

🐍
pip Cache (Python)

Caches ~/.cache/pip. Key: hash of requirements.txt. Only reinstalls when dependencies change. Saves ~2 minutes per build.

🐳
Docker Layer Cache

Each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer. Unchanged layers are REUSED. Key: the Dockerfile instruction itself. COPY requirements.txt only rebuilds if that file changed.

📦
npm/Yarn Cache (Node.js)

Caches node_modules or ~/.npm. Key: hash of package-lock.json. Saves 1-3 minutes per build.

🔑
Cache Key Design

Key = hash of dependency file. Changes only when deps change. Restore-keys: partial match fallback. Never cache secrets or build outputs as cache.

🐙 GitHub Actions YAMLCaching — pip + Docker Layer Example
# ─── PYTHON PIP CACHE ───
- uses: actions/cache@v4
  with:
    path: ~/.cache/pip
    key: pip-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}
    restore-keys: |
      pip-${{ runner.os }}-   # Fallback: any pip cache for this OS
  # Result: pip install reads from cache. Only downloads NEW packages.

# ─── DOCKER LAYER CACHING (buildx) ───
- uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
- uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
  with:
    cache-from: type=gha      # GitHub Actions cache backend
    cache-to: type=gha,mode=max
    # Each Dockerfile layer cached. Only changed layers rebuild.
    # FROM python:3.12 → cached (unchanged)
    # COPY requirements.txt → rebuilt if file changed
    # RUN pip install → cached if requirements.txt unchanged

Docker Layer Caching — How It Actually Works

Docker images are built in LAYERS — each instruction (FROM, COPY, RUN) creates one layer. Layers are cached based on the instruction text AND the context (files being copied). Understanding which layers get invalidated is THE key to fast Docker builds:

📊 DOCKER LAYER CACHE — Which Layers Rebuild When
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              DOCKERFILE LAYER CACHE — anihpj/jobpost                   │
│                                                                       │
│  FROM python:3.12-slim         ← Layer 1: CACHED (image never changes)│
│  WORKDIR /app                  ← Layer 2: CACHED (instruction static) │
│                                                                       │
│  COPY requirements.txt .       ← Layer 3: REBUILDS if .txt changed   │
│  RUN pip install -r reqs.txt   ← Layer 4: REBUILDS if Layer 3 changed │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │ 💡 THE KEY INSIGHT:                                             │ │
│  │ COPY requirements.txt runs BEFORE COPY . (the whole app).       │ │
│  │ This means: pip install is cached UNLESS requirements change.   │ │
│  │ If you did COPY . first → ANY file change invalidates cache.    │ │
│  │ Order matters: copy dependencies FIRST, copy app code LAST.     │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  COPY . /app                   ← Layer 5: REBUILDS on ANY code change│
│  RUN python manage.py collectstatic  ← Layer 6: Usually cached       │
│  CMD ["gunicorn", "..."]       ← Layer 7: CACHED (instruction static)│
│                                                                       │
│  RESULT of a typical push (only app code changed):                    │
│  ✅ Layers 1-4: CACHE HIT (FROM, WORKDIR, pip install all cached)    │
│  🔄 Layer 5: REBUILT (COPY . detected changed files)                │
│  🔄 Layer 6: REBUILT (depends on Layer 5)                           │
│  ✅ Layer 7: CACHE HIT                                             │
│  Total build: ~30s (only 2 layers rebuild, not all 7)               │
│                                                                       │
│  RESULT of a dependency change (requirements.txt changed):            │
│  ✅ Layers 1-2: CACHE HIT                                           │
│  🔄 Layers 3-7: ALL REBUILT (COPY reqs → pip install → COPY app...)│
│  Total build: ~4min (dependency changes are expensive)              │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Dockerfile Optimization for CI — Beyond Layer Caching

Layer caching helps, but the Dockerfile STRUCTURE itself determines whether caching works at all. A poorly structured Dockerfile invalidates the cache on EVERY build — even when nothing meaningful changed. Here are the optimization rules that turn a 4-minute build into a 30-second build:

❌ Bad Dockerfile (Always Rebuilds)
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
# BAD: COPY . copies EVERYTHING first
# Any file change (even README.md)
# invalidates ALL subsequent layers
COPY . /app
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
RUN python manage.py collectstatic
# Result: Change a comment in views.py →
# pip install runs AGAIN. 4 min wasted.
✅ Good Dockerfile (Maximizes Cache)
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
# GOOD: Copy deps FIRST (rarely change)
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install -r requirements.txt
# THEN copy app code (changes often)
COPY . /app
RUN python manage.py collectstatic
# .dockerignore: exclude __pycache__,
# .git, *.md, venv/ — only copy
# what's NEEDED for the build.
# Result: Change views.py → only
# COPY + collectstatic rebuild. 30s.
🐳 Dockerfile.dockerignore — Exclude Files That Invalidate Cache Unnecessarily
# ─── .dockerignore — Essential for Fast CI Builds ───
# Without this file, COPY . sends EVERYTHING to Docker daemon.
# Every gitignore'd file, every venv, every cache = slow build.

# Python
__pycache__/
*.pyc
*.pyo
*.egg-info/
dist/
build/
.venv/
venv/

# Git
.git/
.gitignore
.gitattributes

# Docs & Config (don't affect the build)
README.md
docs/
*.md
docker-compose.yml

# CI/CD (don't belong in the image)
.github/
.circleci/

# Tests (run in CI, not in the image — unless needed for smoke tests)
tests/
*.test.py

# RESULT: COPY . now copies ~50 files instead of ~500.
# Build context is smaller → docker build is faster.
# Layer cache is more effective (fewer spurious changes).

Artifacts — What the Pipeline Produces

Artifacts are the pipeline's OUTPUT — the things it creates that other systems consume. A CI pipeline that builds and throws away its outputs is useless. Artifacts must be STORED, VERSIONED, and ACCESSIBLE to downstream systems (CD pipelines, security scanners, developer workstations):

ArtifactFormatStored WhereConsumed By
Docker ImageOCI image (layers)ECR / Docker Hub / GHCRK8s (pull on deploy), ArgoCD, developers
SBOMSPDX / CycloneDX JSONGitHub artifact storeKyverno (policy check), security audit, compliance
Container SignatureCosign signature (in registry)OCI registry (alongside image)Kyverno / Notary (verify before deploy)
Test ReportJUnit XML / coverage.xmlGitHub artifact storeCodecov, SonarQube, developer review
Vulnerability ReportSARIF / Trivy JSONGitHub Security tabSecurity team, compliance audit
Helm Chart.tgz packageOCI registry / Chart MuseumArgoCD, Helm CLI, Flux
📖 Artifact vs Cache — Don't Confuse Them

Cache: Temporary. Can be evicted anytime. Used to SPEED UP builds (pip cache, Docker layers). Cache miss = slower build but still works. Artifact: Permanent (within retention policy). The OUTPUT of the pipeline. Uploaded explicitly. Artifact loss = pipeline run was wasted. CNPA Rule: Cache dependencies, upload artifacts. Never use artifacts as cache. Never rely on cache for pipeline correctness.

Environment Variables & Secrets — How Data Flows Through the Pipeline

CI pipelines need configuration: database URLs for tests, registry credentials for pushing images, API tokens for notifications. Understanding how these values flow — and where they SHOULDN'T appear — is essential for pipeline security:

📊 SECRETS & ENV FLOW — GitHub Actions Security Model
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              SECRETS & ENVIRONMENT VARIABLES FLOW                      │
│                                                                       │
│  SOURCES (where values come from):                                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  🔒 GitHub Secrets     🌐 Workflow ENV     📋 Job ENV           │ │
│  │  Settings → Secrets    env: at workflow   env: at job level     │ │
│  │  ${{ secrets.X }}      level              DB_URL: postgres://   │ │
│  │  Encrypted at rest     visible in YAML    visible in YAML       │ │
│  └───────────────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                  │                                    │
│                                  ▼                                    │
│  HOW VALUES REACH THE JOB:                                           │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  secrets:                    env:                                │ │
│  │  DOCKER_USERNAME: ${{ sec...  DATABASE_URL: postgresql://...    │ │
│  │  ↓                            ↓                                  │ │
│  │  Available as:               Available as:                      │ │
│  │  $DOCKER_USERNAME            $DATABASE_URL                      │ │
│  │  (echo: *** hidden)          (echo: visible in logs!)           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  ⚠️  SECURITY RULES:                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  ✅ DO:                      ❌ DON'T:                           │ │
│  │  • Use ${{ secrets.X }}     • Hardcode passwords in YAML       │ │
│  │    for ALL sensitive data    • echo $SECRET (leaks to logs)     │ │
│  │  • Use env: for non-        • Pass secrets to untrusted        │ │
│  │    sensitive config          third-party actions                │ │
│  │  • Limit GITHUB_TOKEN       • Store secrets in artifacts       │ │
│  │    permissions per job      • Use secrets in if: conditions    │ │
│  │  • Use Environments for     • Share secrets across repos       │ │
│  │    production secrets        without proper review              │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  ANIHPJ EXAMPLE:                                                      │
│  • DATABASE_URL: env (non-sensitive — test DB only)                  │
│  • DOCKER_USERNAME/PASSWORD: secrets (registry credentials)          │
│  • SLACK_WEBHOOK: secrets (could spam if leaked)                     │
│  • AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID: secrets (cloud credentials — HIGH impact)      │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

12.4 CI Notifications & Git Integration

A CI pipeline that runs silently is a pipeline nobody knows about. Notifications tell the team what happened. Git integration makes pipeline status VISIBLE where developers already work — in pull requests and on the main branch. Together, they close the feedback loop.

Notification Channels — Where Pipeline Status Appears

💬
Slack / Teams Notifications

"❌ Build #1247 failed — anihpj-api tests (main)" or "✅ Deploy #312 to production succeeded." Posted to #platform or #deployments channel. Team sees failures without opening GitHub.

🐙
GitHub Status Checks

Every PR shows ✅ green check or ❌ red X next to each pipeline stage. Required checks BLOCK merge until they pass. Developers see pipeline status without leaving the PR page.

📧
Email (Last Resort)

Only for critical failures on main branch. "Production CI is broken — all deploys blocked." NOT for every PR failure (that's what status checks are for).

🪝
Webhooks

HTTP POST to external systems on pipeline events. ArgoCD webhook triggers sync. PagerDuty creates incident. Monitoring records deploy event for correlation.

🐙 GitHub Actions YAMLSlack Notification — Alert on Failure
# ─── SLACK NOTIFICATION (runs regardless of success/failure) ───
notify:
  needs: [lint, test, build-scan]
  if: always()  # Run even if previous jobs failed
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - name: Notify Slack on Failure
      if: failure()
      uses: slackapi/slack-github-action@v2
      with:
        webhook: ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK }}
        webhook-type: incoming-webhook
        payload: |
          {
            "text": "❌ *anihpj/jobpost* CI FAILED\n
            Branch: `${{ github.ref_name }}`\n
            Commit: `${{ github.sha }}`\n
            Author: ${{ github.actor }}\n
            Run: <${{ github.server_url }}/${{ github.repository }}/actions/runs/${{ github.run_id }}|View Logs>"
          }

    - name: Notify Slack on Success (main only)
      if: success() && github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
      uses: slackapi/slack-github-action@v2
      with:
        webhook: ${{ secrets.SLACK_WEBHOOK }}
        webhook-type: incoming-webhook
        payload: |
          {"text": "✅ *anihpj/jobpost* CI passed on main\n
          Image: `anihpj/jobpost:${{ github.sha }}`"}

Git Integration — Branch Protection and Status Checks

Git integration closes the loop between CI and the development workflow. Status checks are the mechanism: CI sets a status (success/failure/pending) on each commit. Branch protection rules REQUIRE certain statuses to pass before merge. This is how "CI must pass" becomes a non-negotiable rule:

📊 GIT INTEGRATION FLOW — PR → CI → Status Check → Merge
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    GIT + CI INTEGRATION                                │
│                                                                       │
│  1. Developer opens PR: feature/add-job-filter → main                 │
│       │                                                               │
│  2. GitHub triggers CI workflow (on: pull_request)                   │
│       │                                                               │
│  3. CI runs: lint → test → build-scan                                │
│       │                                                               │
│  4. CI reports status to GitHub via API:                              │
│       ✅ "lint / lint — Success"                                      │
│       ✅ "test / test (3.12) — Success"                               │
│       ✅ "build-scan / build-scan — Success"                          │
│       │                                                               │
│  5. GitHub PR shows: All checks have passed ✅                        │
│       │                                                               │
│  6. Branch protection rule: "Require status checks to pass"          │
│       → lint, test, build-scan must all be ✅                         │
│       → Merge button is GREEN (enabled)                               │
│       │                                                               │
│  7. Developer clicks Merge → code enters main                        │
│       │                                                               │
│  WHAT IF CI FAILS?                                                    │
│  ❌ "test / test — Failure"                                           │
│  → PR shows red X                                                      │
│  → Merge button is GREY (disabled)                                    │
│  → Developer MUST fix tests before merge                             │
│                                                                       │
│  This is the "CI as gatekeeper" pattern. Git enforces it.            │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Pipeline Status Badges — Building Trust Through Visibility

A green badge on the README says: "This code builds. This code is tested. You can trust it." Status badges are the public face of CI — they make pipeline status visible OUTSIDE the CI system. A red badge is a warning. A green badge is confidence:

🟢
README Badge

[![CI](https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost/actions/workflows/ci.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/anihpj/jobpost/actions) — Shows live pipeline status on the repo's README. First thing visitors see. Green = project is maintained and working.

📊
Dashboard Badge

Embed pipeline status in Backstage, Confluence, or internal dashboards. "Is the platform CI passing right now?" — answered at a glance without opening GitHub.

🔴
Red Badge Psychology

A red badge should be RARE and URGENT. If the badge is red for days, it becomes wallpaper — ignored. The team must have a culture of "red badge = drop everything and fix."

🤝
Trust Through Transparency

Status badges build trust between teams. "Can I depend on their API?" → Check their CI badge. Green = they test their code. Red = proceed with caution. Badges are lightweight SLAs.

Pipeline Metrics — Measuring Your CI Pipeline's Health

A CI pipeline is itself a system that should be measured. If the pipeline is slow or flaky, developers lose trust and start bypassing it. Track these metrics to keep your pipeline healthy:

⏱️
Pipeline Duration

Median time from push to all checks passing. Target: < 10 minutes. If duration creeps up → investigate: slower tests? larger Docker images? cache misses?

📊
Success Rate

% of pipeline runs that pass all stages. Target: > 80%. Low success rate = flaky tests, unstable environment, or developers pushing broken code.

⚡
Time-to-Feedback

Time from push to FIRST failure (if any). Target: < 2 minutes. This is WHY cheap checks run first. Measures how fast developers learn something is wrong.

🔄
Cache Hit Rate

% of cache restore attempts that succeed. Target: > 90%. Low cache hits = wasted compute and slower pipelines. Check cache key design.

💡 Make Pipeline Metrics Visible

Build a simple Grafana dashboard showing pipeline duration trend (line chart), success rate (gauge), and time-to-feedback (bar chart). When developers complain "CI is slow," look at the data — is it actually slower, or does it just FEEL slower? Pipeline metrics turn subjective complaints into objective data for improvement.

12.5 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

CD Q1 of 10
What is the primary purpose of ordering CI pipeline stages from cheapest to most expensive?
A) To make the pipeline YAML file easier to read
B) Fail-fast: cheap checks run first so failures are caught quickly. Lint (30s) → Test (2min) → Build (4min). A lint failure gives feedback in 30 seconds, not 6.5 minutes. This saves compute time and developer waiting time.
C) To reduce Docker image size
D) To satisfy regulatory compliance requirements
✅ B — Fail-fast: cheap gates first for faster feedback

The CI pipeline is ordered by cost: lint (30s, cheapest) → test (2min, medium) → build+scan (4min, most expensive). If lint catches an unused import, the developer gets feedback in 30 seconds instead of waiting 6.5 minutes for the full pipeline. Each stage is a GATE — if it fails, everything after it is skipped. This is the "stop early" philosophy that makes CI pipelines efficient.

CD Q2 of 10
Which GitHub Actions event should trigger a CI pipeline that runs on every commit to any branch?
A) on: workflow_dispatch (manual trigger only)
B) on: schedule with cron (runs at fixed times, not on push)
C) on: push (triggers on every git push to any branch). Combined with on: pull_request for PR status checks. This is the standard CI trigger pattern.
D) on: release (only triggers on GitHub Release creation)
✅ C — on: push triggers on every commit

The standard CI trigger pattern: (1) on: push → runs CI on every commit to any branch. Developers get immediate feedback. (2) on: pull_request → runs CI when a PR is opened or updated. Status checks appear on the PR. (3) on: schedule → nightly full scans. (4) on: workflow_dispatch → manual trigger for one-off operations. The combination of push + pull_request covers the full development workflow.

CD Q3 of 10
Why use `needs: [lint]` in a GitHub Actions job definition?
A) It creates a DEPENDENCY: the test job only runs if the lint job succeeds. This implements the "gate" pattern — don't waste compute on tests if the code doesn't even pass lint. Without needs, all jobs run in parallel regardless of failures.
B) It makes the job run faster
C) It gives the job higher priority in the queue
D) It's required by GitHub for all jobs
✅ A — needs creates job dependencies (gates)

needs: [lint] means "this job only runs after lint completes successfully." If lint fails, the dependent job is SKIPPED — not failed, just never started. This implements the gate pattern: each stage is a prerequisite for the next. Without needs, all jobs run in parallel (faster but wasteful — why run 4-minute builds on code that fails 30-second lint?). The anihpj pipeline: test needs lint, build needs test.

CD Q4 of 10
What is the difference between a CI pipeline cache and a CI artifact?
A) They are the same thing — interchangeable terms
B) Cache is permanent; artifacts are temporary
C) Artifacts are only for Docker images
D) Cache = temporary speed boost (pip cache, Docker layers). Can be evicted anytime. Cache miss = slower build but pipeline still works. Artifact = permanent pipeline OUTPUT (Docker image, SBOM, test report). Stored explicitly. Artifact loss = wasted pipeline run.
✅ D — Cache = speed (evictable). Artifact = output (must survive).

Cache: stores dependencies between runs for speed. Key = hash of dependency file. Can be evicted by the CI system at any time. Cache miss = slower build but still works. Artifact: the pipeline's output — Docker images, SBOMs, signatures, test reports. Explicitly uploaded with retention policies. Downstream systems (CD, security scanners) depend on artifacts. Never confuse the two: don't store artifacts in cache, don't rely on cache for correctness.

CD Q5 of 10
What does a good cache key look like for Python pip dependencies?
A) A random string — any cache is better than no cache
B) pip-${{ runner.os }}-${{ hashFiles('requirements.txt') }}. The key includes: (1) cache type (pip), (2) OS (different OS = different packages), (3) hash of requirements.txt (changes only when deps change). With restore-keys fallback for partial matches.
C) The current date — ensures fresh cache daily
D) The branch name — different branches get different caches
✅ B — Type + OS + hash(deps) with restore-keys fallback

A good cache key: (1) Prefix identifies the cache type (pip, npm, docker). (2) OS included because compiled packages differ (Linux vs macOS). (3) Hash of the dependency file (requirements.txt, package-lock.json) — key changes ONLY when deps change. (4) restore-keys provides a fallback: if the exact key doesn't match, use the most recent cache for that prefix. This means: exact match = perfect cache. Partial match = use cache from slightly different deps (pip install will update what changed). No match = full reinstall.

CD Q6 of 10
anihpj's CI pipeline takes 8 minutes. The lint stage takes 30 seconds. How would you restructure it for faster failure feedback?
A) Remove the lint stage — it's too fast to matter
B) Run all stages in parallel to reduce total time
C) Keep lint FIRST (30s). If lint fails, SKIP test and build — total time for failure = 30s, not 8min. The pipeline is already properly ordered. The goal is faster FAILURE feedback, not faster SUCCESS time. Most pipelines succeed — but when they fail, every second of waiting is frustration.
D) Move lint to run after the build for better accuracy
✅ C — Lint first, skip rest on failure. Already optimized.

The pipeline is already correctly ordered: cheapest check (lint, 30s) runs first. If lint catches an issue, the developer gets feedback in 30 seconds — not 8 minutes. Parallelizing all stages would make successes ~4.5 minutes BUT failures would also take ~4.5 minutes (because you'd discover the lint error after the build finished). Sequential gates optimize for the FAILURE case — because fast failure feedback is more valuable than slightly faster success. Developer time waiting for failures is the metric to optimize.

CD Q7 of 10
What is an SBOM and why does the CI pipeline produce one?
A) Software Bill of Materials — a machine-readable list of EVERY dependency, library, and component in your container image. The CI pipeline generates it so that: (1) Security scanners can check for known vulnerabilities in specific versions. (2) Compliance audits can verify license compliance. (3) Supply chain attacks can be traced ("was log4j 2.14 in our image?"). Required by executive orders and frameworks like SLSA.
B) Source Build Output Manifest — a log of the build process
C) Secure Binary Output Module — an encrypted version of the image
D) System Backup Operations Manual — disaster recovery documentation
✅ A — SBOM = machine-readable list of all dependencies

An SBOM (Software Bill of Materials) answers: "What's IN this container image?" It lists every package (Django 5.0.1, psycopg2 2.9.9, Python 3.12.1) with versions, licenses, and suppliers. Formats: SPDX or CycloneDX (JSON). Generated by tools like Syft, Trivy, or anchore/sbom-action. The CNPA relevance: Kyverno can verify SBOMs at admission time (block deployment if prohibited licenses found). SBOM + vulnerability scan = complete supply chain security picture. Without an SBOM, you don't know what's in your images — and you can't assess risk when new CVEs are announced.

CD Q8 of 10
How do GitHub branch protection rules enforce CI as a gatekeeper?
A) Branch protection rules are optional — anyone can merge regardless
B) They slow down the merge process without adding security
C) They only protect against force pushes, not CI failures
D) "Require status checks to pass before merging" — the CI jobs (lint, test, build-scan) must ALL report ✅ success. If any check is ❌ failure, the Merge button is DISABLED. Developers CANNOT merge broken code. CI status becomes a non-negotiable gate enforced by GitHub itself.
✅ D — Required status checks disable merge on CI failure

Branch protection rules make CI enforcement automatic: (1) Configure "Require status checks to pass" on the main branch. (2) Select specific checks: "lint", "test", "build-scan". (3) Now: any PR to main must have ALL selected checks green. If CI fails → Merge button greyed out. If CI hasn't run yet → Merge button shows "Waiting for status checks." This removes human judgment from the equation — the machine enforces the policy. It's the "CI as gatekeeper" pattern made concrete.

CD Q9 of 10
Why sign container images with Cosign in the CI pipeline?
A) Signing compresses the image for faster downloads
B) Cryptographic proof that THIS image was built by OUR CI pipeline and hasn't been tampered with. Kyverno/Notary verifies the signature before deployment — rejecting unsigned or modified images. This prevents supply chain attacks where an attacker replaces your image with a malicious one.
C) Signing encrypts the image contents for security
D) Signing is only required for open-source projects
✅ B — Cryptographic proof of origin + integrity

Cosign (Sigstore project) signs container images using OIDC-based keyless signing: (1) CI pipeline authenticates via OIDC to Sigstore's Fulcio CA. (2) Fulcio issues a short-lived certificate tied to the GitHub repository and workflow. (3) Cosign signs the image digest with this certificate. (4) The signature is stored in the OCI registry alongside the image. Verification: Kyverno checks the signature before allowing deployment. If the signature is missing or invalid (image was replaced or modified after build), deployment is BLOCKED. This is SLSA Level 2 compliance — proof that the image came from your trusted CI pipeline.

CD Q10 of 10
anihpj wants to add a nightly security scan that runs even if nobody pushes code. How?
A) Add a pre-commit hook that runs the scan locally
B) Require developers to manually run the scan daily
C) Add a scheduled workflow: on: schedule: [{cron: "0 2 * * *"}]. This runs the pipeline at 2 AM UTC every day, pulling the latest vulnerability databases. Separate from the push-triggered pipeline — different trigger, same quality gates.
D) Run the scan as part of the Docker build every time
✅ C — Scheduled workflow with cron trigger

Scheduled CI pipelines run on a timer, not on code changes. Use case: vulnerability databases update daily — an image that was "clean" yesterday might have NEW known vulnerabilities today. A nightly scan with `on: schedule: [{cron: "0 2 * * *"}]` rebuilds the SBOM and re-scans with the latest database. If new CRITICAL vulnerabilities are found, the pipeline fails and alerts the team. This is defense-in-depth: push-triggered CI catches issues in new code; scheduled CI catches issues in existing images as new vulnerabilities are discovered. Both are needed for a complete security posture.

📊 Chapter 12 Summary — Key Takeaways

⚙️CI PipelinePush → Lint → Test → Build+Scan → Artifacts. Each stage a GATE. Fail-fast ordering.
🔀TriggersPush, PR, schedule, manual, tag. Different triggers for different purposes.
⚡Cachingpip cache, Docker layers. Hash-based keys. Cache = speed, not correctness.
📦ArtifactsImage, SBOM, signature, test report. Pipeline OUTPUT. Must survive.
💬NotificationsSlack on failure. Status checks on PR. Branch protection enforces CI.
✍️SigningCosign keyless signing. Proves origin + integrity. SLSA Level 2.

Chapter 13: Incident Response in Platform Engineering

No platform is perfect. Services crash, databases fill up, certificates expire, and cloud regions fail. Incident Response is the structured process for detecting, responding to, resolving, and learning from these failures. A mature platform doesn't just prevent incidents — it handles them gracefully, recovers quickly, and gets BETTER after each one. This chapter covers the full incident lifecycle: detection through Prometheus alerts, triage through PagerDuty, resolution through runbooks, and continuous improvement through blameless postmortems — all applied to the anihpj platform.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~1.5 hours🚨 Incidents🎯 Domain 3: 16%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ Incident Response Lifecycle — Detect → Respond → Resolve → Learn. Structured failure handling
  • ✅ Incident Management — Severity levels (P1-P4), triage, mitigation, resolution. Who does what when
  • ✅ Alerting & Monitoring — Prometheus Alertmanager routing, silencing, inhibition. Alert on symptoms not causes
  • ✅ Runbooks & Postmortems — Step-by-step recovery guides. Blameless culture. Action items that get done
  • ✅ Incident Metrics — MTTR, MTBF, MTTD, MTTA. Measuring what makes your platform reliable
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Continuous Delivery 16% Foundation for Observability (Ch 7-8) Foundation for Measuring (Ch 25-26)

13.1 What is Incident Response? — Detect → Respond → Resolve → Learn

Incident Response is a structured process — not a panic. When an alert fires, every person involved knows exactly what to do, who to call, and how to escalate. The process has four phases: Detect (monitoring identifies a problem), Respond (on-call engineer acknowledges and triages), Resolve (fix the root cause and restore service), and Learn (blameless postmortem drives system improvements).

For the anihpj platform: Prometheus detects that the jobpost-api error rate has spiked above 5% → Alertmanager routes the alert to PagerDuty → PagerDuty pages the on-call platform engineer → Engineer acknowledges within 5 minutes, diagnoses within 10, resolves within 15 → Within 24 hours, a blameless postmortem is written with concrete action items.

📊 INCIDENT RESPONSE LIFECYCLE — The Four Phases
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                  🚨 INCIDENT RESPONSE LIFECYCLE                        │
│                                                                       │
│  🔔 DETECT              🏃 RESPOND             🔧 RESOLVE            │
│  ┌──────────────┐     ┌──────────────┐       ┌──────────────┐       │
│  │ Prometheus   │────▶│ PagerDuty    │──────▶│ Engineer     │       │
│  │ Alert Fires  │     │ Pages On-Call│       │ Fixes Issue  │       │
│  │              │     │              │       │              │       │
│  │ "error_rate  │     │ "CRITICAL:   │       │ • Rollback   │       │
│  │  > 5% for   │     │  anihpj-api  │       │ • Scale up   │       │
│  │  5 minutes"  │     │  error rate  │       │ • Restart    │       │
│  │              │     │  spiking"    │       │ • Failover   │       │
│  └──────────────┘     └──────────────┘       └──────┬───────┘       │
│                                                     │                │
│  📝 LEARN (Blameless Postmortem — within 24 hours)  │                │
│  ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────▼────────────┐  │
│  │  • Timeline:    14:32 Alert → 14:35 Ack → 14:38 ID → 14:47   │  │
│  │  • Root Cause:  v2.4.1 N+1 query → DB pool exhaustion        │  │
│  │  • Impact:      3% of users saw 500 errors (15 min duration)  │  │
│  │  • Resolution:  Rolled back to v2.4.0 via ArgoCD             │  │
│  │  • Action:      Add query review to CI (@alice, by Friday)   │  │
│  │                 NO BLAME — focus on system improvement.       │  │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
│                                                                       │

Why Platform Incidents Are Different

Platform teams own SHARED infrastructure that ALL developer teams depend on. When the CI pipeline is down, EVERY team is blocked. This makes platform incidents higher-stakes than individual service incidents:

📢
Communicate Widely

Platform incidents affect ALL teams. Post to #platform-status immediately. Update every 15 minutes. "We know. We're on it." Silence breeds frustration and shadow IT.

⚡
Recovery First, Root Cause Later

During the incident: RESTORE SERVICE. Figure out WHY afterwards. A 15-minute outage with a perfect postmortem is worse than a 5-minute outage with a rough one.

🔄
Automate Recovery

ArgoCD rollback, K8s self-healing, Crossplane drift correction should auto-resolve common failures. Fewer incidents needing human intervention = more reliable platform.

📝
Document Everything

Every incident → postmortem → action items → owner + deadline. Platform reliability = sum of completed action items. Track them like bugs — they ARE bugs in the platform.

13.2 Incident Management Lifecycle — From Alert to Resolution

Every incident follows the same lifecycle. Standardizing this lifecycle means every engineer — regardless of experience — knows what to do when an alert fires. No guessing. No panic. Just follow the process:

1
DETECT

Alert fires. Prometheus Alertmanager evaluates rules every 15s. When a condition is true for the configured duration, the alert fires.

2
TRIAGE

On-call acknowledges within 5 min. Assess severity (P1-P4). Is this a real incident or a false alarm? Who needs to be involved?

3
MITIGATE

Stop the bleeding. Rollback. Scale up. Failover. The goal is NOT to fix the root cause — it's to restore service NOW. Root cause comes later.

4
RESOLVE

Fix the root cause. Deploy the fix. Verify monitoring is green. Close the incident. Service is restored AND the underlying issue is addressed.

5
LEARN

Postmortem within 24 hours. Timeline. Root cause. Impact. Action items with owner + deadline. No blame — focus on system improvement.

Severity Levels — How Urgent Is This?

Not all incidents are equal. Severity levels determine WHO responds, HOW they're notified, and HOW FAST they must act. Standardizing severity prevents "everything is critical" alert fatigue:

LevelNameDefinitionResponseNotification
P1CriticalPlatform is DOWN. All deploys blocked. Users affected.Immediate (all hands). Resolve within 15 min.PagerDuty (wake up). Escalate after 5 min no ack.
P2MajorMajor feature broken. Degraded performance. One tenant affected.Within 30 min. Dedicated engineer.PagerDuty (during business hours). Slack #incidents.
P3MinorNon-critical feature broken. Workaround exists. Low impact.Within 4 hours (business hours).Slack #platform-alerts. Email to team.
P4CosmeticVisual glitch. Typo. Documentation error. No user impact.Next sprint. Backlog.Jira ticket. No immediate notification.
⚠️ The "Everything is P1" Anti-Pattern

If every alert is P1, then NO alert is P1. Alert fatigue kills incident response. When engineers are woken up at 3am for a P4 cosmetic issue, they learn to ignore pages. Standardize severity definitions. Enforce them. A P1 means: "Users are affected RIGHT NOW and service is degraded." Everything else is P2 or lower. The CNPA exam tests your ability to classify incidents correctly — not everything is an emergency.

On-Call Rotations — Always Someone Responsible

An incident at 3am needs a human to respond. But that human shouldn't be the same person every night. On-call rotations distribute the burden fairly and ensure there's ALWAYS someone responsible — no "I thought YOU were on call" confusion:

🔄
Weekly Rotation

One engineer is primary on-call for 7 days. Secondary as backup. Most common pattern. Predictable: "I'm on call next week." Handoff happens Monday morning with a brief sync.

🌍
Follow-the-Sun

Teams in multiple time zones share on-call. APAC team handles daytime. EU team handles daytime. US team handles daytime. Nobody works nights. Requires 3+ regional teams.

📋
Escalation Policy

Primary doesn't ack in 5 min → Secondary gets paged. Secondary doesn't ack in 5 min → Manager gets paged. This ensures incidents NEVER go unanswered, even if the primary slept through their phone.

💰
Compensation

On-call is WORK. Pay engineers for being available (stipend) AND for being paged (per-incident pay). Unpaid on-call leads to burnout and resentment. The CNPA recognizes on-call as a platform responsibility that must be funded.

Incident Command System — Who Does What During a Major Incident

For P1 incidents affecting the entire platform, a single engineer can't handle everything. The Incident Command System (borrowed from firefighting) assigns clear ROLES so everyone knows their responsibility. This prevents the "everyone is diagnosing, nobody is communicating" chaos:

Incident Communication — What to Say and When

During a platform incident, communication is as important as technical response. Developers are blocked, managers are nervous, and silence breeds panic. A structured communication cadence keeps everyone informed without distracting the resolver:

💬 SlackIncident Communication Templates — anihpj Platform
# ─── INCIDENT DECLARATION (posted immediately) ───
🚨 INCIDENT: anihpj-api returning 500 errors
Severity: P1 (Critical)
Status: INVESTIGATING
On-call: @bob (primary), @alice (secondary)
Channel: #incident-2024-0315 (join for real-time updates)

What we know:
• Alert fired at 14:32 UTC: "HighErrorRate > 5% for 5 minutes"
• ~3% of users affected. Deploys are NOT blocked.
• Investigating now. Next update in 15 minutes.

# ─── STATUS UPDATE (every 15 minutes) ───
🔄 UPDATE (14:47 UTC): Still investigating
• Narrowed down to v2.4.1 deployment at 14:23
• DB connection pool shows exhaustion
• Considering rollback to v2.4.0
• No ETA yet. Next update in 15 minutes.

# ─── RESOLUTION (when service is restored) ───
✅ RESOLVED (15:02 UTC): Service restored
• Duration: 30 minutes (14:32 → 15:02)
• Root cause: v2.4.1 introduced N+1 query
• Resolution: Rolled back to v2.4.0 via ArgoCD
• Impact: 3% of users saw errors. 4,200 failed requests.
• Postmortem: Will be published within 24 hours in #platform-postmortems
• Thank you for your patience. 🙏

# ─── KEY RULES ───
# 1. Post the FIRST update within 2 minutes of alert.
# 2. Update every 15 minutes — even if the update is "still investigating."
# 3. "No update" is the worst update. Silence = "nobody is working on this."
# 4. Always include: what we know, what we're doing, when the next update comes.
# 5. After resolution: thank the team. Incidents are stressful. Gratitude matters.

13.3 Alerting & Monitoring for Incidents

Monitoring tells you something is wrong. Alerting tells the RIGHT person, through the RIGHT channel, at the RIGHT time. A perfectly configured monitoring stack with badly configured alerts is worthless — you'll either miss real incidents or drown in false alarms.

Prometheus Alertmanager — Intelligent Alert Routing

Alertmanager sits between Prometheus (which fires alerts) and the notification channels (PagerDuty, Slack, Email). It handles: routing (which alert goes where), grouping (combine similar alerts into one notification), inhibition (suppress dependent alerts when the root cause is already firing), and silencing (temporarily mute alerts during maintenance):

📊 ALERTMANAGER — Intelligent Alert Routing Architecture
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    🔔 ALERTMANAGER ROUTING                             │
│                                                                       │
│  Prometheus Alert Fires (multiple alerts may fire simultaneously)     │
│       │                                                               │
│  ┌────▼──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐  │
│  │                      ALERTMANAGER                               │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │  ROUTING (based on severity label):                             │  │
│  │  ┌────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │  │
│  │  │  P1 (severity=critical) ──▶ PagerDuty (wake on-call)      │ │  │
│  │  │  P2 (severity=warning)  ──▶ Slack #platform-alerts         │ │  │
│  │  │  P3 (severity=info)     ──▶ Email daily digest             │ │  │
│  │  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │  GROUPING: Multiple alerts for the SAME incident → ONE page.    │  │
│  │  "anihpj-api down" + "anihpj-api latency high" +                │  │
│  │  "anihpj-api error rate" → GROUPED into ONE PagerDuty alert.    │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │  INHIBITION: Dependent alerts SUPPRESSED when root fires.       │  │
│  │  "K8sNodeDown" fires → SUPPRESS "PodNotReady" for pods          │  │
│  │  on that node. Don't page for pods when the node IS the issue.  │  │
│  │                                                                  │  │
│  │  SILENCING: Maintenance window? Silence alerts temporarily.     │  │
│  │  "Database migration 2-3 AM Saturday" → silence DB alerts.      │  │
│  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Alerting on Symptoms, Not Causes

The golden rule of alerting: alert on SYMPTOMS (what users experience), not CAUSES (what broke internally). A user doesn't care that a pod crashed — they care that the API is slow. Alert on the API latency. Let the dashboard show the pod crash as context for diagnosis:

❌ Alerting on Causes
  • "Pod anihpj-api-7f8g9 has restarted 3 times"
  • "K8s node i-abc123 CPU > 90%"
  • "PostgreSQL replication lag > 2 seconds"
  • "Redis memory usage > 80%"
  • Problem: These are INTERNAL details. Users don't experience them directly. Generates noise. Engineers get paged for transient blips that self-resolve.
✅ Alerting on Symptoms
  • "API p95 latency > 500ms for 5 minutes"
  • "API error rate > 5% for 5 minutes"
  • "Job posting endpoint returning 500 errors"
  • "User login success rate < 95%"
  • Benefit: These are USER-VISIBLE symptoms. Every alert means "users are affected." No alert means "users are fine" — even if pods restarted internally.

anihpj Alert Rules — Concrete PromQL Examples

Prometheus alert rules define WHAT triggers an alert. They combine a PromQL expression (the condition) with a duration (how long it must persist) and labels (severity, routing). These are the actual rules that protect the anihpj platform:

🔥 PromQLPrometheus Alert Rules — anihpj Production Alerts
# ─── PROMETHEUS ALERT RULES (alerts.yml) ───
groups:
  - name: anihpj-platform
    rules:
      # P1 — CRITICAL: API is failing for users
      - alert: HighErrorRate
        expr: |
          rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5.."}[5m])
          / rate(http_requests_total[5m]) > 0.05
        for: 5m  # Must persist for 5 minutes (not a momentary spike)
        labels:
          severity: critical
          component: api
        annotations:
          summary: "anihpj-api error rate > 5%"
          description: "Error rate is {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} over the last 5 minutes. Check Grafana dashboard: anihpj-api Health."

      # P1 — CRITICAL: API is slow for users
      - alert: HighLatency
        expr: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket[5m])
          ) > 1.0
        for: 5m
        labels:
          severity: critical
          component: api
        annotations:
          summary: "anihpj-api p95 latency > 1 second"
          description: "p95 latency is {{ $value }}s. DB pool might be exhausted. Check connection count."

      # P2 — WARNING: Database connections approaching limit
      - alert: DBConnectionPoolHigh
        expr: |
          pg_stat_database_numbackends{datname="anihpj"}
          / pg_settings_max_connections > 0.90
        for: 10m
        labels:
          severity: warning
          component: database
        annotations:
          summary: "PostgreSQL connections > 90% of max"
          description: "{{ $value | humanizePercentage }} of connections used. If it reaches 100%, new connections will be rejected."

      # P3 — INFO: Disk filling up (non-urgent)
      - alert: DiskSpaceLow
        expr: |
          (node_filesystem_avail_bytes{mountpoint="/"}
          / node_filesystem_size_bytes) < 0.20
        for: 30m
        labels:
          severity: info
        annotations:
          summary: "Disk space < 20% on {{ $labels.instance }}"
          description: "Only {{ $value | humanizePercentage }} disk remaining. Auto-create Jira ticket."

# KEY PATTERNS IN THESE RULES:
# • rate(...[5m]) — averages over 5 minutes (smooths spikes)
# • for: 5m — alert only fires if condition persists (prevents flapping)
# • severity label — determines routing (P1→PagerDuty, P2→Slack, P3→Email)
# • annotations — human-readable context for the on-call engineer
🔥 PromQLAlertmanager Configuration — anihpj Alert Routing
# ─── ALERTMANAGER CONFIG (alertmanager.yml) ───
route:
  group_by: ['alertname', 'cluster']   # Group similar alerts
  group_wait: 30s                       # Wait 30s for more alerts in group
  group_interval: 5m                    # Send group updates every 5 min
  repeat_interval: 4h                   # Re-send if still firing after 4h
  receiver: 'slack-platform'            # Default receiver
  routes:
    - match:
        severity: critical              # P1 alerts
      receiver: 'pagerduty-oncall'
      continue: true                    # Also send to Slack
    - match:
        severity: warning               # P2 alerts
      receiver: 'slack-platform'
    - match:
        severity: info                  # P3 alerts
      receiver: 'email-digest'

receivers:
  - name: 'pagerduty-oncall'
    pagerduty_configs:
      - routing_key: 'abc123...'
        severity: critical
        description: '{{ .CommonAnnotations.description }}'

  - name: 'slack-platform'
    slack_configs:
      - api_url: 'https://hooks.slack.com/...'
        channel: '#platform-alerts'
        title: '🚨 {{ .GroupLabels.alertname }}'
        text: '{{ .CommonAnnotations.description }}'

  - name: 'email-digest'
    email_configs:
      - to: 'platform-team@anihpj.io'
        send_resolved: true

# ─── INHIBITION RULES ───
inhibit_rules:
  - source_match:
      alertname: 'K8sNodeDown'
    target_match:
      alertname: 'PodNotReady'
    # If NodeDown fires, don't ALSO page for PodNotReady on that node.
    equal: ['node']

Alert Fatigue Prevention — Keeping Alerts Meaningful

Alert fatigue is the #1 killer of effective incident response. When engineers receive 50 alerts a day — 48 of which are false alarms or self-resolving — they stop paying attention. Then a REAL incident fires... and nobody notices. Preventing alert fatigue is a platform engineering responsibility:

❌ Causes of Alert Fatigue
  • Too-low thresholds: "CPU > 70% for 1 minute" — spikes are normal. Pages for every transient blip.
  • No duration: Alert fires immediately on threshold breach. A 30-second CPU spike triggers a page.
  • Alerting on causes: "Pod restarted" — but the service was healthy (other pods handled traffic). False alarm.
  • No silencing: Maintenance window triggers 20 alerts. Engineers learn to ignore ALL alerts during maintenance.
  • Un-actionable alerts: "Disk will be full in 7 days" — create a Jira ticket, don't page someone at 3am.
✅ Preventing Alert Fatigue
  • Appropriate thresholds: "Error rate > 5% for 5 minutes" — must be sustained, not a blip.
  • Required duration: for: 5m in Prometheus rules. Alert only fires if condition persists.
  • Alert on symptoms: "API returning 500 errors" not "Pod restarted." Every alert = user impact.
  • Silence during maintenance: Alertmanager silence for planned work. Zero alerts during known-good downtime.
  • Ticket non-urgent issues: Disk at 80%? Auto-create Jira. Don't page. Page at 95% with 30min projection.
📖 The CNPA Alert Design Rule

Every alert must pass this test: "If this alert fires at 3am, will the on-call engineer: (a) Immediately get out of bed and start investigating, or (b) Mute it and go back to sleep?" If the answer is (b), it should NOT be a page. It should be a Slack message, an email, or a Jira ticket. Pages are for "users are affected RIGHT NOW." Everything else is a notification. The CNPA exam tests your ability to distinguish between page-worthy alerts and notification-worthy alerts.

13.4 Runbooks, Playbooks & Blameless Postmortems

When an incident fires at 3am, the on-call engineer should NOT be figuring out what to do. A runbook is a step-by-step guide for common incidents. A postmortem is the document that ensures the incident never happens again. Together, they form the platform's institutional memory.

Playbooks vs Runbooks — What's the Difference?

The blueprint mentions both terms. They're related but serve different purposes. The CNPA exam expects you to know the distinction:

📋 Runbook (Tactical)
  • Scope: ONE specific alert. "PostgreSQLDown → do these 5 steps."
  • Audience: On-call engineer during an active incident.
  • Content: Exact commands. Copy-paste. No thinking required.
  • Example: "Step 1: kubectl get pods. Step 2: kubectl logs. Step 3: kubectl delete pod."
  • Goal: Reduce MTTR. Follow instructions, don't improvise.
📖 Playbook (Strategic)
  • Scope: An entire INCIDENT CLASS. "How we handle ANY database incident."
  • Audience: Team leads, incident commanders, new team members.
  • Content: Roles, communication plan, escalation path, decision framework.
  • Example: "DB incidents: IC = on-call engineer. Comms = post to #platform-status every 15min. Escalate to DBA team if >30min."
  • Goal: Ensure the RIGHT PROCESS is followed for the incident CLASS.

Runbooks — What to Do When the Alert Fires

A good runbook answers: "The alert is firing. Now what?" It should be so clear that a sleep-deprived engineer at 3am can follow it without thinking. Every alert should have a corresponding runbook:

📋 MarkdownRunbook — anihpj-db is Down (Example)
# Runbook: anihpj-db is Down
**Alert:** `PostgreSQLDown` (Prometheus Alertmanager)
**Severity:** P1 (Critical — all deploys and API calls blocked)
**Owner:** Platform Team (on-call rotation)

## Step 1: Verify the Incident (2 min)
- [ ] Open Grafana dashboard: "anihpj-db Health"
- [ ] Check: Is the DB actually down or is monitoring broken?
- [ ] Run: `kubectl get pods -l app=anihpj-db -n production`
- [ ] If pods are Running but health check fails → go to Step 2
- [ ] If pods are CrashLoopBackOff → go to Step 3
- [ ] If PVC is full → go to Step 4

## Step 2: Pods Running but Unhealthy (5 min)
- [ ] `kubectl logs -l app=anihpj-db --tail=100`
- [ ] Check for: "too many connections", "disk full", "replication lag"
- [ ] If "too many connections": `kubectl scale deploy anihpj-api --replicas=2` (reduce load)
- [ ] If still unhealthy: restart primary `kubectl delete pod anihpj-db-0`

## Step 3: CrashLoopBackOff (5 min)
- [ ] `kubectl describe pod anihpj-db-0 | tail -30`
- [ ] Check Events for OOMKilled (increase memory limit) or Liveness probe failure
- [ ] If OOMKilled: `kubectl patch statefulset anihpj-db -p '{"spec":{"template":{"spec":{"containers":[{"name":"postgres","resources":{"limits":{"memory":"4Gi"}}}]}}}}'`

## Step 4: PVC Full (10 min)
- [ ] `kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -- df -h /var/lib/postgresql/data`
- [ ] If > 90%: Expand PVC `kubectl patch pvc data-anihpj-db-0 -p '{"spec":{"resources":{"requests":{"storage":"50Gi"}}}}'`
- [ ] If PVC can't expand: Delete old WAL logs `pg_archivecleanup`

## Step 5: If All Else Fails — Restore from Backup (15 min)
- [ ] `velero restore create --from-backup anihpj-db-daily --wait`
- [ ] Verify restore: `kubectl exec anihpj-db-0 -- psql -c "SELECT count(*) FROM jobpost_job;"`
- [ ] Update DNS if needed: `kubectl apply -f service-update.yaml`

## Post-Resolution
- [ ] Update #platform-status: "✅ anihpj-db restored. RCA pending."
- [ ] Create postmortem document within 24 hours
- [ ] Update this runbook if anything was missing or wrong

Blameless Postmortems — Learning Without Blame

A postmortem is NOT about finding who to blame. It's about finding what in the SYSTEM allowed the failure — and fixing that system so it never happens again. The CNPA philosophy: "The question is not 'Who caused this?' but 'How did our system ALLOW this to happen, and how do we prevent it?'":

📊 BLAMELESS POSTMORTEM — Structure & Philosophy
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              📝 BLAMELESS POSTMORTEM TEMPLATE                          │
│                                                                       │
│  INCIDENT SUMMARY                                                     │
│  • Date/Time:  2024-03-15 14:32 UTC                                  │
│  • Duration:   15 minutes (14:32 → 14:47)                            │
│  • Severity:   P1 — anihpj-api returning 500 errors                  │
│  • Impact:     3% of users affected. 2,400 failed requests.          │
│  • Detected:   Prometheus alert "HighErrorRate" fired at 14:32       │
│                                                                       │
│  TIMELINE (key events in order)                                       │
│  14:23  v2.4.1 deployed to production via ArgoCD                     │
│  14:30  DB connection pool utilization spikes to 100%                │
│  14:32  Prometheus alert fires: error_rate > 5%                      │
│  14:33  PagerDuty pages on-call (@bob)                               │
│  14:35  @bob acknowledges, opens incident                            │
│  14:38  @bob identifies v2.4.1 as cause (new N+1 query)             │
│  14:40  @bob rolls back to v2.4.0 via ArgoCD UI                     │
│  14:45  Error rate returns to normal                                 │
│  14:47  Incident resolved. Monitoring green.                         │
│                                                                       │
│  ROOT CAUSE ANALYSIS (5 Whys)                                         │
│  1. Why did the API return 500 errors? — DB pool exhausted.          │
│  2. Why was the pool exhausted? — v2.4.1 added N+1 query.            │
│  3. Why did the N+1 query pass review? — No query review in CI.      │
│  4. Why was there no query review? — Not part of PR checklist.       │
│  5. Why wasn't it in the checklist? — Never defined as a requirement.│
│  → ROOT CAUSE: No automated query review in CI pipeline.             │
│                                                                       │
│  ACTION ITEMS (OWNER + DEADLINE — no blame, just fix)                 │
│  ✅ #1 Add Django-querycount to CI (@alice, Mar 22)                  │
│  ✅ #2 Block PRs with >50% query increase (@bob, Mar 22)             │
│  ✅ #3 Add DB pool utilization alert at 70% warning (@carol, Mar 29) │
│  ✅ #4 Runbook: update "DB Pool Exhausted" section (@bob, Mar 20)    │
│                                                                       │
│  PRINCIPLE: No names in the "why" section. Focus on SYSTEM fixes.     │
│  "Bob deployed bad code" → WRONG. "CI allowed bad code" → RIGHT.     │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Postmortem Action Item Tracking — Closing the Loop

A postmortem without completed action items is a postmortem that failed. The most common failure mode: action items are written, assigned, and... forgotten. The postmortem process must include a TRACKING mechanism that ensures items get done:

1
Create Tickets

Each action item from the postmortem becomes a Jira/GitHub issue. Link back to the postmortem. Priority = P2 (not P1 — these are improvements, not emergencies).

2
Assign Owner + Deadline

Every action item has ONE owner. Not "the platform team" — a specific person. Deadline is within 2 weeks for P2 items. "By Friday" is not a deadline — "March 22" is.

3
Weekly Review

Platform team standup includes: "Postmortem action items status." Open items are reviewed. Blocked items are escalated. Nothing slips through cracks.

4
Postmortem Follow-up

30 days after the incident: review the postmortem. Are all action items COMPLETE? If not, WHY? If yes, has the failure class been prevented? Close the loop formally.

📖 The Action Item Completion Rate Metric

Track what percentage of postmortem action items are completed within their deadline. Target: >90%. If completion rate drops below 70%, your postmortem process is broken — you're identifying fixes but not implementing them. This is worse than not doing postmortems at all, because it creates the ILLUSION of improvement without the reality. The CNPA exam expects you to understand that postmortems without action item tracking are performative — they feel good but don't improve reliability.

13.5 Incident Metrics — MTTR, MTBF, and Beyond

"You can't improve what you don't measure." Incident metrics turn subjective "the platform feels unreliable" into objective data that drives improvement. The four key incident metrics form a pipeline from failure to recovery:

│  │            (Mean Time         │                                     │

│                                                                       │
│  │◀────────────────── MTTA ─────────────────────▶│                     │
