MetricAbbreviationDefinitionanihpj Target
Mean Time to DetectMTTDTime from issue START to alert FIRING. Measures monitoring effectiveness.< 1 minute
Mean Time to AcknowledgeMTTATime from alert FIRING to human ACKNOWLEDGING. Measures on-call readiness.< 5 minutes
Mean Time to RecoverMTTRTime from alert FIRING to service RESTORED. The most important incident metric.< 15 minutes
Mean Time Between FailuresMTBFAverage time BETWEEN incidents. Measures overall platform reliability.> 30 days

How the Platform Reduces Each Metric

🔍
Reduce MTTD

Better monitoring: Prometheus scrapes every 15s (not every 5 min). Alert on symptoms (user-facing). Set appropriate thresholds and durations to avoid false positives that cause alert fatigue.

📱
Reduce MTTA

PagerDuty mobile app with loud notification. Escalation policies: if primary doesn't ack in 5 min → secondary gets paged. Clear on-call rotation — always someone responsible.

⚡
Reduce MTTR

Automated rollback (ArgoCD one-click). AIOps correlation (identifies root cause in seconds). Runbooks with exact commands. Pre-scripted recovery for common failures.

🛡️
Increase MTBF

Postmortem action items actually get done. Progressive delivery (canary → small blast radius). Policy as code (Kyverno blocks known-bad patterns). Automated testing catches issues before production.

📖 MTTR Is THE Metric — Here's Why

MTTR (Mean Time to Recover) is the most important incident metric because it directly measures USER IMPACT. MTTD and MTTA are internal — users don't care how fast you detected the issue, they care how fast you FIXED it. A platform with 1-minute MTTD and 30-minute MTTR is worse than a platform with 10-minute MTTD and 5-minute MTTR. The CNPA exam prioritizes MTTR for this reason. Focus platform improvements on recovery speed: automated rollback, AIOps correlation, runbook automation. Every second of MTTR reduction is a second users aren't experiencing an outage.

Fire Drills & Chaos Engineering — Practice Makes Perfect

You don't want the FIRST time your team handles a database failure to be at 3am in production. Fire drills are SIMULATED incidents — the team practices responding to a realistic scenario in a safe environment. Chaos engineering takes this further: intentionally inject failures into production to verify the system handles them gracefully:

🔥 Fire Drills (Practice)
  • Simulated incident: "The anihpj-db primary has failed. Respond."
  • Safe environment: Staging cluster. No users affected.
  • Measured: Time from alert to recovery. Compare to MTTR target.
  • Debrief: What went well? What was confusing? Update runbooks.
  • Frequency: Monthly. Rotate scenarios (DB failure, network partition, cert expiry).
🌪️ Chaos Engineering (Verify)
  • Real failure: Terminate a random pod in production. Does the system self-heal?
  • Controlled blast radius: Start small (one pod). Expand gradually.
  • Hypothesis-driven: "If we kill the primary DB, the replica should promote within 30s."
  • Abort condition: If users ARE affected, stop immediately.
  • Tools: Chaos Mesh, LitmusChaos, Gremlin. K8s-native chaos engineering.
💡 The CNPA Fire Drill Pattern

1. Pick a scenario from a PAST postmortem (it already happened once — it could happen again). 2. Schedule a 1-hour fire drill. 3. One person is the "simulator" (injects the failure). The rest are responders. 4. Run the drill. Measure MTTR. 5. Debrief: What went well? What was slow? Update runbooks. 6. Repeat monthly with different scenarios. After 6 months, your team has practiced the top 6 failure modes. MTTR in real incidents drops dramatically because response is practiced, not improvised.

Error Budgets — How Many Failures Are "Acceptable"?

Platforms don't aim for 100% uptime — that's impossible and counterproductive (you'd never deploy anything). An Error Budget is the amount of "acceptable" downtime or errors before action must be taken. It bridges incident metrics (MTTR) with business decisions (should we pause deployments to improve reliability?):

📊 ERROR BUDGET — From SLO to Action
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    💰 ERROR BUDGET CONCEPT                              │
│                                                                       │
│  SLO (Service Level Objective): "99.9% uptime per month"              │
│       │                                                               │
│       ▼                                                               │
│  ERROR BUDGET = 100% - SLO = 0.1% of the month                        │
│              = 43 minutes of acceptable downtime per month            │
│       │                                                               │
│       ▼                                                               │
│  HOW IT'S USED:                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Week 1: 0 min downtime     → Budget: 43 min remaining  ✅      │ │
│  │  Week 2: 5 min downtime     → Budget: 38 min remaining  ✅      │ │
│  │  Week 3: 15 min downtime    → Budget: 23 min remaining  ⚠️      │ │
│  │  Week 4: 0 min downtime     → Budget: 23 min remaining  ✅      │ │
│  │  Monthly total: 20 min      → SLO MET (within 43 min budget)   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  BUDGET BURN RATE — When to Take Action:                              │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Normal burn: Using <50% of monthly budget → keep deploying   │ │
│  │  • Elevated burn: >50% in first week → INVESTIGATE              │ │
│  │  • Budget exhausted: 100% used → FREEZE DEPLOYMENTS             │ │
│  │    Focus ALL engineering time on reliability improvements.      │ │
│  │  • The error budget gives you a DATA-DRIVEN reason to pause     │ │
│  │    feature work and fix reliability — not a gut feeling.        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  CNPA INSIGHT: Error budgets are the bridge between incident metrics  │
│  (MTTR) and business decisions (deploy vs. fix). They turn             │
│  "we should probably make things more reliable" into "we've used      │
│  80% of our error budget — NO MORE DEPLOYS until we fix this."        │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Alert Storm Management — When Everything Fires at Once

An alert storm happens when a single root cause (e.g., network partition, cloud region failure) triggers dozens of alerts simultaneously. The on-call engineer's phone becomes a brick of notifications. Managing alert storms is a critical platform skill:

🌪️
What Causes Alert Storms
  • Network partition: All cross-AZ communication fails → 50+ alerts
  • Cloud region outage: AWS us-east-1 down → everything in that region fails
  • K8s control plane failure: All controllers stop → cascading alerts
  • DNS failure: Service discovery breaks → every service appears "down"
🛡️
How to Manage Alert Storms
  • Inhibition rules: NodeDown suppresses PodNotReady. One root alert, not 50.
  • Alert grouping: Alertmanager groups by alertname. One Slack message, not 50.
  • Dependency mapping: Know which services depend on which. Focus on the ROOT.
  • Status dashboard: ONE page showing overall platform health. Don't triage alerts individually.
⚠️ Alert Storm Protocol

When your phone has 50 PagerDuty notifications: (1) DON'T try to acknowledge each one. (2) Open the platform status dashboard. (3) Identify the ROOT cause (usually ONE thing — network, cloud, control plane). (4) Acknowledge the ROOT alert. (5) Verify inhibition rules are suppressing dependents. If not, manually silence dependent alerts. (6) Fix the root cause. All dependent alerts will auto-resolve. The key insight: in an alert storm, 49 of 50 alerts are CONSEQUENCES, not causes. Focus on the ONE root alert.

13.6 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

CD Q1 of 10
What are the four phases of the Incident Response lifecycle?
A) Plan → Build → Test → Deploy
B) Alert → Panic → Google → Fix
C) Detect → Respond → Resolve → Learn. Every incident follows this structured lifecycle: monitoring detects, on-call responds, engineer resolves, postmortem drives learning.
D) Monitor → Log → Trace → Debug
✅ C — Detect → Respond → Resolve → Learn

The four phases: (1) DETECT: Prometheus alert fires. (2) RESPOND: On-call acknowledges and triages. (3) RESOLVE: Fix root cause and restore service. (4) LEARN: Blameless postmortem with action items. This structured lifecycle removes panic from incidents — everyone knows their role and the process.

CD Q2 of 10
During an active P1 incident, what should the on-call engineer prioritize FIRST?
A) Finding the root cause and documenting it thoroughly
B) RESTORING SERVICE. Mitigate first (rollback, scale up, failover). Root cause analysis comes AFTER users are no longer affected. A 15-minute outage with a rough postmortem is better than a 45-minute outage with a perfect one.
C) Notifying all stakeholders before taking any action
D) Writing the postmortem while the incident is fresh
✅ B — Restore service FIRST. Root cause comes AFTER.

The priority during an incident: (1) Mitigate — stop the bleeding (rollback, failover, scale). (2) Resolve — fix the root cause. (3) Learn — postmortem. Users don't care WHY the service is broken — they care that it's fixed. A quick rollback that restores service in 2 minutes is BETTER than spending 20 minutes understanding the root cause while users suffer. MTTR is the metric that matters during an incident.

CD Q3 of 10
What is the difference between alerting on symptoms vs alerting on causes?
A) Symptoms = what USERS experience (API latency > 500ms, error rate > 5%). Causes = internal details (pod restarted, CPU > 90%). Alert on SYMPTOMS — every alert means "users are affected." Alerting on causes generates noise (pod restarted but service still healthy → unnecessary page).
B) There is no difference — they mean the same thing
C) Causes are more important — always alert on the root issue
D) Symptoms are for developers; causes are for operations
✅ A — Symptoms = user-visible. Causes = internal details. Alert on symptoms.

The golden rule: alert on what users EXPERIENCE, not what broke internally. "API error rate > 5%" → users ARE getting errors. "Pod restarted 3 times" → users might be fine (no errors if other pods covered). Alerting on causes creates noise and alert fatigue. The internal details (pod restart, CPU spike) go on dashboards for diagnosis — not into alerts that wake people up.

CD Q4 of 10
What is Alertmanager inhibition and why is it important?
A) It permanently disables alerts for maintenance windows
B) It speeds up alert delivery to PagerDuty
C) It combines multiple alerts into a single notification
D) Inhibition SUPPRESSES dependent alerts when the ROOT CAUSE alert is already firing. Example: "K8sNodeDown" fires → suppress "PodNotReady" for pods on that node. Without inhibition, one node failure generates 20 alerts (1 node down + 19 pods not ready). With inhibition: ONE page.
✅ D — Suppress dependent alerts when root cause is already firing

Inhibition prevents alert storms. When a K8s node goes down, ALL pods on that node become "NotReady." Without inhibition: 1 NodeDown alert + 19 PodNotReady alerts = 20 PagerDuty pages. The on-call engineer is flooded. With inhibition: only the NodeDown alert fires. The PodNotReady alerts are suppressed because they're CONSEQUENCES of the node failure, not independent issues. Alertmanager inhibition rules: source_match (root alert) → target_match (dependent alerts to suppress).

CD Q5 of 10
What makes a postmortem "blameless"?
A) It doesn't mention any names or teams involved
B) It focuses on SYSTEM improvements, not individual fault. Instead of "Bob deployed bad code," it asks "Why did our CI pipeline ALLOW bad code to reach production?" Action items fix the SYSTEM (add query review to CI), not the person (don't let Bob deploy). The goal is to prevent the CLASS of failure from recurring — not to punish the individual.
C) It assigns blame equally to everyone involved
D) It's written by someone not involved in the incident
✅ B — Focus on SYSTEM fixes, not individual fault

Blameless postmortems follow a simple rule: "The question is not 'Who caused this?' but 'How did our system ALLOW this to happen, and how do we prevent it?'" If Bob deployed bad code, the postmortem doesn't say "Bob made a mistake." It asks: "Why didn't CI catch this? Why didn't code review catch this? Why didn't canary deployment catch this?" The answer is always a SYSTEM gap — missing checks, missing automation, missing processes. Fixing the system prevents the ENTIRE CLASS of failure (anyone could deploy bad code). Blaming Bob fixes nothing — next time, Alice might make the same mistake.

CD Q6 of 10
What is a runbook and when should it be used?
A) A step-by-step guide for responding to a SPECIFIC alert. When "PostgreSQLDown" fires, the runbook says: Step 1: verify, Step 2: check logs, Step 3: restart, Step 4: restore from backup. Runbooks remove guesswork from incident response — the on-call engineer follows instructions, not intuition.
B) A document describing the platform architecture
C) A script that automatically fixes all incidents
D) A log of all past incidents for reference
✅ A — Step-by-step guide for a specific alert. Follow, don't improvise.

A runbook is the operational manual for an alert. It answers: "The alert is firing. Now what?" A good runbook: (1) Is specific to ONE alert type. (2) Has numbered steps in order. (3) Includes exact commands (copy-paste, not type-from-memory). (4) Has escalation paths ("If Step 3 doesn't work → call the DBA"). (5) Is tested regularly (fire drills). Runbooks transform incident response from "figure it out" to "follow the instructions" — which is faster, more reliable, and less stressful at 3am.

CD Q7 of 10
A P1 incident is declared. The CI pipeline goes down. Who should be notified and how?
A) No notification needed — just fix it quietly
B) Email the platform team and wait for a response
C) PagerDuty pages the on-call engineer IMMEDIATELY. Post to #platform-status: "🚨 CI pipeline down. On-call responding. Updates every 15 min." Escalate if no ack in 5 min. Platform incidents affect ALL teams — communicate widely and frequently.
D) File a Jira ticket for the next sprint
✅ C — Immediate PagerDuty page + public status update. Communicate widely.

Platform incidents have a LARGE blast radius. When CI is down, EVERY team is blocked from deploying. Communication protocol: (1) PagerDuty pages on-call (immediate). (2) Post to #platform-status with incident declaration. (3) Update every 15 minutes — even if the update is "still investigating." (4) Escalate if no acknowledgment in 5 minutes. (5) When resolved: "✅ CI pipeline restored. Postmortem within 24h." Silence during a platform incident breeds frustration. Visibility builds trust — even when things are broken.

CD Q8 of 10
What is the difference between MTTR, MTTD, and MTBF?
A) They all measure the same thing — incident frequency
B) MTTR = detection time. MTTD = recovery time. MTBF = failure rate.
C) They are only relevant for hardware failures, not software
D) MTTD = issue start → alert fires (detection speed). MTTR = alert fires → service restored (recovery speed — MOST important). MTBF = average time between incidents (reliability). Together they measure: how fast you notice, how fast you fix, and how often things break.
✅ D — MTTD = detect. MTTR = recover. MTBF = reliability between failures.

The incident metric pipeline: MTTD (Mean Time to Detect) = how fast monitoring catches issues. Target: < 1 min. MTTA (Mean Time to Acknowledge) = how fast humans respond. Target: < 5 min. MTTR (Mean Time to Recover) = how fast service is restored — the most important metric. Target: < 15 min. MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) = how often incidents occur. Target: > 30 days. These four metrics answer: "How good is our monitoring? How ready is our team? How fast do we recover? How reliable is our platform?"

CD Q9 of 10
How does ArgoCD help reduce MTTR during platform incidents?
A) ArgoCD automatically writes postmortems
B) One-click ROLLBACK: ArgoCD syncs from Git. A bad deployment = a bad Git commit. Rolling back = syncing to the PREVIOUS commit. ArgoCD shows the diff, one click reverts. No kubectl commands. No manual YAML editing. Recovery in seconds, not minutes.
C) ArgoCD sends alerts when deployments fail
D) ArgoCD prevents all incidents from happening
✅ B — One-click rollback to previous Git commit. Recovery in seconds.

ArgoCD as incident response tool: When a bad deployment causes an incident, ArgoCD shows the deployment history. The engineer identifies the last HEALTHY commit. Clicks "Rollback." ArgoCD syncs the cluster to that commit. K8s rolling update restores the previous version. Recovery time: < 2 minutes (mostly K8s pod startup time). Without ArgoCD: engineer must find the old manifest, run kubectl commands, update multiple resources — 10+ minutes. GitOps = fast rollback = low MTTR.

CD Q10 of 10
anihpj wants to reduce MTTR from 30 minutes to under 10 minutes. What changes should they make?
A) (1) Automated rollback via ArgoCD (no manual kubectl). (2) AIOps correlation for faster diagnosis (identify root cause in seconds). (3) Runbooks with exact copy-paste commands for top 5 incidents. (4) Pre-scripted recovery for common failures. (5) Fire drills to practice — speed comes from practice, not theory.
B) Hire more on-call engineers to respond faster
C) Add more monitoring dashboards for better visibility
D) Increase alert thresholds so fewer incidents trigger
✅ A — Automate recovery. Speed diagnosis. Pre-script fixes. Practice regularly.

MTTR reduction is a platform engineering problem: (1) Automate recovery — ArgoCD rollback, Crossplane drift correction, K8s self-healing. Fewer incidents need human intervention. (2) Speed diagnosis — AIOps correlation, unified dashboards, standardized logging. The slowest part of incident response is FIGURING OUT what's wrong. (3) Pre-script recovery — runbooks with copy-paste commands. Don't make engineers type commands from memory at 3am. (4) Practice — fire drills. Run simulated incidents. Measure MTTR. Improve. Adding more engineers doesn't reduce MTTR significantly (coordination overhead). Better tooling and automation does.

📊 Chapter 13 Summary — Key Takeaways

🚨LifecycleDetect → Respond → Resolve → Learn. Structured, not panicked.
📊SeverityP1 (critical) to P4 (cosmetic). Not everything is an emergency.
🔔AlertmanagerRoute, group, inhibit, silence. Alert on symptoms, not causes.
📋RunbooksStep-by-step per alert. Copy-paste commands. No guessing at 3am.
📝PostmortemsBlameless. System fixes. Action items with owner + deadline.
⏱️MTTRTHE metric. Recovery speed = user impact. Target: < 15 minutes.

Chapter 14: CI/CD & Deployment Strategies

CI builds it. CD ships it. This chapter draws the bright line between Continuous Integration and Continuous Delivery — where one ends and the other begins — and explores the deployment strategies that determine HOW your code reaches users. From rolling updates (the K8s default) to blue/green (instant rollback) to canary (gradual traffic shift) to feature flags (decoupling deploy from release), each strategy trades speed, safety, and complexity differently. Understanding these tradeoffs is the core of CNPA deployment design. Every example uses the anihpj/jobpost application deployed through ArgoCD.

🟡 Intermediate⏱️ ~2 hours🚀 CD🎯 Domain 3: 16%

🎯 What You'll Learn

  • ✅ CI vs CD — Where the build pipeline ends and the deployment pipeline begins. The artifact is the handoff
  • ✅ Delivery vs Deployment — Manual approval gate vs fully automated. When to use which
  • ✅ Deployment Strategies — Rolling, Blue/Green, Canary, A/B Testing. Tradeoffs for each
  • ✅ Feature Flags — Decouple deploy from release. Deploy hidden code, enable gradually
  • ✅ Deployment Automation Tools — ArgoCD, Flux, Spinnaker, Harness. CNPA tool selection
🎓 CNPA Relevance
Continuous Delivery 16% Foundation for GitOps (Ch 15-16) Foundation for Progressive Delivery (Ch 15)

14.1 What is Continuous Delivery (CD)? — Always Deployable

Continuous Delivery means your software is ALWAYS in a deployable state. Every merge to main produces a tested, scanned, signed artifact that COULD go to production. The decision to actually deploy becomes a business decision — not a technical one. CD doesn't mean "deploy everything automatically." It means "everything COULD be deployed automatically." The actual deploy may require a manual approval — but the technical work is done.

For anihpj: every merge to main triggers CI (lint → test → build → scan → sign). The resulting Docker image is deployed to staging automatically. The platform team verifies staging (smoke tests, metrics check). When ready, they click "Promote to Production" in ArgoCD or Slack. Production deployment takes 2 minutes because the artifact is already built, tested, and staged. This is Continuous Delivery: the pipeline is automated; the business decision to release is manual.

📊 CONTINUOUS DELIVERY PIPELINE — CI → Staging → Production
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    🚀 CONTINUOUS DELIVERY — anihpj Flow                │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌─────────────────── CI (automated) ───────────────────┐            │
│  │  Push → Lint → Test → Build → Scan → Sign → Artifact │            │
│  └──────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┘            │

│  ┌──────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────┐            │
│  │              CD — CONTINUOUS DELIVERY                 │            │
│  │                                                       │            │
│  │  ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────────┐    ┌──────────┐│            │
│  │  │ Deploy to    │───▶│  Automated   │───▶│ MANUAL   ││            │
│  │  │ STAGING      │    │  Smoke Tests │    │ APPROVAL ││            │
│  │  │ (automatic)  │    │  + Metrics   │    │  GATE    ││            │

│  │                                               │✅     │            │

CD Maturity Model — Where Does Your Platform Stand?

Not all CD is created equal. The CD Maturity Model defines four stages of deployment automation — from manual deploys with downtime to fully automated canary deployments. Understanding where your platform sits on this spectrum tells you what to improve next:

Level 1
Manual Deploy

SSH to server. git pull. Restart. Downtime between deploys. No rollback.

❌ Pre-CD
Level 2
Scripted Deploy

Shell scripts or Ansible. Some automation. Still manual trigger. Inconsistent.

🟡 Basic
Level 3
Continuous Delivery

Automated pipeline. Rolling updates. Manual prod approval. Fast rollback.

🟢 anihpj
Level 4
Continuous Deployment

Fully automated to prod. Canary + auto-rollback. Zero human gates.

✅ Elite
💡 The CNPA Maturity Insight

Most organizations should target Level 3 (Continuous Delivery). Level 4 (Continuous Deployment) requires exceptional test coverage, canary deployments, automated rollback, and a culture that accepts occasional production failures as the price of speed. anihpj operates at Level 3 with manual production approval — this is the CNPA-recommended target for business-critical platforms. The exam won't ask you to achieve Level 4 — it asks you to understand the tradeoffs at each level and choose appropriately for the business context.

📖 The CD Golden Rule: Build Once, Deploy Many

The same Docker image that passed tests in CI is deployed to staging, then production. You do NOT rebuild between environments. Rebuilding introduces risk: different dependency versions, different timestamps, different build environment. The artifact is IMMUTABLE. The only thing that changes between environments is CONFIGURATION (environment variables, feature flags, resource limits) — never the artifact itself. This is why CD pipelines promote artifacts, not rebuild code.

Deployment Verification — How Do You Know the Deploy Is Healthy?

Deploying is not the same as delivering value. After the pods are running, you must VERIFY that the new version is actually working correctly. Deployment verification combines automated checks with human judgment to answer: "Is this deployment healthy, or should we roll back?":

🏥
Health Checks (Automatic)

K8s liveness/readiness probes. Pod is "Ready" only when it passes HTTP health check. If probe fails → pod removed from Service. ArgoCD marks Application "Healthy" or "Degraded."

📊
Metrics Comparison (Automatic)

Compare error rate, latency, and throughput BEFORE vs AFTER deploy. If error rate triples → deployment is suspect. Argo Rollouts does this automatically via AnalysisTemplate.

🧪
Smoke Tests (Automatic)

Run a quick automated test against the NEW deployment: "Can users log in? Can they create a job post? Does the homepage load?" If smoke tests fail → deployment is broken regardless of what K8s probes say.

👁️
Human Verification (Manual)

For major releases: a human checks key flows manually. "Does the new dashboard render correctly? Does the API return the new field?" This is the "approval gate" in Continuous Delivery.

💡 The Verification Pipeline

Layer verification in order of speed: (1) Health checks (seconds — K8s probes). (2) Smoke tests (1-2 minutes). (3) Metrics comparison (5-10 minutes — need enough data). (4) Human verification (2-5 minutes — major releases only). If ANY layer fails → stop the deployment. Don't proceed to the next environment. This is how CD pipelines catch problems BEFORE they affect all users.

14.2 CI vs CD — Where One Ends, the Other Begins

CI and CD are often confused. The boundary is clear: CI ends with a tested artifact. CD begins with that artifact and delivers it to users. CI answers "is this code good?" CD answers "is this code in production?" The artifact — the Docker image, the SBOM, the signature — is the handoff between the two worlds:

📊 CI vs CD — THE BOUNDARY
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    ⚡ CI vs CD — THE BOUNDARY                           │
│                                                                       │
│  ┌────────────────────── CI (Continuous Integration) ──────────────┐ │
│  │                                                                    │ │
│  │  Push → Lint → Test → Build → Scan → Sign → 🐳 ARTIFACT         │ │
│  │                                                                    │ │
│  │  GOAL: "Is this code good?"                                       │ │
│  │  OUTPUT: Docker image + SBOM + signature (tested, scanned)        │ │
│  │  OWNER: Developer (writes code, CI validates it)                  │ │
│  │  SPEED: < 10 minutes (fast feedback on every commit)              │ │
│  └────────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                               │                                        │
│                    🐳 ARTIFACT (immutable)                             │
│                               │                                        │
│  ┌────────────────────────────▼───────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │                    CD (Continuous Delivery)                        │ │
│  │                                                                    │ │
│  │  Artifact → Deploy Staging → Verify → Approve → Deploy Production │ │
│  │                                                                    │ │
│  │  GOAL: "Is this code in production?"                               │ │
│  │  OUTPUT: Running application serving users                         │ │
│  │  OWNER: Platform team (manages deployment pipeline)                │ │
│  │  SPEED: Minutes to hours (depends on approval gates)               │ │
│  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  💡 "CI builds it. CD ships it." The artifact is the contract.        │
│  CI guarantees the artifact is good. CD guarantees it reaches users.  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🔧 CI Responsibilities
  • Runs on every push. Fast feedback (< 10 min).
  • Linting, testing, building, scanning
  • Produces: Docker image + SBOM + signature
  • Fails if: code doesn't compile, tests fail, vulnerabilities found
  • Owner: Developer. "My code passes CI."
🚀 CD Responsibilities
  • Runs after CI passes. Deployment pipeline.
  • Deploy to staging → verify → approve → production
  • Produces: Running application in target environment
  • Fails if: deployment fails, health checks fail, metrics degrade
  • Owner: Platform. "The platform deployed my code."

Environment Promotion — How Artifacts Flow Through Environments

The same artifact moves through environments, but each environment has DIFFERENT configuration. This is the "promotion" pattern: the artifact is promoted, configuration is environment-specific. Understanding this separation is the key to designing CD pipelines that don't accidentally promote staging database credentials to production:

📊 ENVIRONMENT PROMOTION — Same Artifact, Different Config

│              🔄 ENVIRONMENT PROMOTION — anihpj Flow                     │

│       ├──────────────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┐     │

│  Auto-deploy         Auto-deploy        Auto-deploy       MANUAL    │

│  CONFIG SOURCES (environment-specific, NOT in the artifact):          │
│  • K8s Secrets (External Secrets Operator → AWS/GCP)                 │

14.3 Continuous Delivery vs Continuous Deployment — The Approval Gate

The difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment is one manual approval gate. Both automate the pipeline up to production. Delivery keeps a human in the loop. Deployment removes the human entirely. The choice depends on your risk tolerance and business requirements:

📋 Continuous Delivery (Manual Gate)
  • CI → Auto-deploy to staging → Verify → MANUAL APPROVAL → Deploy to production
  • Human decides WHEN to release. Business timing matters (after marketing launch, during low-traffic window).
  • Used by anihpj: staging is auto-deployed, but production requires platform team approval.
  • Best for: Business-critical apps, regulated industries, B2B products where customers need notice.
⚡ Continuous Deployment (Fully Automated)
  • CI → Auto-deploy to staging → Verify → Auto-deploy to production (no human)
  • Every merged PR reaches production automatically within minutes.
  • Requires: exceptional test coverage, canary deployments, automated rollback, feature flags.
  • Best for: SaaS products, consumer apps, teams with high DevOps maturity (ELITE DORA performers).
💡 anihpj's Choice: Continuous Delivery (Manual Approval)

anihpj is a B2B job posting platform. Customers expect stability and advance notice of changes. Continuous Delivery with a manual approval gate gives the platform team control over WHEN changes reach users. Staging auto-deploys for fast internal feedback. Production deploys require a Slack command: /anihpj promote jobpost-api to production. This is the CNPA-recommended pattern for business-critical platforms: automate everything EXCEPT the final business decision to release.

Deployment Pipeline Stages — What Actually Happens During a Deploy

A deploy is not one action — it's a PIPELINE of stages. Understanding each stage helps you diagnose WHERE a deployment failed and design better pipelines. Here's what happens when anihpj promotes a release to production:

1
Pre-Deploy Checks

Are all required approvals granted? Is the target environment healthy? Are there active incidents? If any check fails → deploy is BLOCKED before anything changes.

2
Config Injection

Environment-specific config is injected into the artifact: K8s Secrets, ConfigMaps, feature flags. The artifact itself is unchanged — config is layered ON TOP at deploy time.

3
Rollout

New pods are created. Old pods are terminated (rolling) or kept (blue/green). Traffic is shifted according to the strategy. K8s readiness probes control when pods receive traffic.

4
Health Verification

Post-deploy checks: Are pods Ready? Are health checks passing? Is the application responding? If any check fails within the verification window → auto-rollback.

5
Metrics Validation

Compare error rate, latency, and throughput 5 minutes BEFORE vs 5 minutes AFTER deploy. If metrics degraded beyond threshold → auto-rollback (Argo Rollouts).

6
Cleanup

Old pods fully terminated. Old ReplicaSets scaled to 0 (kept for rollback). Deployment marked "Successful." Notification sent to #platform-deploys.

📖 What Happens at EACH Failure Point

Stage 1 fails: Nothing was changed. Safe. Fix the approval/permission and retry. Stage 3 fails: K8s automatically stops the rollout (maxUnavailable). Some pods are new, some old. Mixed state. Stage 4 fails: Auto-rollback triggers. New pods are terminated, old pods restored. Brief mixed state. Stage 5 fails: Degraded metrics detected AFTER rollout. Argo Rollouts auto-rolls back. Users experienced degradation for the verification window. This is why verification windows should be SHORT (5-10 minutes).

Deployment Windows & Change Freezes — When NOT to Deploy

Knowing WHEN to deploy is as important as knowing HOW. Deployment windows define allowed times for production changes. Change freezes block ALL deployments during critical periods. These aren't technical limitations — they're business policies enforced by the CD pipeline:

🪟
Deployment Windows

Allowed: Monday-Thursday, 9am-5pm (business hours). Why: Full team available if something goes wrong. No 3am solo debugging. The CD tool can enforce: "Deploy button disabled outside window."

🔒
Change Freezes

Blocked: Black Friday week, Christmas holidays, fiscal year-end. Why: Business can't afford ANY disruption during critical periods. Emergency fixes require VP approval. CD tool enforces automatically.

🚑
Emergency Deploys

Always allowed, even during freezes. Requires: (1) P1 incident declared. (2) Manager approval. (3) Full post-deploy monitoring. "Break glass" procedure. Audited after the fact.

📊
Metrics-Based Gating

Don't deploy if: (1) Active P1/P2 incidents. (2) Error budget > 80% burned. (3) System is already degraded. CD tool checks metrics BEFORE allowing deploy — automated gatekeeping.

14.4 Deployment Strategies — How Code Reaches Users

A deployment strategy determines HOW a new version replaces the old version while users are actively using the application. Each strategy trades off speed, safety, resource usage, and complexity differently. Choosing the right strategy for each deployment scenario is a core CNPA design skill:

Strategy 1: Rolling Update — The K8s Default

Kubernetes replaces pods one at a time. Old pods are terminated only AFTER new pods are ready. Users experience zero downtime. Simple, built-in, no extra tooling needed. The tradeoff: for a brief period, both old and new versions run simultaneously — if the new version has a bug, some users hit it while others don't:

📊 ROLLING UPDATE — Gradual Pod Replacement
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    🔄 ROLLING UPDATE (K8s Default)                      │
│                                                                       │
│  BEFORE:    ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐    All v1 (3 replicas)              │
│             │ v1 │ │ v1 │ │ v1 │                                     │
│             └────┘ └────┘ └────┘                                     │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 1:    ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐    New v2 pod created               │
│             │ v1 │ │ v1 │ │ v2 │    Traffic: 2/3 v1, 1/3 v2          │
│             └────┘ └────┘ └────┘                                     │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 2:    ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐    Second v2 pod created            │
│             │ v1 │ │ v2 │ │ v2 │    Traffic: 1/3 v1, 2/3 v2          │
│             └────┘ └────┘ └────┘                                     │
│                                                                       │
│  AFTER:     ┌────┐ ┌────┐ ┌────┐    All v2 (3 replicas)              │
│             │ v2 │ │ v2 │ │ v2 │                                     │
│             └────┘ └────┘ └────┘                                     │
│                                                                       │
│  ✅ Zero downtime    ✅ Simple, built-in    ✅ No extra resources     │
│  ⚠️  Mixed versions briefly    ⚠️  Rollback = another rolling update │
│  anihpj: Used for PATCH releases (v2.4.0→v2.4.1). Low risk.          │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Strategy 2: Blue/Green — Instant Switch, Instant Rollback

Deploy the new version COMPLETELY alongside the old version. When ready, switch ALL traffic at once. If something goes wrong — switch back instantly. The tradeoff: double the resources (both versions run simultaneously):

📊 BLUE/GREEN — Parallel Environments
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    🔵🟢 BLUE/GREEN DEPLOYMENT                           │
│                                                                       │
│  BEFORE:                          AFTER SWITCH:                       │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐           │
│  │   🔵 BLUE (v1)       │        │   🔵 BLUE (v1)       │           │
│  │   ┌────┐ ┌────┐     │        │   ┌────┐ ┌────┐     │           │
│  │   │ v1 │ │ v1 │     │        │   │ v1 │ │ v1 │     │           │
│  │   └────┘ └────┘     │        │   └────┘ └────┘     │           │
│  │   ◀── 100% traffic  │        │   (standby, no traffic)           │
│  └──────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘           │
│  ┌──────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────┐           │
│  │   🟢 GREEN (v2)      │        │   🟢 GREEN (v2)      │           │
│  │   ┌────┐ ┌────┐     │        │   ┌────┐ ┌────┐     │           │
│  │   │ v2 │ │ v2 │     │        │   │ v2 │ │ v2 │     │           │
│  │   └────┘ └────┘     │        │   └────┘ └────┘     │           │
│  │   (standby, no traffic)       │   ◀── 100% traffic  │           │
│  └──────────────────────┘        └──────────────────────┘           │
│                                                                       │
│  ✅ Instant switch    ✅ Instant rollback (switch back to Blue)      │
│  ⚠️  2× resources during deploy    ⚠️  Database migrations tricky   │
│  anihpj: Used for MAJOR releases (v2.0→v3.0). Full validation first.│
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Strategy 3: Canary — Gradual Traffic Shift

Send a SMALL percentage of traffic to the new version. Monitor metrics. If healthy, increase gradually. If metrics degrade, auto-rollback. This is the safest strategy — problems affect only a fraction of users:

📊 CANARY DEPLOYMENT — Gradual Traffic Shift
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    🐤 CANARY DEPLOYMENT                                 │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 1: 5% canary          STEP 2: 25% canary                       │
│  ┌──────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐                    │
│  │  v1: 95% ████████│       │  v1: 75% ██████  │                    │
│  │  v2:  5% ▏       │       │  v2: 25% ██      │                    │
│  └──────────────────┘       └──────────────────┘                    │
│  Monitor: error rate,        Monitor: still healthy?                 │
│  latency, CPU for 10 min     ✅ → continue                           │
│                                                                       │
│  STEP 3: 50% canary         STEP 4: 100% (complete)                  │
│  ┌──────────────────┐       ┌──────────────────┐                    │
│  │  v1: 50% ████    │       │  v2: 100%████████│                    │
│  │  v2: 50% ████    │       │                  │                    │
│  └──────────────────┘       └──────────────────┘                    │
│  Monitor again              Deployment complete ✅                   │
│                                                                       │
│  AT ANY STEP: If error_rate > baseline → AUTO-ROLLBACK to v1.        │
│  ✅ Safest strategy    ✅ Gradual validation    ✅ Auto-rollback     │
│  ⚠️  Complex setup (Istio/Argo Rollouts needed)                     │
│  anihpj: Used for RISKY changes (DB schema change, new dependency).  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Strategy 4: A/B Testing — User-Specific Routing

Unlike canary (random % of traffic), A/B testing routes SPECIFIC users to the new version based on headers, cookies, or user IDs. Used for testing features with target audiences — not for gradual rollout:

How Traffic Routing Works — The Engine Behind Deployments

All deployment strategies (except rolling update) require a TRAFFIC ROUTING layer that controls which requests go to which version. Understanding this layer explains WHY some strategies are more complex than others:

📊 TRAFFIC ROUTING — How Requests Reach the Right Version
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🚦 TRAFFIC ROUTING LAYER                                  │
│                                                                       │
│  USERS ──▶ ┌──────────────┐                                          │
│            │  TRAFFIC      │  Routes requests to v1 or v2 based on:   │
│            │  ROUTING      │  • Weight: 90% v1, 10% v2 (canary)      │
│            │  LAYER        │  • Header: X-User-Type: beta → v2        │
│            │               │  • Cookie: canary=true → v2              │
│            └───┬───────┬───┘                                          │
│                │       │                                               │
│        90%     ▼       ▼     10%                                      │
│            ┌──────┐ ┌──────┐                                          │
│            │  v1  │ │  v2  │   (canary: 10% to v2)                   │
│            │ 3 pods│ │ 1 pod│                                          │
│            └──────┘ └──────┘                                          │
│                                                                       │
│  IMPLEMENTATIONS:                                                     │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  K8s Service (basic):                                            │ │
│  │  • Round-robin across ALL Ready pods. No weight control.        │ │
│  │  • Rolling update: new pods join Service when Ready.            │ │
│  │  • Cannot do canary or blue/green without extra tooling.       │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  Istio/Envoy (service mesh):                                     │ │
│  │  • VirtualService: route 90% to v1 subset, 10% to v2 subset.   │ │
│  │  • Header-based routing: X-User-Type:beta → v2.                 │ │
│  │  • Required for: canary, A/B testing, traffic mirroring.        │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  Argo Rollouts (without service mesh):                           │ │
│  │  • Manipulates K8s Service by scaling pods:                     │ │
│  │    v1 has 9 pods, v2 has 1 pod → ~10% to v2.                   │ │
│  │  • Simpler than Istio but coarser control (pod count, not %)    │ │
│  │  • Works with standard K8s Services. No mesh required.          │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  CNPA INSIGHT: Rolling update needs NO traffic routing layer.        │
│  Blue/Green needs a Service switch. Canary needs weighted routing.   │
│  A/B Testing needs header/cookie routing. Choose the simplest        │
│  routing layer your strategy requires.                                │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Argo Rollouts in Practice — Canary Deployment YAML

Argo Rollouts extends the K8s Deployment with canary and blue/green strategies. Instead of a standard Deployment, you define a Rollout resource that specifies the strategy AND the analysis to perform at each step:

☸️ YAMLArgo Rollouts — Canary with Automated Analysis
# ─── ROLLOUT: Replaces K8s Deployment ───
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Rollout
metadata:
  name: anihpj-api
spec:
  replicas: 5
  strategy:
    canary:
      steps:
      - setWeight: 5     # Step 1: 5% canary
      - pause: {duration: 10m}  # Wait 10 min, monitor metrics
      - setWeight: 25    # Step 2: 25% canary
      - pause: {duration: 10m}
      - setWeight: 50    # Step 3: 50% canary
      - pause: {duration: 10m}
      - setWeight: 100   # Step 4: 100% (complete)
      # AT ANY STEP: AnalysisTemplate can abort the rollout
  template:
    # ... same pod spec as a Deployment

---
# ─── ANALYSIS TEMPLATE: Monitors metrics during canary ───
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: AnalysisTemplate
metadata:
  name: canary-analysis
spec:
  metrics:
  - name: error-rate
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: |
          rate(http_requests_total{status=~"5..",app="anihpj-api"}[5m])
          / rate(http_requests_total{app="anihpj-api"}[5m])
    successCondition: result < 0.05  # Error rate must be < 5%
    failureLimit: 2                   # Fail if condition breached twice
  - name: p95-latency
    provider:
      prometheus:
        address: http://prometheus.monitoring:9090
        query: |
          histogram_quantile(0.95,
            rate(http_request_duration_seconds_bucket{app="anihpj-api"}[5m]))
    successCondition: result < 0.5   # p95 must be < 500ms
    failureLimit: 2
# RESULT: Each canary step runs these analyses. If error_rate > 5%
# or p95 > 500ms → canary ABORTED → weight set to 0%. Auto-recovery.
StrategyTraffic ControlRollback SpeedResource CostComplexityanihpj Use Case
RollingPod-by-podSlow (another rolling update)No extraLowPatch releases (v2.4.0→v2.4.1)
Blue/GreenAll-at-once switchInstant (switch back)2× during deployMediumMajor releases (v2.0→v3.0)
CanaryGradual % shiftInstant (set % to 0)Small extraHighRisky changes (DB migration)
A/B TestingUser/header-basedInstant (change rule)Small extraHighFeature experiments (new UI)
📖 The CNPA Strategy Selection Rule

Choose the LEAST complex strategy that meets your safety requirements: (1) If the change is low-risk (patch, config change) → Rolling update. K8s does it for free. (2) If instant rollback is critical → Blue/Green. Pay the resource cost for safety. (3) If you need gradual validation with real users → Canary. Invest in the tooling (Argo Rollouts + Istio). (4) If you're testing a feature with a specific audience → A/B Testing. The CNPA exam tests your ability to MATCH the strategy to the scenario — not to use canary for everything.

Deployment Strategies with Real Numbers — What Actually Happens

The diagrams show the concept. Here's what actually happens with concrete numbers — how many pods, how much traffic, how long each step takes. These are the details the CNPA exam tests:

AspectRolling (5 replicas)Blue/GreenCanary (5 replicas)
Resources during deploy5→6 pods max (1 extra)10 pods (5 v1 + 5 v2)6 pods (5 v1 + 1 v2 at 10%)
Deploy duration~2 min (5 × 30s per pod)~30s (switch traffic)30+ min (gradual steps)
Users on new versionSome immediately, all within 2 minAll at once (after switch)5%→25%→50%→100% over time
Rollback time~2 min (reverse rolling update)Seconds (switch back)Seconds (set weight=0)
Users affected if bugA fraction (gradually all)ALL (after switch — fast rollback mitigates)Only canary % (5%→25%)
DB migration compatible⚠️ Risky (mixed versions)✅ Yes (one version at a time)✅ Yes (old version still serves)
K8s native✅ Built-in (Deployment)❌ Needs Service switch❌ Needs Argo Rollouts
anihpj uses forPatch releasesMajor releasesDB migrations, risky changes
💡 The "Fix Forward vs Rollback" Decision

When a deployment fails, you have two choices: (1) Rollback — revert to the previous version. Fast (seconds to minutes). Safe (known-good state). But the bad code is still in the repo. (2) Fix Forward — deploy a NEW version that fixes the bug. Keeps moving forward. But takes longer (new CI build + deploy). The CNPA rule: if the bug is user-impacting → ROLLBACK first (restore service). Then fix forward at your leisure. If the bug is cosmetic/non-impacting → fix forward. The decision is about USER IMPACT, not engineering convenience.

Database Migrations and Deployment — The Hardest Problem in CD

Database schema changes are the #1 source of deployment failures. Unlike application code (which can run multiple versions simultaneously), a database has ONE schema. The solution is the Expand-Contract pattern: make changes backward-compatible so both old AND new application code can work with the database during the transition:

📊 EXPAND-CONTRACT — Safe Database Migrations
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🗄️  EXPAND-CONTRACT — Database Migration Pattern           │
│                                                                       │
│  PHASE 1: EXPAND (add, don't remove)                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Add new column (nullable, with default):                     │ │
│  │    ALTER TABLE jobpost_job ADD COLUMN department VARCHAR(100);  │ │
│  │  • v1 code IGNORES the column. v2 code USES it.                │ │
│  │  • Both v1 and v2 can run simultaneously.                      │ │
│  │  • Deploy v2 via Rolling update. No downtime.                  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  PHASE 2: MIGRATE (backfill data, if needed)                          │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Run background migration to populate new column for old rows │ │
│  │  • Both versions still work. No rush.                           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  PHASE 3: CONTRACT (remove old, after all v1 gone)                    │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • ONLY after ALL v1 pods are gone:                             │ │
│  │    ALTER TABLE jobpost_job DROP COLUMN old_field;               │ │
│  │  • Remove old column. Clean up.                                 │ │
│  │  • v2 (only version) now owns the schema.                       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  RULE: NEVER rename a column. ALWAYS add new → migrate → drop old.   │
│  RULE: NEVER make a column NOT NULL without a default (breaks v1).   │
│  RULE: EXPAND in one deploy. CONTRACT in a SEPARATE deploy (later).  │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

Rollback Strategies — Beyond "Just Switch Back"

A rollback isn't always as simple as reverting to the previous version. Database migrations, API changes, and configuration updates all complicate rollback. Understanding what CAN and CAN'T be rolled back is critical deployment design:

✅
Easy to Roll Back
  • Application code: Revert to previous image. K8s handles the rolling update.
  • Config changes: Revert ConfigMap/Secret to previous version.
  • Feature flags: Disable the flag. Instant. No redeploy needed.
  • Blue/Green: Switch traffic back to Blue. Seconds.
⚠️
Hard to Roll Back
  • DB schema changes: DROP COLUMN destroys data. ADD COLUMN is safe. Plan migrations to be backward-compatible.
  • API changes: Removing a field that clients depend on. Use API versioning (/v1/, /v2/) — deprecate before removing.
  • Data migrations: Transforming data irreversibly. Always make migrations reversible or accept data loss as a calculated risk.

Deployment Strategy Decision Tree — Which Strategy When?

When faced with a deployment decision, follow this decision tree. It formalizes the intuition of "match strategy to risk" into a repeatable process:

📊 DEPLOYMENT STRATEGY DECISION TREE
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│              🌳 DEPLOYMENT STRATEGY DECISION TREE                      │
│                                                                       │
│  START: "I need to deploy a change."                                  │
│       │                                                               │
│  ┌────▼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Q1: Does the change have USER-VISIBLE impact?                  │ │
│  │  ├── NO → Patch/config/internal change → ROLLING UPDATE         │ │
│  │  └── YES → Continue to Q2                                       │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│       │                                                               │
│  ┌────▼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Q2: Does the change affect the DATABASE SCHEMA?                │ │
│  │  ├── YES → HIGH RISK → CANARY deployment (5%→25%→100%)         │ │
│  │  │         + Expand-Contract migration pattern                  │ │
│  │  └── NO → Continue to Q3                                        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│       │                                                               │
│  ┌────▼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Q3: Is INSTANT ROLLBACK required (SLA < 1 min recovery)?       │ │
│  │  ├── YES → BLUE/GREEN (double resources, instant switch-back)   │ │
│  │  └── NO → Continue to Q4                                        │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│       │                                                               │
│  ┌────▼────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Q4: Is this a NEW FEATURE that needs gradual user validation?  │ │
│  │  ├── YES → FEATURE FLAG + ROLLING UPDATE                        │ │
│  │  │         (deploy hidden, enable gradually via flag)            │ │
│  │  └── NO → ROLLING UPDATE (default, simplest, zero extra cost)   │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  RULE: Start from the SIMPLEST strategy. Only escalate complexity     │
│  when the RISK justifies it. Don't use canary for a typo fix.         │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

14.5 Feature Flags — Decoupling Deploy from Release

A feature flag separates two concepts that traditional deployment conflates: deploying code (making it available on servers) and releasing a feature (making it visible to users). With feature flags, you can deploy code that's HIDDEN — then enable it gradually, for specific users, or on a schedule. If something goes wrong, you disable the FLAG (instant), not roll back the CODE (slow):

📊 FEATURE FLAGS — Deploy vs Release
┌──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│                    🏁 FEATURE FLAGS — DEPLOY ≠ RELEASE                  │
│                                                                       │
│  WITHOUT FEATURE FLAGS:                                               │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Deploy v2 = Release dark mode to ALL users                      │ │
│  │  Problem: Users see the feature IMMEDIATELY. No gradual rollout. │ │
│  │  Rollback = redeploy v1 (slow).                                  │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  WITH FEATURE FLAGS:                                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  Deploy v2 (dark mode code present but HIDDEN behind flag)      │ │
│  │       │                                                          │ │
│  │       ▼                                                          │ │
│  │  Enable for 10% of users → monitor → 50% → 100%                 │ │
│  │       │                                                          │ │
│  │       ▼ (if issues detected)                                     │ │
│  │  DISABLE flag (instant — no redeploy needed)                     │ │
│  │  All users back to v1 experience. Code stays deployed.           │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
│                                                                       │
│  anihpj EXAMPLE: "Dark Mode" feature                                  │
│  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐ │
│  │  • Deploy: v2.5.0 includes dark mode code (hidden)              │ │
│  │  • Release: Enable dark_mode flag for beta testers (5% users)   │ │
│  │  • Verify: No increase in error rate. Users like it.            │ │
│  │  • Expand: 25% → 50% → 100% over 1 week                        │ │
│  │  • Emergency: If 500 errors spike → DISABLE flag. Instant fix.  │ │
│  │                                                                  │ │
│  │  Tools: LaunchDarkly (managed), Unleash (self-hosted),          │ │
│  │  or custom ConfigMap: {dark_mode: {enabled: true, pct: 25}}    │ │
│  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘ │
└──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
🚀
Deploy = Technical

Code is on the servers. Containers are running. The binary/artifact is present. But users can't see the feature. This is a TECHNICAL operation — CI/CD handles it.

📢
Release = Business Decision

The feature is VISIBLE to users. Marketing announces it. Support is trained. This is a BUSINESS decision — product managers handle it. The flag controls it.

⚠️ Feature Flag Technical Debt

Feature flags are TEMPORARY. A flag that exists for 6+ months becomes technical debt: the code has two paths (flag ON and flag OFF), tests must cover both, and complexity grows. Every flag should have an OWNER and an EXPIRY DATE. When the feature is fully rolled out (100% for 2+ weeks), REMOVE the flag and the old code path. The CNPA exam expects you to understand that flags enable safe deployment but create maintenance burden if not cleaned up.

14.6 Deployment Automation Tools — The CD Toolchain

CI produces the artifact. CD needs tools to deploy it. The CNCF ecosystem provides several options, each with different philosophies and tradeoffs. The CNPA exam focuses on ArgoCD as the K8s-native GitOps standard:

ToolApproachBest ForStrengthsWeaknesses
ArgoCDGitOps (Pull-based)K8s-native CD. The CNPA standard.Declarative Git→Cluster sync. Rich Web UI. Auto-sync. Rollback = git revert. Multi-cluster.K8s only. Learning curve for non-K8s teams.
FluxGitOps (Pull-based)GitOps purists. Lighter weight.K8s-native. Helm controller. Image automation. Smaller footprint than ArgoCD.Less mature UI. Smaller community.
SpinnakerPipeline-based (Push)Multi-cloud, complex deployment pipelinesAdvanced strategies (canary, red/black). Multi-cloud (AWS, GCP, K8s).Complex setup. Heavy. Netflix-maintained (less active).
HarnessAI-powered (Push)Enterprise CD with continuous verificationAI-driven verification (compares metrics before/after deploy). Built-in rollback.Commercial (not open source). Vendor lock-in.
💡 Why ArgoCD is the CNPA Standard

The CNPA exam favors ArgoCD because: (1) It's K8s-native (everything is a CRD). (2) It's GitOps (pull-based — the cluster converges to Git state). (3) It's declarative (Application CRD defines WHAT, not HOW). (4) It's the most widely adopted GitOps tool in the CNCF ecosystem. (5) Rollback = git revert (auditable, versioned, peer-reviewed). For the exam: when asked about CD tools for K8s, ArgoCD is the default answer unless the scenario specifically requires multi-cloud (Spinnaker) or enterprise AI verification (Harness).

CD Anti-Patterns — What NOT to Do in Continuous Delivery

The CNPA exam tests your ability to identify broken CD implementations. Here are the most common anti-patterns seen in real platforms — and what to do instead:

🚫
❌ Rebuilding Between Environments

"Build for staging, rebuild for production." Breaks the CD guarantee. Staging tested image A; production runs image B. Different pip versions, different timestamps, different bugs. Fix: build ONCE, tag with git SHA, promote the SAME image.

🚫
❌ Deploying Without Health Checks

Pods are "Running" but returning 500 errors. Without readiness probes, K8s sends traffic anyway. Without post-deploy verification, nobody notices for hours. Fix: readiness probe + smoke tests + metrics comparison after every deploy.

🚫
❌ No Rollback Plan

"We'll figure it out if something goes wrong." Under pressure, figuring it out means 30 minutes of frantic kubectl commands. Fix: ArgoCD one-click rollback. Blue/Green for instant switch-back. Document the rollback process BEFORE you need it.

🚫
❌ Manual Deployment Steps

"After the automated deploy, manually run these 3 SQL migration scripts and update the CDN cache." These steps WILL be forgotten. Fix: automate EVERY step. If it can't be automated, it's a deployment risk that needs engineering investment.

🚫
❌ Environment Drift

"Staging has 2 replicas, production has 5. Staging uses Redis 6, production uses Redis 7." Configurations diverge over time. Bugs appear only in production. Fix: GitOps — environments defined as code in Git. Drift detected and corrected automatically.

🚫
❌ Deploying on Fridays

"Let's deploy at 5pm Friday and go home." If something breaks, nobody is available until Monday. Fix: deploy during business hours when the full team is available. If you're afraid to deploy during the day, fix the deployment process — don't hide it at night.

14.7 Practice Lab — 10 CNPA Exam-Style Questions

CD Q1 of 10
What is the boundary between CI and CD?
A) CI is for testing; CD is for monitoring
B) There is no boundary — they are the same thing
C) CI ends with a tested ARTIFACT (Docker image + SBOM + signature). CD begins with that artifact and delivers it to users. CI answers "is this code good?" CD answers "is this code in production?" The artifact is the handoff.
D) CI handles infrastructure; CD handles applications
✅ C — CI → artifact → CD. The artifact is the boundary.

CI (Continuous Integration): Push → Lint → Test → Build → Scan → Sign → Artifact. CD (Continuous Delivery): Artifact → Deploy → Verify → Approve → Production. The artifact (Docker image) is IMMUTABLE — it flows through environments unchanged. CI guarantees the artifact is tested. CD guarantees the artifact reaches users. "CI builds it. CD ships it."

CD Q2 of 10
What is the difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
A) Delivery uses containers; Deployment uses VMs
B) ONE manual approval gate. Delivery: auto to staging → MANUAL approval → production. Deployment: auto ALL THE WAY to production (no human). Both automate the pipeline; only Deployment removes the human from the final decision.
C) Delivery is slower; Deployment is faster
D) They are exactly the same — the terms are interchangeable
✅ B — One manual approval gate is the difference

Continuous Delivery: the pipeline is fully automated up to production, but a HUMAN approves the final deploy. Continuous Deployment: the pipeline is fully automated INCLUDING production — no human gate. Delivery is safer for business-critical apps (anihpj uses this). Deployment requires exceptional test coverage, canary deployments, and automated rollback. Both are "CD" — the distinction is whether the final business decision is manual or automated.

CD Q3 of 10
A K8s Deployment with 5 replicas is updated from v1 to v2 using the default strategy. How many pods run v1 and v2 during the update?
A) Rolling update: pods are replaced one at a time. During the update, you'll have a MIX of v1 and v2 pods. With maxSurge=1 and maxUnavailable=0 (default), at most 6 pods exist (5 old + 1 new), gradually transitioning to 5 v2 pods. Both versions serve traffic simultaneously for a brief period.
B) All 5 switch simultaneously — there's no mixed state
C) v1 pods are deleted first, then v2 pods are created — brief downtime
D) The number depends on the cluster size, not the strategy
✅ A — Rolling update: mixed v1/v2 during transition. No downtime.

K8s rolling update default: maxSurge=25% (round up), maxUnavailable=25% (round down). With 5 replicas: maxSurge=1 (up to 6 pods during update), maxUnavailable=1 (up to 1 pod can be unavailable). The controller: (1) Creates 1 new v2 pod (total: 5v1 + 1v2 = 6). (2) When v2 is ready, terminates 1 v1 (total: 4v1 + 1v2 = 5). (3) Repeats until all 5 are v2. During the transition, BOTH versions serve traffic. This is why rolling updates are safe for stateless apps but risky for API changes — clients may hit either version.

CD Q4 of 10
When should anihpj use Blue/Green deployment instead of Rolling update?
A) Blue/Green is always better — use it for everything
B) For patch releases where risk is minimal
C) When you want to save on infrastructure costs
D) When INSTANT rollback is critical. Blue/Green runs both versions simultaneously. If v2 has a problem, switch traffic back to v1 in SECONDS. Rolling update rollback requires another rolling update (minutes). Blue/Green costs 2× resources during deploy but gives you an instant undo button.
✅ D — When instant rollback is critical. Pay 2× resources for safety.

Blue/Green tradeoff: PRO = instant rollback (switch traffic back to Blue). CON = double resources during deployment (both Blue and Green run). Use Blue/Green when: (1) The deployment is high-risk (major version change). (2) Rollback speed matters (SLAs require < 1 minute recovery). (3) You can afford double resources temporarily. Don't use Blue/Green for routine patches — Rolling update is sufficient and doesn't require extra resources.

CD Q5 of 10
In a canary deployment, 10% of traffic goes to v2. Error rate spikes. What should Argo Rollouts do?
A) Continue the canary — the error might be a false positive
B) AUTO-ROLLBACK: Argo Rollouts AnalysisTemplate detects the error rate spike → sets canary weight back to 0% → all traffic returns to v1. The canary is aborted. This is the ENTIRE point of canary — detect problems with minimal user impact and auto-recover.
C) Increase canary to 50% to get more data
D) Page the on-call engineer and wait for manual intervention
✅ B — Auto-rollback: canary weight → 0%. Problem detected, auto-recovered.

Argo Rollouts with AnalysisTemplate: (1) Deploy canary at 10%. (2) Analysis runs: query Prometheus for error_rate. (3) If error_rate > baseline → analysis FAILS. (4) Argo Rollouts automatically sets canary weight to 0% — all traffic back to stable v1. (5) The canary is marked "Degraded." No human intervention needed. This is why canary requires tooling (Argo Rollouts + metrics) — the automation makes it safe. Without auto-rollback, canary is just "hope nothing goes wrong while I watch dashboards."

CD Q6 of 10
How do feature flags enable decoupling deploy from release?
A) Deploy the code HIDDEN behind a flag. Release by ENABLING the flag for users. Deploy is technical (code on servers). Release is business (feature visible). If the feature breaks, DISABLE the flag (instant), don't roll back the deployment (slow).
B) Feature flags make deployments faster by skipping tests
C) Feature flags automatically test new features in production
D) Feature flags replace the need for staging environments
✅ A — Deploy hidden code. Release by enabling flag. Kill switch = disable flag.

Feature flags separate deploy (technical) from release (business). Without flags: deploy v2 → ALL users see new feature immediately. Rollback = redeploy v1 (slow). With flags: deploy v2 (feature hidden) → enable flag for 5% → verify → 100%. If issue: disable flag (instant — no redeploy). The feature flag is a KILL SWITCH. This is the CNPA pattern for safe feature rollout: always deploy behind a flag, enable gradually, clean up the flag after full rollout.

CD Q7 of 10
anihpj is deploying a database schema migration. Which deployment strategy should they use?
A) Rolling update — it's the default and simplest
B) A/B Testing — route specific users to test the migration
C) Canary deployment. DB migrations are HIGH RISK — they can't be rolled back easily. Canary sends a small % of traffic to the new version. If queries fail or performance degrades, auto-rollback before most users are affected. Rolling update is dangerous for DB migrations because ALL pods eventually run the new code.
D) Feature flags — disable the database entirely during migration
✅ C — Canary: gradual traffic shift with auto-rollback for risky changes.

Database migrations are the riskiest deployments because: (1) They're hard to roll back (schema changes are not easily reversible). (2) They affect ALL users if something goes wrong. (3) Performance impact is hard to predict. Canary deployment mitigates this: 5% of traffic tests the new schema. If query performance degrades or errors spike → auto-rollback. Only 5% of users were affected. Rolling update would eventually run the migration for ALL users with no safety net. Blue/Green works but requires double the database resources.

CD Q8 of 10
Why does the CNPA exam favor ArgoCD over other CD tools?
A) ArgoCD is the only CD tool for Kubernetes
B) ArgoCD is the cheapest option
C) ArgoCD was created by the CNCF
D) ArgoCD is K8s-native (everything is a CRD), GitOps pull-based (cluster converges to Git), declarative (Application CRD), has the largest CNCF ecosystem adoption, and rollback = git revert (auditable, versioned). The CNPA tests GitOps as the standard CD pattern for K8s, and ArgoCD is the reference implementation.
✅ D — K8s-native CRDs + GitOps + largest ecosystem + auditable rollback.

ArgoCD is the CNPA standard for K8s CD because: (1) Application CRD — define your deployment declaratively. (2) Pull-based GitOps — ArgoCD pulls from Git, not CI pushing to cluster. (3) Auto-sync — cluster continuously converges to Git state. (4) Rollback = git revert — auditable, peer-reviewed, versioned. (5) Multi-cluster — one ArgoCD instance manages many clusters. (6) CNCF Graduated project — proven, stable, widely adopted. For the exam: when asked "how should we deploy to K8s?" → ArgoCD with GitOps.

CD Q9 of 10
Why is "Build Once, Deploy Many" the CD golden rule?
A) It reduces CI pipeline time by skipping rebuilds
B) The same artifact (Docker image) flows through staging→production UNCHANGED. If you rebuild between environments, you risk: different dependency versions, different timestamps, different build environment. Staging tested image X. Production must run the EXACT same image X — not a rebuild. Only CONFIG changes between environments.
C) It saves storage space in the container registry
D) It's a convention without technical benefit
✅ B — Same artifact everywhere. Only config changes per environment.

"Build Once, Deploy Many" is the CD guarantee: "What you tested IS what you deploy." The Docker image built in CI is tagged with the git SHA. That exact SHA-tagged image is deployed to staging (tested), then promoted to production (same image). Rebuilding between environments breaks this guarantee: pip install might resolve different versions, timestamps differ, the build environment might have different tools. The CNPA exam tests this: the artifact is IMMUTABLE. Environments differ only in CONFIG (env vars, feature flags, resource limits).

CD Q10 of 10
Design the complete deployment strategy for anihpj: patch releases, major releases, and risky DB changes.
A) Patch (v2.4.0→v2.4.1): Rolling update — low risk, no extra resources. Major (v2.0→v3.0): Blue/Green — instant rollback if v3 breaks. Risky (DB migration): Canary with Argo Rollouts — 5%→25%→100% with auto-rollback on metric degradation. Feature experiments: A/B Testing with feature flags. One size does NOT fit all.
B) Use Rolling update for everything — it's the simplest
C) Use Canary for everything — it's the safest
D) Use Blue/Green for everything — instant rollback always
✅ A — Match strategy to risk: Rolling for patches, Blue/Green for majors, Canary for risky.

The CNPA deployment strategy matrix: (1) Patch releases (bug fixes, config changes) → Rolling update. K8s does it natively. Low risk, zero extra cost. (2) Major releases (breaking changes, new architecture) → Blue/Green. Full validation of v2 before switching traffic. Instant rollback if needed. (3) Risky changes (DB migration, new dependency, performance-sensitive) → Canary with Argo Rollouts. Gradual traffic shift with automated metric analysis. Auto-rollback on degradation. (4) Feature experiments (new UI, A/B test) → Feature flags + A/B Testing. Deploy hidden, enable for specific users. The key: match the strategy to the RISK — don't use one strategy for everything.

Chapter 15: GitOps Basics & Workflows

GitOps is the operating model for cloud native delivery — Git is the single source of truth, and automated agents reconcile the cluster to match Git. Everything you built in Chapters 12-14 (CI pipelines, delivery strategies, deployment automation) converges here into one unified workflow: merge to Git → auto-sync to cluster. This chapter covers the four Weaveworks principles, Push vs Pull models, ArgoCD architecture, the Application CRD, sync strategies, and the repository structure that powers anihpj/jobpost across dev, staging, and production.

15.1 What is GitOps? — Git is the Source of Truth

GitOps is an operating model for cloud native applications that uses Git repositories as the single source of truth for declarative infrastructure and application configuration. An automated process ensures that the running cluster state matches the desired state defined in Git. If there's a drift — the agent corrects it automatically. If you need to change the application — you change Git, not the cluster:

🔍 The Problem GitOps Solves — Before and After

To truly understand WHY GitOps exists, you need to see the operational nightmare it replaces. Before GitOps, platform teams lived in a world of manual kubectl commands, snowflake clusters, and deployment anxiety. GitOps doesn't just automate — it fundamentally changes the relationship between developers, operators, and the cluster:

ProblemBefore GitOpsAfter GitOps
"What's running in production?"Nobody knows exactly. Someone ran kubectl apply 3 weeks ago. Another person scaled replicas manually during an incident. The cluster is a snowflake — unique and irreproducible.Git IS the answer. git log shows every change. ArgoCD ensures the cluster matches Git. The cluster is cattle — disposable and reproducible.
"Who changed the replicas from 3 to 10?"Slack archaeology. "I think Alice did it during the outage?" No audit trail. No accountability. Changes happen directly on the cluster with no record.git log -- apps/anihpj/overlays/prod/ shows the commit, author, timestamp, PR number, and reviewer. Complete audit trail in one command.
"How do we recover from a disaster?"Hope the Terraform state is current. Hope someone documented the manual steps. Rebuild from memory. Recovery takes hours or days. Some things are permanently lost.Point ArgoCD at a new cluster. All 45+ applications auto-sync within minutes. Recovery = redeploy from Git. No state lost. No tribal knowledge needed.
"Is staging the same as production?"Probably not. Someone patched production directly. Staging has different resource limits. "It worked in staging!" is a meaningless statement because environments have diverged.Same Git repo, same manifests, different Kustomize overlays. The ONLY difference is the overlay values (replicas, resources). What you test in staging IS what runs in production.
"How do we deploy?"Run the CI pipeline. Hope the KUBECONFIG secret is still valid. Hope nobody changed the cluster between the last deploy and now. Deployment is an event — with anxiety attached.Merge a PR. ArgoCD detects the change. Syncs automatically. Deployment is a state — the cluster continuously converges to Git. No ceremony. No credentials outside the cluster.
💡 The Mental Model Shift

Traditional ops thinks: "I TELL the cluster what to do" (imperative). GitOps thinks: "I DECLARE what the cluster SHOULD BE, and an agent makes it so" (declarative, reconciled). This shift from pushing commands to declaring state is the fundamental insight behind GitOps. Once you internalize this, every GitOps concept — pull model, self-heal, pruning, drift detection — becomes obvious.
